58045.e: The hypocentre is also called the earthquake focus. It is the point inside the Earth where the rupture begins.
58045.m: The hypocentre is also called the focus.

58046.q: Where do earthquakes with foci several hundred kilometres below the surface mainly occur?
a: In sinking plates at subduction zones
In the middle of stable continents
58046.e: Deep-focus earthquakes from around 300 km down occur almost only where a cold, brittle plate sinks into the mantle, for example beneath Japan or the Andes.
58046.m: Deep-focus earthquakes happen in sinking plates.

58047.q: Roughly down to what depth do the deepest known earthquakes occur?
58047.e: The deepest earthquakes happen in sinking lithospheric plates down to a depth of around 700 km. Below that the rock is too plastic for brittle fractures.
58047.m: Below about 700 kilometres there are no more earthquakes.

58048.q: Why do shallow earthquakes usually cause more damage than deep ones of the same magnitude?
a: The waves travel a shorter distance
Deep earthquakes produce no S waves
58048.e: The closer the focus is to the surface, the less the waves are weakened on their way. The shaking at the ground is therefore stronger.
58048.m: Shallow earthquakes are usually more destructive than deep ones.

58049.q: A focus is 30 km deep and the station is 40 km from the epicentre. What is the hypocentral distance?
58049.e: The focal depth and the epicentral distance form the two shorter sides of a right-angled triangle. The square root of 30² plus 40², that is of 2,500, gives 50 km.
58049.m: You calculate the hypocentral distance with Pythagoras' theorem.

58050.q: How do the rock particles move in a P wave?
a: Back and forth in the direction of travel
At right angles to the direction of travel
58050.e: P waves are longitudinal or compression waves. The rock is alternately squeezed and stretched, similar to sound.
58050.m: P waves are pressure waves like sound waves.

58051.q: Roughly what speed does a P wave have in the Earth's crust?
58051.e: In the crust, P waves travel at around 5 to 7 km/s. In the mantle they become even faster with increasing depth.
58051.m: P waves travel about six kilometres per second in the Earth's crust.

58052.q: What causes the P-wave shadow zone between about 103 and 142 degrees of epicentral distance?
a: Refraction at the liquid outer core
58052.e: At the core-mantle boundary, the P-wave speed drops sharply. The waves are refracted and do not reach this part of the surface directly.
58052.m: The Earth's core bends P waves and so creates a shadow zone.

58053.q: Which seismologist discovered the solid inner core in 1936 using P waves?
58053.e: The Dane Inge Lehmann interpreted weak P-wave signals in the shadow zone as reflections from an inner core. This showed that the Earth's core consists of two parts.
58053.m: Inge Lehmann discovered the inner core in 1936.

58054.q: What did Andrija Mohorovičić discover in 1909 from a jump in wave speed?
a: The boundary between crust and mantle
The boundary between mantle and core
58054.e: After an earthquake in Croatia, he noticed two groups of P waves. He concluded that the speed suddenly increases at a boundary deep down, the so-called Moho.
58054.m: The Moho separates the Earth's crust from the mantle.

58055.q: What are earthquake early warning systems, such as in Japan, based on?
a: They detect the fast P wave before the destructive waves
They measure gas leaks days before the earthquake
They calculate earthquakes from the phase of the moon
58055.e: The P wave is faster but does little damage. If it is detected near the focus, trains can be braked and people warned before the stronger waves arrive.
58055.m: Early warning systems use the head start of the P wave.

58056.q: What kind of wave is an S wave?
58056.e: In S waves, the particles move at right angles to the direction of travel. The rock is sheared, not squeezed.

58057.q: Roughly how fast is an S wave compared with a P wave in the same rock?
58057.e: In typical rock, the S-wave speed is around the P-wave speed divided by the square root of 3, so about 58 per cent.
58057.m: S waves are much slower than P waves.

58058.q: What was concluded from the fact that no direct S waves arrive beyond about 103 degrees?
a: The crust is thin under the oceans
58058.e: Direct S waves are missing on the opposite side of the Earth. This shows that they cannot pass through a layer with no shear strength: the liquid outer core.
58058.m: The S-wave shadow proves that the outer core is liquid.

58059.q: At what depth did Beno Gutenberg determine the boundary between the mantle and the core in 1914?
58059.e: From the travel times of earthquake waves, Gutenberg calculated a core boundary at a depth of around 2,900 km. Today it is called the Gutenberg discontinuity.
58059.m: The core-mantle boundary lies at a depth of about 2,900 kilometres.

58261.q: What are the channels formed by solution on bare limestone surfaces called, often known in Switzerland as Schratten?
58261.e: Rainwater dissolves limestone at the surface and forms sharp-edged channels and ridges. Fields of karren like this can be found, for example, on the Schrattenfluh in the Entlebuch.
58261.m: Karren or Schratten are solution channels on limestone rock.

58262.q: What do you call a place where a river in karst suddenly disappears underground?
58262.e: A ponor or swallow hole carries surface water into underground cavities. The water often comes out again far away at a karst spring.
58262.m: In a ponor, a river sinks into the karst underground.

58263.q: Where does the water that seeps underground at Lac de Joux come back to the surface?
a: At the source of the Orbe near Vallorbe
At the Rhine Falls near Schaffhausen
At the source of the Aare on the Grimsel
58263.e: The water of Lac de Joux and Lac Brenet seeps into the limestone of the Jura. It comes out again near Vallorbe as the source of the Orbe.
58263.m: The Orbe rises near Vallorbe from karst water from Lac de Joux.

58264.q: Why is karst groundwater particularly vulnerable to pollution?
a: It flows quickly and is hardly filtered
It naturally contains a lot of salt
It is always warm and encourages bacteria
It stands completely still in the rock
58264.e: In karst areas, water flows quickly through open cracks and caves to the spring. Pollutants are hardly held back or broken down on the way.
58264.m: In karst, pollutants reach spring water quickly and unfiltered.

a: A dry valley in the desert
58265.e: Dolines are rounded, bowl-shaped or funnel-shaped hollows in soluble rock. They form through solution or through the collapse of underground cavities.
58265.m: A doline is a funnel-shaped hollow in karst areas.

58266.q: Which two main types of doline are distinguished by how they formed?
58266.e: Solution dolines form when limestone is dissolved from above. Collapse dolines form when the roof of a cave falls in.
58266.m: Dolines form through solution from above or collapse from below.

58267.q: What are the water-filled collapse dolines on the Yucatán Peninsula in Mexico called?
58267.e: Cenotes are karst holes that reach down to the groundwater. For the Maya they were important sources of water and sacred places.
58267.m: Cenotes are water-filled collapse dolines in Yucatán.

58268.q: Why do dolines form mainly in limestone areas?
a: Limestone is dissolved by water containing carbonic acid
Limestone is worn away by the wind
58268.e: Rainwater takes up carbon dioxide and forms weak carbonic acid. This dissolves the limestone and creates cavities that appear as hollows or collapse.
58268.m: Water containing carbonic acid dissolves limestone and shapes dolines.

58269.q: Which language does the word doline come from?
58269.e: Doline comes from the Slovenian word “dolina”, which means valley. Many karst terms come from the Dinaric Karst.
58269.m: The word doline comes from Slovenian and means valley.

58270.q: What is a dripstone that hangs down from the ceiling of a cave called?
58270.e: Stalactites grow downwards from the ceiling. Stalagmites grow upwards from the floor, and when the two join, a column forms.
58270.m: Stalactites hang from the ceiling, stalagmites stand on the floor.

58271.q: Why is limestone deposited from dripping water in caves?
a: The water releases CO₂ into the cave air
The water freezes in the cave
The cave air contains a lot of salt
The water becomes more acidic in the cave
58271.e: Seepage water contains a lot of dissolved CO₂ from the soil. In the cave, CO₂ escapes, the balance shifts and calcium carbonate is deposited.
58271.m: When CO₂ escapes from dripping water, limestone is deposited as dripstone.

58272.q: What is the limestone that dripstones are made of called?
58272.e: Dripstones consist of calcium carbonate deposited from water. This deposit is called calcareous sinter or simply sinter.
58272.m: Dripstones are made of calcareous sinter.

58273.q: Roughly how long is the Hölloch cave system in the Muota valley (canton of Schwyz) (as of 2022)?
58273.e: As of 2022, the Hölloch is about 210 kilometres long. It is considered the second longest known cave system in Europe.
58273.m: The Hölloch in the Muota valley is over 200 kilometres long.

58274.q: What are thin, hollow dripstones that hang from the ceiling like drinking straws called?
58274.e: In soda straws, the drop runs down inside a thin tube of limestone and deposits limestone at the rim. Because of their shape they are also called macaroni.
58274.m: Soda straws are hollow, thin dripstones like drinking straws.

58275.q: How fast do dripstones typically grow?
a: Usually only fractions of a millimetre per year
58275.e: The growth rate depends on the amount of water, CO₂ and temperature. It is often less than one millimetre per year, which is why large dripstones are often thousands of years old.
58275.m: Dripstones grow very slowly and are often thousands of years old.

58276.q: Why are dripstones valuable for climate research?
a: Their layers store clues about past climates
They show the direction of the Earth’s magnetic field
58276.e: Dripstones grow in layers. Isotopes and trace elements in these layers allow conclusions about the temperature and rainfall of earlier times.
58276.m: Dripstones are climate archives covering many thousands of years.

58277.q: Which cave on Lake Thun is a well-known show cave with dripstones?
58277.e: The St Beatus Caves lie above Lake Thun near Sundlauenen. They are named after Saint Beatus and are open to visitors as a show cave.
58277.m: The St Beatus Caves on Lake Thun are a well-known Swiss dripstone cave.

58278.q: What shape is a barchan dune?
58278.e: A barchan is a crescent-shaped or half-moon-shaped dune. Its two tips are called horns.
58278.m: A barchan is a crescent-shaped dune.

58279.q: In which direction do the horns of a barchan point?
58279.e: At the low edges the sand moves faster than in the higher centre. That is why the horns race ahead and point in the direction the wind is blowing.
58279.m: The horns of a barchan point downwind.

58280.q: How do the windward and leeward sides of a barchan differ?
58280.e: On the gentle windward side, the wind drives the sand upwards. On the leeward side it slides down and forms a steep slip face.
58280.m: A barchan has a gentle windward side and a steep leeward side.

58281.q: Roughly how steep is the slip face on the leeward side of a dune?
58281.e: Dry sand slides down as soon as the slope is steeper than its natural angle of repose. This is around 30 to 35 degrees.
58281.m: The lee slope of a dune is as steep as the angle of repose of dry sand.

58282.q: Under which conditions do barchans most often form?
a: Wind from one direction and little sand
Changing winds and lots of sand
Wind from one direction and a great deal of sand
Almost no wind and damp sand
58282.e: Barchans form on firm ground with a limited supply of sand and a steady wind direction. With lots of sand, transverse dunes tend to form; with changing winds, star dunes.
58282.m: Barchans need a steady wind and little sand.

58283.q: Why do small barchans move faster than large ones?
a: They consist of less sand that has to be moved
They are heavier and roll faster
They are always sheltered from the wind
58283.e: A dune moves when sand is carried from the windward side to the leeward side. In small dunes, less sand has to be moved for this.
58283.m: The smaller a barchan is, the faster it moves.

58284.q: How do grains of sand mainly move when dunes form?
58284.e: Most grains of sand are briefly lifted by the wind and bounce over the ground in flat arcs. This saltation usually happens only a few tens of centimetres above the ground.
58284.m: In saltation, sand grains bounce over the ground in flat arcs.

58285.q: Which language does the word wadi come from?
58285.e: Wadi is the Arabic word for valley or riverbed. It is part of many place names in North Africa and Arabia.
58285.m: The word wadi comes from Arabic.

58286.q: What do you call the flow of a wadi that only happens after irregular heavy rain?
58286.e: Episodic streams carry water only occasionally and irregularly. Periodic rivers, on the other hand, carry water every year at a particular season.

58287.q: Why are many wadis larger than today’s rainfall can explain?
a: Some of them formed in wetter climate phases
They were dug out by people
They were blown out by the wind
58287.e: In wetter times in the past, parts of the Sahara were green and crossed by rivers. Many wadis are therefore relics of an earlier climate.
58287.m: Many wadis date from wetter climate phases in the past.

58288.q: Which desert valley in Jordan has been a UNESCO World Heritage Site since 2011?
58288.e: Wadi Rum in southern Jordan is known for its sandstone mountains and rock carvings. It was listed in 2011 as a mixed natural and cultural heritage site.
58288.m: Wadi Rum in Jordan is a UNESCO World Heritage Site.

58289.q: Why are wells and oases often found in wadis?
a: Groundwater collects beneath the wadi floor
Wadis are always by the sea
It rains every day in wadis
58289.e: The rare floodwater seeps into the loose gravel of the wadi floor. Groundwater stays there longer and can be used through wells.
58289.m: Beneath dry wadis there is often usable groundwater.

a: A mountain rising alone from a plain
A mountain on an island in the sea
A hill made of glacial debris
58290.e: Inselbergs rise steeply and in isolation above a wide planation surface. They look like islands in a sea of plain.
58290.m: An inselberg rises like an island from a flat plain.

58291.q: Which famous inselberg rises from the plain in central Australia?
58291.e: Uluru, formerly Ayers Rock, rises about 350 metres above the flat surroundings. The term inselberg was coined around 1900 by the German geologist Wilhelm Bornhardt in East Africa.

58292.q: Who was Henry Ayers, after whom Uluru was named “Ayers Rock” in 1873?
58292.e: The surveyor William Gosse named the rock after Sir Henry Ayers, then Chief Secretary of South Australia. Today the official name is Uluru / Ayers Rock.
58292.m: The name Ayers Rock goes back to the politician Henry Ayers.

58293.q: How do the rock layers in Uluru lie today?
a: Horizontal, as when they were deposited
58293.e: The layers were once deposited horizontally and later tilted to about 85 degrees during mountain building. That is why the edges of the layers can be seen today as fine ribs on Uluru.
58293.m: In Uluru the rock layers stand almost vertically.

58294.q: What does deflation mean in geomorphology?
58294.e: In deflation, the wind lifts fine, loose material such as dust and sand from the ground and carries it away. The term comes from the Latin “deflare”, meaning to blow away.
58294.m: Deflation means the wind blows loose material away.

58295.q: What is the wearing away of rock by wind-driven sand grains called, as opposed to deflation?
58295.e: In corrasion, the wind acts like a sandblaster and grinds rocks down. In deflation, on the other hand, only loose material is blown away.
58295.m: Corrasion grinds rock down, deflation blows loose material away.

58296.q: Which surface is left behind when the wind blows all the fine material out of a mixture of gravel and fine material?
58296.e: The coarse stones are too heavy for the wind and stay where they are. They form a dense desert pavement that protects the ground beneath.
58296.m: Deflation leaves behind a protective desert pavement.

58297.q: What is the gravel desert that often forms through deflation called?
58297.e: Serir or reg is a gravel desert in which the wind has blown out the fine material. Erg is the sand desert, hamada the rock or stone desert.
58297.m: In a serir, mainly gravel is left after deflation.

58298.q: Which large depression in Egypt is an example of a hollow partly shaped by deflation?
58298.e: The Qattara Depression lies in Egypt’s Western Desert and reaches about 133 metres below sea level. Over a long time the wind blew out the weathered material.
58298.m: The Qattara Depression was blown out deeply by the wind.

58299.q: Which event in Switzerland shows that dust blown out by deflation is carried a long way?
a: The foehn brings rain to Ticino
The bise dries out the Swiss Plateau
Fog lies over the Swiss Plateau
58299.e: Storms in the Sahara lift fine dust high into the air. South winds carry it as far as the Alps, where it colours snow and sky yellowish to reddish.
58299.m: Saharan dust can travel thousands of kilometres to Switzerland.

58300.q: Which wind-deposited fine sediment is the counterpart to deflation and forms fertile soils?
58300.e: Fine dust blown out by the wind is deposited elsewhere as loess. Loess soils are among the most fertile farmland soils.
58300.m: Loess forms from dust that the wind has blown out elsewhere.

58301.q: What was the environmental disaster of the 1930s in the USA called, when wind blew away huge amounts of farmland soil?
58301.e: After droughts and intensive ploughing of the prairie, the soil was unprotected. Storms blew the topsoil away and many farming families had to move away.
58301.m: The Dust Bowl shows how destructive deflation can be on unprotected farmland.

58302.q: Which process mainly shapes the narrow base of a mushroom rock in the desert?
a: Sandblasting by wind near the ground
58302.e: The wind carries sand grains mainly close to the ground. There it acts like a sandblaster and grinds the base of the rock more than the upper part.
58302.m: A mushroom rock is ground away at its base by sand.

58303.q: Why is wind abrasion strongest close to the ground?
a: Most sand grains bounce close to the ground
The wind is fastest at the ground
The rock is always softer at the ground
The air is driest at the ground
58303.e: Heavy sand grains are lifted only a little by the wind. The grinding effect is therefore limited to a zone near the ground.
58303.m: Sand grains mostly fly low, so the wind grinds mainly at the bottom.

58304.q: Which difference in the rock helps a mushroom rock to form?
a: A hard top layer over softer rock
A soft top layer over hard rock
58304.e: A resistant layer at the top forms the cap. The softer rock beneath is worn away faster and forms the narrow stem.
58304.m: A hard cap over soft rock allows a mushroom rock to form.

58305.q: Which kind of weathering, besides the wind, can further weaken the base of mushroom rocks?
a: Salt weathering due to ground moisture
58305.e: Near the ground, the rock is often a little damper and saltier. Salt weathering loosens the rock there, which the wind can then remove more easily.
58305.m: Salt weathering near the ground helps shape the stem of a mushroom rock.

58306.q: In which Egyptian desert landscape are mushroom-shaped limestone rocks a well-known sight?
58306.e: The White Desert near the Farafra oasis is known for its white chalk rocks shaped by the wind. Many of them are shaped like mushrooms or animals.
58306.m: In Egypt’s White Desert, the wind shaped limestone rocks into mushrooms.

58307.q: Which similar-looking forms in Valais were not created by wind but by rain washing away soft moraine material?
a: The karren fields of the Schrattenfluh
The dripstones of the St Beatus Caves
58307.e: At Euseigne, large capstones protect the moraine material beneath them from rain. Tall pillars with a stone as a cap were left standing.
58307.m: The earth pyramids of Euseigne are pillars with a protective capstone.

58308.q: How are the long, streamlined rock ridges in deserts called yardangs formed?
a: By rivers in the rainy season
58308.e: Sand-laden wind grinds the rock in its direction. This creates ridges lying parallel to the wind direction, which, like mushroom rocks, are a form of wind erosion.
58308.m: Yardangs are rock ridges ground by the wind.

58309.q: Besides the river’s erosion, which geological process was crucial for the great depth of the Grand Canyon?
a: The uplift of the Colorado Plateau
58309.e: As the Colorado Plateau rose, the river cut deeper and deeper. This combination of uplift and downcutting created the gorge.
58309.m: Uplift of the plateau and downcutting by the river created the Grand Canyon.

58310.q: Who led the first documented boat expedition through the Grand Canyon in 1869?
58310.e: In 1869 the geologist John Wesley Powell travelled down the Green River and the Colorado River with a small group. On the way he explored the Grand Canyon.
58310.m: In 1869 John Wesley Powell made the first documented trip through the Grand Canyon.

58311.q: In which year was the Grand Canyon declared a national park of the USA?
58311.e: Grand Canyon National Park was founded in 1919. Since 1979 it has also been a UNESCO World Heritage Site.
58311.m: The Grand Canyon has been a national park since 1919.

58312.q: Why do the walls of the Grand Canyon show a typical stepped profile?
a: Hard and soft layers weather differently
The river changed direction every year
58312.e: Resistant layers such as limestone and sandstone form steep walls. Softer shales weather faster and form gentler slopes.
58312.m: Layers of different hardness create the steps in the Grand Canyon.

58313.q: Where does the water of many wadis often end up after a flood?
a: In a basin with no outlet
58313.e: Many wadis never reach the sea because the water seeps away and evaporates on the way. It often collects in basins where salt pans (sabkhas) can form.
58313.m: Many wadis end in basins with no outlet in the middle of the desert.

58314.q: Which group of conglomerate rocks lies about 25 kilometres west of Uluru in the same national park?
58314.e: Kata Tjuta, also called the Olgas, consists of 36 dome-shaped rocks. Together with Uluru it forms Uluru-Kata Tjuta National Park.
58314.m: Kata Tjuta lies in the same national park as Uluru.

58315.q: Roughly how long is the circumference of Uluru at its base?
58315.e: Uluru is about 3.6 kilometres long and almost 2 kilometres wide. Its circumference is about 9.4 kilometres.
58315.m: Walking around Uluru means walking about nine kilometres.

58316.q: Roughly how old are the oldest rocks at the bottom of the Grand Canyon?
58316.e: Right at the bottom of the Inner Gorge are metamorphic rocks such as the Vishnu Schist. They are about 1.7 billion years old.
58316.m: At the bottom of the Grand Canyon lie rocks about 1.7 billion years old.

58317.q: Why are fossils of sea creatures found in the limestone at the top rim of the Grand Canyon?
a: The area used to lie beneath a sea
Birds carried the animals from the Pacific
The Colorado River washed them upstream
A tsunami threw them onto the plateau
58317.e: The Kaibab Limestone at the rim of the gorge formed about 270 million years ago on the floor of a shallow sea. Later the area was uplifted and today lies over 2000 m high.
58317.m: Sea fossils high up show that the land was once under water.

58318.q: In the Grand Canyon, what is the boundary called where hundreds of millions of years of rock history are missing?
58318.e: At this unconformity, young sedimentary layers lie directly on much older basement rock. The rocks in between were eroded or never deposited.
58318.m: The Great Unconformity shows a huge gap in the sequence of rocks.

58319.e: Karst forms only in rocks that dissolve in water. These include carbonate rocks such as limestone and dolomite as well as sulphate and salt rocks.
58319.m: Karst forms only in rocks that water can dissolve.

58320.q: In which climate do inselbergs above planation surfaces typically form?
a: In the high mountains of the Alps
58320.e: In the savannas of the seasonally wet tropics, rock weathers deeply and is worn down over wide areas. Hard cores of rock are left standing as inselbergs.
58320.m: Inselbergs are typical of the savannas of the seasonally wet tropics.

58321.q: In which type of dune do the arms point into the wind, unlike a barchan?
58321.e: Parabolic dunes are often held in place at the arms by plants, while the middle part keeps moving. That is why their arms point into the wind.
58321.m: In a parabolic dune, the arms point into the wind.

58322.q: What are stones called that the wind has ground to give them sharp edges and smooth faces?
58322.e: Ventifacts form when sand-laden wind strikes a stone over a long time. Depending on the number of edges, they are called, for example, dreikanters (three-edged stones).
58322.m: Ventifacts are stones that sandy wind has ground into sharp edges.

58323.q: Roughly how high does Uluru rise above the surrounding plain?
58323.e: Uluru rises about 348 metres above the plain. Its summit is about 863 metres above sea level.
58323.m: Uluru rises about 350 metres above the plain.

58324.q: Which Aboriginal people are the traditional owners of Uluru?
58324.e: Uluru is a sacred place for the Anangu. Since 1985 the land has officially belonged to them again, and the park is managed jointly.
58324.m: The Anangu are the traditional owners of Uluru.

58325.q: What are the round limestone formations that form in small pools of water in caves called?
58325.e: A grain of sand or a small stone is moved about in the dripping water and coated all round with limestone. This is how smooth, rounded cave pearls grow.
58325.m: Cave pearls form when limestone is deposited all round a moving core.

58326.q: What is the weathering of granite into rounded, cushion-shaped blocks called?
58326.e: Granite weathers along its joints, with the edges of the blocks attacked most strongly. This creates rounded blocks that look like stacked woolsacks.
58326.m: In woolsack weathering, granite turns into round, cushion-shaped blocks.

58327.q: Which cross-section is typical of a glacial trough shaped by a glacier?
58327.e: A valley glacier scours the floor and sides at the same time and so widens the valley. This creates a U-shaped cross-section with a wide valley floor and steep walls.
58327.m: Glaciers form U-shaped valleys, rivers form V-shaped valleys.

58328.q: What is the gentler ledge above the steep walls of a glacial trough called?
58328.e: The trough shoulder lies above the trough wall and often marks the height of an older valley floor or the glacier surface. In the Alps, alpine pastures and villages are often found on it.
58328.m: Alpine pastures and mountain villages are often found on the trough shoulder.

58329.q: Why do hanging valleys open out high above the floor of a glacial trough?
a: The main glacier eroded deeper than the side glaciers
Side valleys were later lifted by tectonic forces
Rivers in side valleys deposit more debris
The main river has filled its bed with gravel
58329.e: The huge main glacier had more ice and therefore more erosive power than the small side glaciers. After the ice melted, the side valleys therefore end at a steep step high above the main valley.
58329.m: Hanging valleys show that the main glacier dug deeper.

58330.q: Which valley in the Bernese Oberland is a textbook example of a glacial trough with waterfalls from hanging valleys?
58330.e: The Lauterbrunnen Valley has almost vertical rock walls over which many streams from hanging valleys plunge, such as the Staubbach Falls. It is considered one of the most impressive glacial troughs in the Alps.
58330.m: The Lauterbrunnen Valley is a classic example of a glacial trough.

58331.q: What is meant by glacial overdeepening of a glacial trough?
a: The glacier scours basins deeper than the later valley exit
A river cuts deeply into the ground after the Ice Age
The valley floor sinks as limestone dissolves
A rockslide dams the valley to form a lake
58331.e: Under pressure, glaciers can also flow uphill and can therefore scour basins below the level of the valley exit. Such overdeepened basins often later fill with lakes or sediments.
58331.m: Glaciers can scour basins deeper than the valley exit.

58332.q: Which national park in California is famous for its ice-shaped glacial trough with granite walls?
58332.e: Yosemite Valley was widened into a glacial trough by Ice Age glaciers. Rock walls such as El Capitan and hanging valleys with waterfalls shape the scenery.
58332.m: Yosemite Valley is a glacial trough with high granite walls.

58333.q: What is a threshold of harder rock lying across a glacial trough, which the glacier could not completely wear away, called?
58333.e: Harder parts of the rock resist glacial erosion and remain as a rock bar across the valley. Behind it there is often an overdeepened basin with a lake or a plain.
58333.m: A rock bar is a hard rock threshold across a glacial trough.

58334.q: How can you tell the maximum height of the glacier surface during the Ice Age on the wall of a glacial trough?
58334.e: Below the trimline the rock has been polished smooth by the ice, above it it is jagged from frost weathering. The line shows how thick the ice once was.
58334.m: The trimline reveals the former height of the glacier ice.

58335.q: What is a cirque in glacial geomorphology?
a: An armchair-shaped hollow on a mountainside
A long hill of ground moraine
A ridge of debris in front of the glacier snout
58335.e: A cirque is a hollow scoured out by a small glacier, with a steep back wall and a flatter floor. It usually lies high up on mountainsides and is often where a valley glacier begins.
58335.m: A cirque looks like an armchair pressed into the mountain.

58336.q: What is a small lake that forms in the floor of a cirque after the ice has melted called?
58336.e: The glacier has overdeepened the cirque floor into a hollow. After the ice melts, water collects in this hollow to form a tarn.
58336.m: Many cirques today hold a small tarn.

58337.q: What is the raised rock edge at the exit of a cirque that dams the tarn called?
58337.e: Because the glacier in a cirque flows with a rotating motion, it scours the middle deeper than the exit. At the edge, a threshold of rock or moraine is left standing.
58337.m: The cirque lip dams the water in the cirque to form a lake.

58338.q: Which mountain shape forms when three or more cirques eat into a peak from different sides?
58338.e: When cirques cut back from several sides, sharp ridges and a pointed summit are left between them. This pyramid shape is called a horn.
58338.m: A horn forms when cirques eat into a peak from all sides.

58339.q: Which Swiss mountain is a well-known example of a horn?
58339.e: The Matterhorn has steep faces and sharp ridges carved out by cirques on several sides. It is therefore regarded worldwide as the classic example of a horn.
58339.m: The Matterhorn is a classic example of a horn.

58341.q: What is a small glacier called that only fills the hollow of a cirque and does not form a distinct tongue?
58341.e: A cirque glacier is a small mass of ice in a shady hollow on a mountainside. It has no clearly formed glacier tongue and can lie lower than valley glaciers.
58341.m: A cirque glacier stays in its hollow on the mountainside.

58342.q: Which process makes the steep back wall of a cirque retreat?
58342.e: Water freezing in cracks breaks rock out of the cirque back wall, and the glacier carries the debris away. In this way the wall gradually retreats and the cirque grows larger.
58342.m: Frost and ice together make the cirque wall retreat.

58343.q: How can you tell moraine material apart from river gravel?
a: It is unsorted, a mix from clay to boulders
It is well sorted and finely layered
It consists only of well-rounded pebbles
58343.e: Ice carries large and small pieces together without separating them by size. Flowing water, on the other hand, sorts and layers the material.
58343.m: Moraine material is a jumbled mix and hardly sorted.

58344.q: What does a terminal moraine show?
a: The furthest advance of a glacier tongue
The place where two glaciers flow together
The height of the snow line
58344.e: The terminal moraine forms at the front of the glacier, where it pushes debris together like a bulldozer and deposits it. It marks the maximum extent of the glacier tongue.
58344.m: The terminal moraine shows how far a glacier once reached.

58345.q: How does a medial moraine form?
a: Two lateral moraines join where two glaciers meet
The glacier deposits debris at its front
Debris falls into a crevasse and freezes
Meltwater deposits sand in the middle of the glacier
58345.e: When two glaciers flow together, their inner lateral moraines join to form a dark band of debris in the middle. The Aletsch Glacier shows such medial moraines particularly clearly.
58345.m: Where two glaciers meet, two lateral moraines become one medial moraine.

58346.q: What is the moraine called that is deposited beneath the glacier and forms flat landscapes?
58346.e: Ground moraine forms at the base of the glacier from ground-up rock. It often forms gently rolling landscapes.
58346.m: Ground moraine lies beneath the glacier and is often very tightly packed.

58347.q: What are large blocks of rock called that were carried far by a glacier and now lie a long way from where they came from?
58347.e: Erratics or erratic boulders were often carried over long distances during the Ice Ages. On the Swiss Plateau, for example, there are granite blocks from the Alps.
58347.m: Erratics prove that glaciers once reached far into the lowlands.

58348.q: In the glacial series, what typically lies directly behind a terminal moraine, on the glacier side?
a: A tongue basin, often with a lake
An outwash plain of meltwater gravel
58348.e: Behind the terminal moraine, the glacier tongue scoured out a basin. Many lakes on the Swiss Plateau, such as Lake Zurich, lie in tongue basins like this.
58348.m: Behind the terminal moraine there is often a lake in the tongue basin.

58349.q: In the glacial series, which deposit lies in front of the terminal moraine, on the side facing away from the glacier?
58349.e: Meltwater flows outwards through the terminal moraine and deposits well-sorted sand and gravel over a wide area. These gravel plains are called outwash plains (sandar).
58349.m: In front of the terminal moraine, meltwater spreads out an outwash plain.

a: A streamlined hill of ground moraine
A ridge of beach sand in front of a lagoon
A pointed peak between several cirques
A rock threshold across a valley
58350.e: Drumlins are long, oval hills formed beneath a glacier from ground moraine material. The ice flowing over them shaped them into streamlined forms.
58350.m: A drumlin is a long moraine hill shaped by ice.

58351.q: How is a drumlin typically aligned with the former direction of glacier flow?
a: Its long axis is parallel to the direction of flow
Its long axis is at right angles to the direction of flow
It is arranged in a ring around the tongue basin
58351.e: The ice moulded the material into a streamlined shape in the direction of flow. That is why drumlins point like arrows in the direction the former glacier moved.
58351.m: Drumlins show the direction in which the former glacier flowed.

58352.q: Which side of a drumlin is usually steeper?
a: The stoss side facing the glacier
The lee side facing away from the glacier
Both long sides are equally steep
The south side facing the sun
58352.e: The blunt, steeper side faces the oncoming glacier. In the direction of flow, the hill tapers off lower and narrower.
58352.m: The steep side of a drumlin faces where the ice came from.

58353.q: Which language does the word drumlin come from?
58353.e: Drumlin comes from the Irish word “druim”, which means back or ridge. Ireland has many distinctive drumlin landscapes.
58353.m: The word drumlin comes from Irish and means a ridge.

58354.q: In which region of Switzerland is there a well-known drumlin landscape protected in the federal inventory?
58354.e: The drumlin landscape in the Zurich Oberland around Wetzikon and Hinwil formed beneath the Ice Age Linth Glacier. It is protected as a landscape of national importance.
58354.m: Drumlins shape the landscape in the Zurich Oberland.

58355.q: What do you call a group of many drumlins with a similar alignment?
58355.e: Drumlins rarely occur alone, but often in dozens or hundreds side by side. This is called a drumlin swarm or drumlin field.
58355.m: Many drumlins together form a drumlin swarm.

58356.q: What forms when a drumlin landscape is later flooded by the sea?
58356.e: When the sea level rises, only the tops of the drumlins stick out of the water. This creates a swarm of small islands, as in Clew Bay in Ireland.
58356.m: Flooded drumlins form swarms of islands.

58357.q: Which everyday object is the shape of a drumlin often compared to?
58357.e: A drumlin is broad and blunt at one end and tapers off at the other. Its shape is therefore reminiscent of an upside-down spoon or half an egg.
58357.m: A drumlin looks like an upside-down spoon.

a: A glacially overdeepened trough is flooded by the sea
A river cuts a gorge into the coastal mountains
A tectonic crack opens up on the coast
The surf eats a bay into a cliff coast
58358.e: Ice Age glaciers scoured deep troughs to below today’s sea level. After the ice melted and the sea level rose, the sea flowed into these valleys.
58358.m: A fjord is a glacial valley flooded by the sea.

58359.q: Why is a fjord often shallower at its mouth than further inland?
a: There is a threshold of rock or moraine at the exit
The tides pile up sandbanks there
The land has risen more there
58359.e: At the exit, the glacier lost thickness and erosive power, and it also deposited terminal moraines there. This created a threshold behind which the basin is deeper.
58359.m: Many fjords have a shallow threshold at the exit and are deeper inside.

58360.q: Which fjord is the longest and deepest in Norway?
58360.e: The Sognefjord is about 200 kilometres long and over 1300 metres deep at its deepest point. This makes it Norway’s longest and deepest fjord.
58360.m: The Sognefjord is Norway’s longest and deepest fjord.

58361.q: Which two Norwegian fjords were jointly added to the UNESCO World Heritage list in 2005?
58361.e: Under the name “West Norwegian Fjords”, the Geirangerfjord and the Nærøyfjord were added to the World Heritage list in 2005. They are regarded as particularly typical fjords with steep walls and waterfalls.
58361.m: The Geirangerfjord and Nærøyfjord are UNESCO World Heritage Sites.

58362.q: How does a förde, like the one at Kiel, differ from a fjord?
a: It is shallower and lined with gentle shores
It was never shaped by glaciers
It was formed by the surf
58362.e: Förden were also formed by glaciers, but in flat terrain from glacier tongue basins and meltwater channels. That is why they do not have steep, high rock walls like fjords.
58362.m: A förde is a shallow flooded glacial valley, a fjord a steep-walled one.

58363.q: In which country is the Scoresby Sund system, one of the largest fjord systems in the world?
58363.e: Scoresby Sund lies on the east coast of Greenland, which belongs to the Kingdom of Denmark. It is considered one of the longest fjord systems on Earth.
58363.m: One of the largest fjord systems in the world is in East Greenland.

58364.q: At which latitudes are most of the world’s fjord coasts found?
a: In middle and high latitudes of both hemispheres
58364.e: Fjords form where Ice Age glaciers reached the sea. This was mainly the case in Norway, Greenland, Canada, Alaska, Chile and New Zealand.
58364.m: Fjords are found where Ice Age glaciers reached the sea.

58365.q: In which bay in Alaska did a rockfall in 1958 trigger a wave that ran more than 500 metres up the slope?
58365.e: An earthquake made rock crash into the fjord-like Lituya Bay. On the opposite slope, the wave tore away the forest up to a height of about 524 metres.
58365.m: In 1958 a wave in Lituya Bay ran more than 500 metres high.

58366.q: Why is the deep water in some fjords low in oxygen?
a: The threshold at the exit hinders water exchange
The water there is particularly warm
Glaciers release oxygen into the air
The surf pushes out the oxygen
58366.e: The shallow threshold prevents oxygen-rich seawater from flowing regularly into the deep basin. The breakdown of organic material uses up the oxygen there.
58366.m: A fjord’s threshold slows down water exchange in the depths.

a: A steep slope on the coast shaped by the surf
A sand ridge that closes off a bay
A flat fan of sediment at a river mouth
58367.e: A cliff forms when the surf attacks a coast of rock or loose material and pushes it back. It forms a steep drop to the sea.
58367.m: A cliff is a steep coast shaped by the surf.

58368.q: What is the notch that the surf washes out at the foot of a cliff called?
58368.e: The waves knock rock out of the foot of the cliff and create a notch. When the overhang becomes too large, the upper part breaks off and the cliff retreats.
58368.m: The wave-cut notch undermines the cliff until it collapses.

58369.q: What is the flat rock surface that forms in front of a retreating cliff called?
58369.e: As the cliff retreats, a rock surface ground down by the surf is left in front of it. It is often visible at low tide and is also called an abrasion platform.
58369.m: A wave-cut platform is left in front of a retreating cliff.

58370.q: When is a cliff called dead or inactive?
a: When the surf no longer reaches the foot of the cliff
When the cliff has completely collapsed
When the cliff lies under water
When it is made of dead coral limestone
58370.e: An inactive cliff lies out of reach of the waves because of new land being built up or a falling sea level. It is then gradually covered by plants and becomes less steep.
58370.m: A dead cliff is no longer reached by the surf.

58371.q: What is a sea stack like the Lange Anna on Heligoland?
a: A rock tower cut off from the retreating cliff
The remains of a coral reef
58371.e: The surf widens cracks in the cliff into caves and arches until a piece of rock is completely cut off. What remains is a free-standing rock tower in the sea.
58371.m: A sea stack is a rock tower cut off from the cliff.

58372.q: Which rock formation on the coast of Normandy is Étretat known for?
58372.e: At Étretat, the surf has carved arches such as the Porte d’Aval into the white chalk cliffs. Next to them stands the rock needle L’Aiguille, a sea stack.
58372.m: At Étretat the surf has carved arches into the chalk cliffs.

58373.q: What rock are the famous cliffs of Dover and on the island of Rügen made of?
58373.e: The white cliffs near Dover and the Königsstuhl on Rügen are made of chalk. This soft limestone is worn away relatively quickly by the surf.
58373.m: The white cliffs of Dover and Rügen are made of chalk.

58374.q: On a coast being straightened by the sea, where does much of the sand that builds spits and barriers come from?
58374.e: On such a coast, cliffs that stick out are worn away. The loosened material is carried along and deposited again elsewhere.
58374.m: What the surf removes from cliffs builds spits and barriers elsewhere.

a: A narrow strip of land that separates a bay from the sea
A steep slope on a rocky coast
58375.e: A barrier spit is a long beach ridge of sand that largely closes off a bay. It forms mainly on coasts being straightened by the sea, such as on the Baltic Sea.
58375.m: A barrier spit is a narrow strip of sand between a bay and the open sea.

58376.q: Which process carries the sand from which barrier spits grow?
58376.e: Waves hitting the coast at an angle shift sand in a zigzag along the beach. In this way a beach ridge gradually grows across the bay.
58376.m: The longshore current carries the sand from which barrier spits grow.

58377.q: What is a narrow tongue of sand called that grows from the shore into the sea and whose end lies free in the water?
58377.e: A spit is a depositional landform that grows from the shore into the sea through longshore drift. Its free end is often curved landwards; a tombolo, by contrast, connects an island to the mainland.
58377.m: A spit grows from the shore into the sea as a tongue of sand.

58378.q: Between which two countries is the Curonian Spit divided today?
58378.e: The northern part of the Curonian Spit belongs to Lithuania, the southern part to the Russian exclave of Kaliningrad. The spit is about 98 kilometres long.
58378.m: The Curonian Spit lies in Lithuania and Russia.

58379.q: Besides its length, what is the Curonian Spit particularly famous for?
58379.e: The Curonian Spit has some of the highest wandering dunes in Europe. Since 2000 the spit has been a UNESCO World Heritage Site.
58379.m: The Curonian Spit is famous for its wandering dunes.

58380.q: Which river flows into the Curonian Lagoon?
58380.e: The Neman, called Nemunas in Lithuanian and Memel in German, flows into the Curonian Lagoon through a delta. Because of its fresh water, the lagoon is only slightly salty.
58380.m: The Neman flows into the Curonian Lagoon.

58381.q: Which lagoon lies at the mouth of the Oder between Germany and Poland?
58381.e: The Szczecin Lagoon is separated from the Baltic Sea by the islands of Usedom and Wolin. The Oder flows through it and reaches the sea through three outlets.
58381.m: The Oder flows through the Szczecin Lagoon into the Baltic Sea.

58382.q: What did Poland have built through the Vistula Spit in 2022?
a: A dam for a tidal power station
58382.e: The canal through the Vistula Spit opened in 2022. Ships can now sail from the Vistula Lagoon directly into the Baltic Sea without having to pass through Russian waters.
58382.m: Since 2022 a canal through the Vistula Spit has connected the lagoon and the Baltic Sea.

a: A shallow body of water separated from the sea by sandbanks or reefs
58383.e: A lagoon is a shallow coastal body of water that is largely cut off from the open sea by spits, islands or reefs. It is connected to the sea through narrow openings.
58383.m: A lagoon is a shallow body of water behind sandbanks or reefs.

58384.q: What is the long sandy island that separates the Venetian Lagoon from the Adriatic and is known for the film festival called?
58384.e: The Lido is a barrier island about eleven kilometres long between the lagoon and the Adriatic. The Venice Film Festival takes place there every year.
58384.m: The Lido separates the Venetian Lagoon from the open sea.

58385.q: What is the system of movable flood barriers at the entrances to the Venetian Lagoon called?
58385.e: MOSE consists of hinged gates on the seabed that rise up during high water. It was first used successfully against a storm surge in 2020.
58385.m: The MOSE flood barrier system protects Venice from high water.

58386.q: Why does the salt content of lagoons often vary so much?
a: Freshwater inflow and evaporation have a strong effect depending on location
Corals remove salt from the water
58386.e: Because exchange with the sea is limited, rivers and evaporation strongly determine the salt content. Depending on the climate, a lagoon can be brackish or saltier than the sea.
58386.m: The salt content of a lagoon depends strongly on inflow and evaporation.

58387.q: Which Latin word does the term lagoon come from?
58387.e: Lagoon goes back via the Italian “laguna” to the Latin “lacuna”. Lacuna means hollow, gap or pond.
58387.m: The word lagoon comes from the Latin lacuna.

58388.q: Which Spanish saltwater lagoon on the Mediterranean is one of the largest in Europe?
58388.e: The Mar Menor in the Murcia region is separated from the Mediterranean by the narrow spit of La Manga. It is one of the largest saltwater lagoons in Europe.
58388.m: The Mar Menor is a large lagoon behind the La Manga spit.

58389.q: What are long, narrow sandy islands off a coast, with lagoons behind them, like the Outer Banks in the USA, called?
58389.e: Barrier islands are long sandy islands parallel to the coast. Between them and the mainland lie shallow lagoons or sounds.
58389.m: Shallow lagoons often lie behind barrier islands.

58390.q: What do lagoons often have in common as a habitat for many sea creatures?
a: They serve as a sheltered nursery for young fish
They are very deep and dark
They freeze to the bottom every winter
58390.e: The calm, shallow and nutrient-rich water offers protection from waves and predators. That is why many fish and crabs spend their youth in lagoons.
58390.m: Lagoons are important nurseries for young sea creatures.

58391.q: In 1952, deep drilling on an atoll hit volcanic rock beneath more than 1000 metres of reef limestone. What did this find confirm?
a: Atolls sit on sunken volcanic islands
Atolls are the remains of a continent
58391.e: The drilling on Enewetak in the Marshall Islands went through thick layers of limestone made of dead corals. Beneath them basalt was found, in other words the sunken volcano, as Darwin had suspected.
58391.m: Drilling on Enewetak found a sunken volcano beneath the reef limestone.

58392.q: What do you call a navigable gap in the ring of reef around an atoll?
58392.e: Water flows through passes between the lagoon and the open sea with the ebb and flow of the tide. They are often the only way for ships to enter the lagoon.
58392.m: Ships enter the lagoon of an atoll through a pass.

58393.q: Which sequence of reef development does Darwin’s theory of how an atoll forms describe?
58393.e: First a fringing reef grows directly on the volcanic island. When the island sinks, a barrier reef forms with a lagoon in between, and when the island sinks completely, an atoll is left.
58393.m: A fringing reef becomes a barrier reef and finally an atoll.

58394.q: On many atoll islands, where does the usable groundwater come from?
a: From a freshwater lens above the salt water
58394.e: Rainwater seeps into the coral sand and, because it is less dense, floats as a lens on the salt water. Overuse or storm surges can make this lens salty.
58394.m: On atolls, a thin freshwater lens floats on the salt water.

58395.q: Which country carried out nuclear weapons tests on Mururoa Atoll between 1966 and 1996?
58395.e: France tested nuclear weapons on Mururoa and Fangataufa in French Polynesia. The last tests in 1995 and 1996 sparked protests around the world.
58395.m: France tested nuclear weapons on Mururoa Atoll.

58396.q: Which atoll in the Marshall Islands has one of the largest lagoons in the world and is home to a US missile test base?
58396.e: With around a hundred small islands, Kwajalein encloses a very large lagoon. The USA has operated a missile test range there for decades.
58396.m: Kwajalein has one of the largest atoll lagoons on Earth.

58397.q: Which raised atoll in the Seychelles is known for its large population of giant tortoises?
58397.e: Aldabra is an atoll raised above sea level and has been a UNESCO World Heritage Site since 1982. Around 100,000 Aldabra giant tortoises live there.
58397.m: Very many giant tortoises live on the raised atoll of Aldabra.

58398.q: What is a sunken seamount with a flat top, on which reef growth could not keep up with the sinking, called?
58398.e: Guyots are former volcanic islands whose summits were flattened by the surf. If they sank too quickly or into water that was too cool, the reef died and the mountain disappeared into the depths.
58398.m: A guyot is a sunken volcano with a flat summit.

58399.q: Which atoll in the Indian Ocean did Darwin study in 1836 on his voyage on the Beagle?
58399.e: On the Cocos Islands, also called the Keeling Islands, Darwin studied the reef in April 1836. His observations fed into his theory of how atolls form.
58399.m: In 1836 Darwin studied an atoll on the Cocos Islands.

58400.q: How has the Great Barrier Reef mainly been protected since 1975?
a: As a large marine park with protected zones
By a complete ban on ships
By an underwater wall in front of the reef
58400.e: Since 1975 the reef has been protected as the Great Barrier Reef Marine Park. A special authority divides it into zones in which different uses, such as fishing or tourism, are allowed.
58400.m: The Great Barrier Reef is a marine park with different protected zones.

58401.q: Since the rezoning of 2004, what share of the Great Barrier Reef Marine Park has been designated as a no-fishing protected zone?
58401.e: With the 2004 zoning plan, the so-called green zones were greatly expanded. Since then about a third of the park has been closed to fishing.
58401.m: Since 2004 about a third of the marine park has been a no-fishing zone.

58402.q: Which status did UNESCO experts propose for the Great Barrier Reef in 2021, without it being adopted?
a: Removal from the World Heritage list
58402.e: Because of repeated coral bleaching, experts recommended adding it to the list of World Heritage in Danger. After objections from Australia, the World Heritage Committee did not follow the recommendation.
58402.m: Experts wanted to classify the Great Barrier Reef as World Heritage in Danger.

58403.q: In which two consecutive years did the Great Barrier Reef suffer two mass bleaching events in a row for the first time?
58403.e: After a marine heatwave in 2016, another mass bleaching followed in 2017. The corals had no time to recover in between.
58403.m: In 2016 and 2017 the corals bleached on a massive scale twice in a row.

58404.q: Which kind of farming on the coast of Queensland is an important source of fertiliser washed onto the reef?
58404.e: A lot of sugar cane is grown on the coastal plains of Queensland. Fertiliser and sediment reach the sea with rivers and, among other things, encourage algae to grow.
58404.m: Fertiliser from sugar cane farming puts strain on the reef.

58405.q: Which living things in the tissue of corals do they lose during coral bleaching?
58405.e: Single-celled algae live in corals, providing food through photosynthesis and giving them their colour. When the water is too warm, the corals expel them and turn white.
58405.m: In coral bleaching, corals lose their colourful algae.

58406.q: On what geological foundation has the Great Barrier Reef grown?
a: On sunken volcanic islands, like an atoll
58406.e: The reef sits on the shallow shelf off Queensland, which was flooded when sea levels rose. At the outer edge, the seabed drops steeply into the deeper Coral Sea.
58406.m: The Great Barrier Reef grows on the continental shelf.

58407.q: Which strait roughly forms the northern end of the Great Barrier Reef?
58407.e: The reef stretches south from the Torres Strait between Australia and New Guinea. In the south it ends at about the latitude of Bundaberg.
58407.m: In the north, the Great Barrier Reef reaches as far as the Torres Strait.

58408.q: Which group of islands on the Great Barrier Reef is known for the white quartz sand beach Whitehaven Beach?
58408.e: The Whitsunday Islands lie off the coast of Queensland in the middle of the reef area. Whitehaven Beach consists of very fine, almost pure quartz sand.
58408.m: Whitehaven Beach is on the Whitsunday Islands.

58409.q: According to which three processes did William Galloway classify deltas in 1975?
58409.e: Galloway arranged deltas in a triangle according to whether river supply, waves or tides determine their shape. The Mississippi delta, for example, is river-dominated, while the Ganges-Brahmaputra delta is strongly influenced by tides.
58409.m: Deltas are classified by the influence of river, waves and tides.

58410.q: Which river has built a large delta into Lake Maggiore between Locarno and Ascona?
58410.e: The Maggia brings a lot of gravel from the Maggia valley and deposits it in Lake Maggiore. Parts of Locarno and Ascona now stand on the delta formed in this way.
58410.m: Locarno and Ascona stand on the delta of the Maggia.

58411.q: Which river is known for its bird’s-foot delta?
58411.e: The Mississippi builds its distributaries with levees far out into the Gulf of Mexico. From above, the shape looks like a bird’s foot.
58411.m: The Mississippi has a delta shaped like a bird’s foot.

58412.q: Why does a delta often form where a river flows into a lake or the sea?
a: The water slows down and deposits the material it carries
The water speeds up and digs a deep basin
The lake water dissolves the rock of the shore
The wind blows sand from the land to the mouth
58412.e: When it enters still water, the river loses speed and therefore its power to carry material. Gravel, sand and mud settle, and the delta grows out into the lake or sea.
58412.m: A delta forms when a river deposits its load at its mouth.

58413.q: What are the channels into which a river splits in its delta called?
58413.e: In the delta, the river branches into several channels that flow separately into the sea. Tributaries, on the other hand, flow into a river.
58413.m: In the delta the river splits into several distributaries.

58414.q: Which region in southern France lies in the Rhône delta?
58414.e: Before reaching the Mediterranean, the Rhône splits into the Grand Rhône and the Petit Rhône. Between them lies the Camargue, with lagoons, salt meadows and flamingos.
58414.m: The Rhône delta forms the Camargue.

58415.q: Where, close to Switzerland, is the Alpine Rhine building a delta?
58415.e: Every year the Alpine Rhine deposits large amounts of gravel and sand in Lake Constance. Its delta is therefore growing steadily into the lake.
58415.m: The Alpine Rhine is building a delta into Lake Constance.

58416.q: Which delta in Romania and Ukraine is a UNESCO World Heritage Site and home to many birds?
58416.e: The Danube Delta on the Black Sea is one of the largest wetlands in Europe. Its Romanian part has been a UNESCO World Heritage Site since 1991.
58416.m: The Danube Delta is a great paradise for birds on the Black Sea.

58417.q: Why has the Nile Delta been partly eroded at the coast since the Aswan High Dam was built?
a: The dam holds back the sediment
The Nile has carried more water since then
The dam has made the tides stronger
The desert is spreading into the delta
58417.e: Since the High Dam was built in the 1960s, the mud has stayed in Lake Nasser. Without new supplies, the Mediterranean is wearing away parts of the delta coast.
58417.m: Without new sediment, a delta shrinks at the coast.

a: A funnel-shaped river mouth influenced by tides
A river mouth area that branches into many channels
A glacial valley flooded by the sea
58418.e: In an estuary, the river mouth widens like a funnel towards the sea. The tides push far upstream and flush out sediment.
58418.m: An estuary is a funnel-shaped river mouth shaped by the tides.

58419.q: Which two rivers flow together into the Río de la Plata estuary?
58419.e: The Río de la Plata is formed where the Paraná and the Uruguay meet. Buenos Aires and Montevideo lie on its shores.
58419.m: The Paraná and the Uruguay together form the Río de la Plata.

58420.q: What kind of water is typical of an estuary?
58420.e: In an estuary, the river’s fresh water mixes with the salt water of the sea. The resulting brackish water has a medium salt content.
58420.m: In an estuary, fresh and salt water mix to form brackish water.

58421.q: On which estuary does the port of Hamburg lie?
58421.e: Hamburg lies about 100 kilometres inland on the Elbe. The tides reach as far as the port, which is why large ships use the high tide.
58421.m: Hamburg lies on the tidal Elbe.

58422.q: Which estuary in France is formed where the Garonne and the Dordogne meet?
58422.e: The Garonne and the Dordogne join north of Bordeaux to form the Gironde. It is considered the largest estuary in Western Europe.
58422.m: The Gironde is the shared estuary of the Garonne and the Dordogne.

58423.q: Which river in Canada forms one of the largest estuaries in the world?
58423.e: The St Lawrence River connects the Great Lakes with the Atlantic. Its estuary widens to many dozens of kilometres towards the gulf.
58423.m: The St Lawrence River has a huge estuary.

58424.q: Why is the water in an estuary often particularly murky?
a: Fine suspended particles collect where fresh and salt water meet
Ships constantly stir up the bottom there
Algae only grow in river mouths
The seawater there is particularly cold
58424.e: When fresh and salt water mix, fine particles clump together. The tides move them back and forth, creating a turbidity zone.
58424.m: In the turbidity zone of an estuary, the water is particularly murky.

58425.q: Which river forms a wide estuary into the North Sea below London?
58425.e: Below London, the Thames widens into a broad estuary leading to the North Sea. The Thames Barrier was built to protect against storm surges.
58425.m: London lies on the estuary of the Thames.

58426.q: How did George Hadley explain the origin of the trade winds in 1735?
a: With rising air at the equator and the Earth’s rotation
With the pull of the Moon
With heat from inside the Earth
With the melting of the polar ice caps
58426.e: At the equator, warmed air rises, and air from the subtropics flows in along the ground to replace it. The Earth’s rotation deflects this flow, creating the trade winds.
58426.m: Hadley explained the trade winds with rising air at the equator and the Earth’s rotation.

58427.q: Roughly how high does the Hadley cell reach in the tropics?
58427.e: The Hadley cell spans the whole troposphere up to the tropopause. In the tropics this lies much higher than in middle latitudes, at about 15 to 18 km.
58427.m: In the tropics the Hadley cell reaches up to the high tropopause.

58428.q: What happens to the air at the poleward edge of the Hadley cell?
58428.e: The high-altitude air cools on its way towards the poles, becomes denser and sinks in the subtropics. As it sinks, it warms up through compression.
58428.m: At the edge of the Hadley cell the air sinks and warms up.

58429.q: Which process supplies particularly large amounts of energy to the rising branch of the Hadley cell?
a: Release of latent heat during condensation
Heat given off by the Earth’s crust
58429.e: When the water vapour in the rising air condenses, the heat stored during evaporation is released again. This latent heat strengthens the uplift.
58429.m: Condensing water vapour releases latent heat and so drives the Hadley cell.

58430.q: What is the poleward high-altitude flow of the Hadley cell called?
58430.e: At altitude, the air that rose at the equator flows back towards the subtropics. Because it blows opposite to the trade wind near the ground, it is called the anti-trade wind.
58430.m: The anti-trade is the high-altitude flow that blows opposite to the trade wind.

58431.q: Which circulation cell joins the Hadley cell on the poleward side in each hemisphere?
a: The Hadley cell of the other hemisphere
58431.e: The three-cell model consists of the Hadley cell, the Ferrel cell and the polar cell. The Ferrel cell lies in the middle latitudes between the other two.
58431.m: In the three-cell model, the Ferrel cell follows the Hadley cell.

58432.q: Why is the Hadley cell considered a thermally direct circulation?
a: Warm air rises, cooler air sinks
Cold air rises, warm air sinks
It is driven by tides alone
It is created only by friction against mountains
58432.e: In a thermally direct cell, the movement is driven directly by differences in temperature. The Ferrel cell, by contrast, is considered thermally indirect.
58432.m: In the Hadley cell warm air rises and cooler air sinks.

58433.q: Which change in the Hadley cell is linked to global warming in many studies?
a: Shrinking to a narrow belt at the equator
A reversal of its direction of rotation
58433.e: Observations since about 1980 suggest that the Hadley cells have expanded towards the poles. This could shift dry subtropical regions.
58433.m: With global warming, the Hadley cells are probably expanding towards the poles.

58434.q: Which desert lies in the area of the sinking branch of the Hadley cell?
58434.e: The Sahara lies in the subtropical zone where dry air sinks. The Gobi and Taklamakan are inland deserts, and the Patagonian Desert lies in the rain shadow of the Andes.
58434.m: The Sahara is a desert of the subtropical zone of sinking air.

58435.q: What flows together in the Intertropical Convergence Zone (ITCZ)?
a: The trade winds of both hemispheres
58435.e: Convergence means flowing together. In the ITCZ, the trade winds of the northern and southern hemispheres meet, and the air is forced to rise.
58435.m: In the ITCZ, the trade winds of the northern and southern hemispheres meet.

58436.q: What weather is typical of the Intertropical Convergence Zone?
a: Towering cumulus clouds with heavy rain
58436.e: The rising, moist air forms huge cumulonimbus clouds. Violent thunderstorms often develop in the afternoon, known as zenithal rains.
58436.m: The ITCZ brings thunderstorms and heavy downpours.

58437.q: What did sailors call the zone of light winds in the area of the ITCZ?
58437.e: In the ITCZ the air mainly rises, and horizontal winds are often weak. Sailing ships were therefore sometimes stuck in the doldrums for days.
58437.m: The doldrums at the equator are known for their lack of wind.

58438.q: What determines the seasonal shift of the ITCZ?
a: Where the sun is directly overhead
The position of the ocean ridges
The strength of the Earth’s magnetic field
58438.e: With some delay, the ITCZ follows the area where the sun is directly overhead at midday. That is why it lies further north in the northern summer and further south in the southern summer.
58438.m: The ITCZ moves with the position of the overhead sun.

58439.q: Where does the ITCZ lie on average over the year?
a: Exactly on the Tropic of Capricorn
58439.e: Because the northern hemisphere has more land and warms up more, the ITCZ lies slightly north of the equator on average over the year, at about 5° north.
58439.m: On average over the year, the ITCZ lies slightly north of the equator.

58440.q: Where does the ITCZ shift particularly far north in the northern summer?
58440.e: The large land mass of Asia warms up strongly in summer. Over South Asia, the ITCZ therefore moves to beyond 20° north.
58440.m: Over South Asia the ITCZ moves far north in summer.

58441.q: What causes the rainy season in the African Sahel?
a: The ITCZ shifting north in the northern summer
Low-pressure areas from the North Atlantic
58441.e: In the northern summer, the ITCZ shifts towards the Sahel and brings rain there. When it moves back south, the long dry season begins.
58441.m: The Sahel gets its rain when the ITCZ moves north in summer.

58442.q: Why do many places near the equator have two rainy seasons a year?
a: The ITCZ passes over them twice a year
Two monsoons blow at the same time
The Earth has two summers a year
58442.e: Over the year, the ITCZ moves north and then south again. Places near the equator are therefore crossed twice and get two rainy seasons.
58442.m: Two passes of the ITCZ bring two rainy seasons near the equator.

58443.q: Which pressure system is linked to the Intertropical Convergence Zone?
a: The equatorial trough of low pressure
58443.e: Where air rises over a large area, the air pressure at the ground falls. That is why a band of low pressure, the equatorial trough, forms along the ITCZ.
58443.m: The equatorial trough of low pressure lies along the ITCZ.

58444.q: From which direction does the trade wind blow in the northern hemisphere?
58444.e: The air flows from the subtropics to the equator and is deflected by the Earth’s rotation. This creates a wind that blows at an angle towards the equator.
58444.m: In the northern hemisphere, the north-east trade wind blows.

58445.q: From which direction does the trade wind blow in the southern hemisphere?
58445.e: In the southern hemisphere, the deflection by the Earth’s rotation works as a mirror image of the northern hemisphere. This gives a different wind direction there from the one in the north.
58445.m: In the southern hemisphere, the south-east trade wind blows.

58447.q: What does the trade wind inversion do?
a: It limits cloud formation at altitude
It strengthens thunderstorms in the trade wind area
It reverses the wind direction every day
58447.e: Sinking, warmed air lies at about 1 to 2 km above cooler, moist air. This temperature inversion acts like a lid, which is why trade wind clouds usually stay flat.
58447.m: The trade wind inversion keeps trade wind clouds low.

58448.q: Why did Columbus first sail south to the Canary Islands in 1492?
a: To reach the zone of the trade winds
58448.e: From the Canaries, the steady trade wind drove the ships westwards across the Atlantic. For the return journey, Columbus chose a more northerly route.
58448.m: Columbus used the trade wind for his voyage west.

58449.q: Which side of the Hawaiian Islands is usually particularly rainy?
a: The windward side facing the trade wind
The leeward side facing away from the trade wind
The southern tip of each island
58449.e: The trade wind brings moist sea air that rises over the mountains and rains out. The windward side is therefore wet, and the leeward side is often dry.
58449.m: On trade wind islands, the windward side is rainier than the leeward side.

58450.q: Between which pressure areas does the trade wind blow?
a: From the subtropical high towards the equator
From the Icelandic Low to the Azores High
From the polar high to the subpolar low
From the equator to the subtropical high
58450.e: Wind blows from high to low pressure. The trade winds therefore flow from the subtropical high-pressure belt to the equator, where the air rises and the pressure is lower.
58450.m: The trade wind blows from the subtropical highs to the equator.

58451.q: Why doesn’t the trade wind in the northern hemisphere blow exactly from the north?
a: Mountains force it to the side
The Earth’s magnetic field deflects it
58451.e: On a rotating Earth, moving masses of air are deflected. The wind flowing south therefore becomes a wind from the north-east.
58451.m: Because of the Earth’s rotation, the trade wind blows at an angle towards the equator.

58452.q: Which ocean current in the Atlantic is driven by the trade wind north of the equator?
58452.e: The steady trade wind pushes the surface water north of the equator westwards. This creates the westward-flowing North Equatorial Current.
58452.m: The trade wind drives the North Equatorial Current.

58453.q: In which range of latitudes do the westerlies prevail?
58453.e: The westerly wind zone lies in the middle latitudes between the subtropical high-pressure belt and the subpolar low-pressure trough. Its boundaries shift with the seasons.
58453.m: The westerlies shape the middle latitudes.

58454.q: In which wind zone does Switzerland lie?
a: In the zone of the polar easterlies
58454.e: Switzerland lies at about 46° to 48° north and therefore in the middle latitudes. Its weather is often shaped by air masses brought in from the Atlantic.
58454.m: Switzerland lies in the westerly wind zone.

58455.q: What do sailors call the stormy westerly winds around 40° south?
58455.e: In the southern hemisphere, the westerlies around 40° south blow almost unchecked across the sea. Because of their strength they are called the “Roaring Forties”.
58455.m: The Roaring Forties are the stormy westerlies of the southern hemisphere.

58456.q: Why are the westerlies in the southern hemisphere stronger and steadier than in the northern hemisphere?
a: There are hardly any land masses to slow them down
The sun shines more strongly there
There are no high-pressure areas there
58456.e: Between 40° and 60° south there is almost nothing but ocean. Without mountains and continents, there is none of the friction that weakens and deflects the wind in the northern hemisphere.
58456.m: Without continents to slow them, the southern westerlies blow particularly strongly.

58457.q: Which ocean current is also called the West Wind Drift?
58457.e: In the Southern Ocean, the westerlies drive a current that flows all the way around Antarctica. This Antarctic Circumpolar Current is also called the West Wind Drift.
58457.m: The Antarctic Circumpolar Current is also called the West Wind Drift.

58458.q: What weather is typical of the westerly wind zone?
a: Half a year of rain and half a year of drought
58458.e: In the westerly wind zone, low-pressure areas with their fronts keep moving from west to east. In between there are spells of high pressure, so the weather changes often.
58458.m: In the westerly wind zone the weather often changes.

58459.q: Why are winters in Western Europe relatively mild?
a: Westerly winds bring mild air from the Atlantic
The sun is high there in winter
Warm air flows in from Siberia
The Alps hold back the cold
58459.e: The Atlantic stores heat, partly thanks to the North Atlantic Current. The westerlies carry this mild sea air far into Europe.
58459.m: The westerlies bring mild Atlantic air to Western Europe.

58460.q: Which climate is typical on the west coasts of continents in the westerly wind zone?
58460.e: On west coasts such as in Ireland or Norway, the air comes straight from the sea. That is why temperature differences are small and rain is frequent.
58460.m: On west coasts in the westerly wind zone there is an oceanic climate.

58461.q: Why is eastern Patagonia very dry despite lying in the westerly wind zone?
a: It lies in the rain shadow of the Andes
It lies in the area of the ITCZ
The trade wind blows there constantly
58461.e: The moist westerlies rain out on the Chilean side of the Andes. On the Argentinian eastern side, the air arrives dry and sinking.
58461.m: The Andes keep the westerlies’ rain away from eastern Patagonia.

58462.q: At roughly what height does the jet stream blow?
58462.e: Jet streams are bands of strong wind in the upper troposphere near the tropopause. Many passenger planes also fly there.
58462.m: The jet stream blows near the tropopause at about 10 km high.

58463.q: What speed can the wind in the jet stream reach?
58463.e: In the core of a jet stream the wind often blows at about 180 km/h, and speeds of up to about 400 km/h have been measured. That is why it has a strong effect on flight times.
58463.m: In the jet stream the wind can reach about 400 kilometres per hour.

58464.q: Which two jet streams are mainly distinguished in each hemisphere?
a: Polar front jet and subtropical jet
Monsoon jet and trade wind jet
Gulf Stream jet and foehn jet
Equatorial jet and polar jet at the pole
58464.e: The polar front jet lies above the boundary between polar and temperate air, the subtropical jet at the poleward edge of the Hadley cell.
58464.m: There is a polar front jet and a subtropical jet.

58465.q: In the 1920s in Japan, how were the strong high-altitude winds of the jet stream discovered?
a: With balloons whose flight paths were tracked
With weather stations on mountain tops
58465.e: The meteorologist Wasaburo Oishi released pilot balloons near Mount Fuji and measured their paths. Because he published in Esperanto, the discovery went unnoticed outside Japan for a long time.
58465.m: The jet stream was discovered in Japan using balloons.

58466.q: Why does a flight from Zurich to New York usually take longer than the return flight?
a: On the outward flight there is a headwind from the jet stream
The Earth turns away beneath the plane
Planes are only allowed to fly more slowly westwards
The route is longer going west
58466.e: On the way west, the plane flies against the high-altitude westerlies. Going east, pilots use the jet stream as a tailwind.
58466.m: The jet stream shortens flights to the east and lengthens flights to the west.

58467.q: What did Japan use the jet stream for in the Second World War?
a: To send balloon bombs to North America
To send radio signals to Europe
To steer weather balloons to Australia
To take planes to the South Pole
58467.e: From 1944 Japan released thousands of balloons carrying explosives, which the strong wind carried across the Pacific. Some actually reached the USA and Canada.
58467.m: In the Second World War, Japan sent balloon bombs across the Pacific with the jet stream.

58468.q: What are the large waves in which the jet stream meanders around the Earth called?
58468.e: The large-scale meanders of the high-altitude flow were named after the meteorologist Carl-Gustaf Rossby. If they stay in place, a type of weather can last for a long time.
58468.m: The jet stream winds its way around the Earth in Rossby waves.

58469.q: What causes the polar front jet?
a: Large temperature contrasts between air masses
58469.e: Where cold and warm air masses meet, the pressure difference increases with height. This creates a strong high-altitude wind along this boundary.
58469.m: Strong temperature contrasts create the jet stream.

58470.q: In which season is the polar front jet usually strongest in the northern hemisphere?
a: It is equally strong all year
58470.e: In winter the temperature difference between the Arctic and the subtropics is greatest. That is why the jet stream blows most strongly then.
58470.m: The northern hemisphere’s jet stream is strongest in winter.

58471.q: Which experiment in Paris in 1851 made visible the rotation of the Earth, which also causes the Coriolis force?
58471.e: In 1851 Léon Foucault set a long pendulum swinging. Its plane of swing slowly turned because the Earth turns beneath it. The same rotation of the Earth produces the Coriolis force.
58471.m: Foucault’s pendulum shows the rotation of the Earth.

58472.q: In which direction does the Coriolis force deflect moving air in the northern hemisphere?
58472.e: In the northern hemisphere, every horizontal movement is deflected to the right when seen in the direction of motion. This shapes the direction of winds and ocean currents.
58472.m: In the northern hemisphere the Coriolis force deflects to the right.

58473.q: In which direction does the Coriolis force deflect moving air in the southern hemisphere?
58473.e: In the southern hemisphere, the deflection is a mirror image of the northern hemisphere. Moving air is deflected to the left when seen in the direction of motion.
58473.m: In the southern hemisphere the Coriolis force deflects to the left.

58474.q: How large is the horizontal deflection by the Coriolis force right at the equator?
a: About half as large as at the poles
The same as at the poles
58474.e: The horizontal component of the Coriolis force depends on the sine of the latitude. At the equator the sine of 0° is zero, and at the poles the effect is greatest.
58474.m: At the equator the Coriolis force does not deflect horizontal movements.

58475.q: In physics, what kind of force is the Coriolis force?
a: A fictitious force in a rotating frame of reference
A frictional force of the air
58475.e: The Coriolis force only arises because we observe movements from the rotating Earth. It is therefore called a fictitious or inertial force.
58475.m: The Coriolis force is a fictitious force caused by the Earth’s rotation.

58476.q: Why do tropical cyclones hardly ever form closer than about 5° to the equator?
a: The Coriolis force is too weak there
The sea is too cold there
There is no humidity at all there
The air pressure is too high there
