58476.e: For a vortex to form, the incoming air has to be deflected. Near the equator, the Coriolis force is too small for this.
58476.m: Without enough Coriolis force, no cyclone forms.

58477.q: Does the Coriolis force decide which way water swirls down the sink?
a: No, it is far too weak for that
Only in places north of the Alps
58477.e: With such small amounts of water and such short times, the Coriolis force is tiny. The shape of the basin and leftover movements in the water decide the direction of the swirl.
58477.m: In a sink, it is not the Coriolis force that decides the direction of the swirl.

58478.q: What does the strength of the Coriolis force depend on?
a: On the time of day and the phase of the Moon
On altitude and the type of rock
58478.e: The Coriolis force increases with the speed of the moving body. In addition, its horizontal effect increases from the equator towards the poles.
58478.m: Fast movements at high latitudes are strongly deflected.

58479.q: Which experiment in Paris in 1851 made the Earth’s rotation visible?
a: The experiment with the Magdeburg hemispheres
58479.e: In 1851 Léon Foucault set a long pendulum swinging, whose plane of swing slowly turned over the course of the day. The cause is the same effect of the Earth’s rotation that also deflects winds.
58479.m: Foucault’s pendulum shows the rotation of the Earth.

58480.q: At which latitudes are the horse latitudes?
58480.e: The horse latitudes lie in the subtropics, roughly between 25° and 35° latitude in both hemispheres. This is where the subtropical high-pressure belt is.
58480.m: The horse latitudes lie in the subtropics around 30° latitude.

58481.q: According to a popular explanation, where does the name horse latitudes come from?
a: Horses were thrown overboard when there was no wind
Many wild horses lived on islands there
A sailor called Horse discovered them
58481.e: Sailing ships in the horse latitudes, with their light winds, often got stuck in long calms. When drinking water ran short, horses are said to have been thrown overboard; however, the origin is not reliably proven.
58481.m: The name horse latitudes is often explained by horses on sailing ships.

58482.q: What weather is typical of the horse latitudes?
58482.e: In the horse latitudes, air sinks over a large area and the air pressure is high. Strong horizontal winds are missing, and hardly any rain clouds form.
58482.m: The horse latitudes are calm and dry.

58483.q: Why does it rarely rain in the horse latitudes?
a: Sinking air warms up and clouds dissolve
The air there is too cold for water vapour
Strong winds blow the clouds away
The ground absorbs all the moisture
58483.e: As it sinks, the air is compressed and warms up. This lowers the relative humidity and clouds evaporate.
58483.m: Sinking air dries out and prevents rain.

58484.q: Which high-pressure area over the Atlantic belongs to the subtropical high-pressure belt of the northern hemisphere?
58484.e: The Azores High lies in the area of the horse latitudes of the North Atlantic. It influences the weather in Europe, especially in summer.
58484.m: The Azores High belongs to the subtropical high-pressure belt.

58485.q: Why are summers on the Mediterranean usually dry?
a: The subtropical high-pressure belt shifts north
The ITCZ lies over the Mediterranean in summer
The Alps keep all the clouds away
The monsoon brings dry air from India
58485.e: In the northern summer, the pressure belts move north with the position of the sun. The Mediterranean comes under the influence of the subtropical highs, and in winter under the influence of the westerlies instead.
58485.m: In summer the Mediterranean is under the influence of the subtropical highs.

58486.q: Which winds flow out of the horse latitudes near the ground?
a: Trade winds towards the equator and westerlies towards the poles
Only polar easterlies towards the poles
Monsoons towards the equator and foehn towards the poles
None at all, the air only rises
58486.e: The horse latitudes are an area of high pressure. From there, air flows out in both directions: towards the equator as the trade wind and into the middle latitudes as the westerlies.
58486.m: Trade winds and westerlies blow out of the horse latitudes.

58487.q: Which sea area, known for calm winds and floating seaweed, lies in the horse latitudes of the North Atlantic?
58487.e: The Sargasso Sea lies in the centre of the North Atlantic gyre under the subtropical high. It is named after the Sargassum seaweed that floats there.
58487.m: The Sargasso Sea lies in the calm horse latitudes.

58488.q: Why is the salt content of seawater in the horse latitudes particularly high?
a: A lot evaporates and little rain falls
Rivers bring a lot of salt there
58488.e: Sunshine and dry air make a lot of water evaporate, while hardly any rain falls. The salt is left behind, which is why the surface water there is particularly salty.
58488.m: Strong evaporation makes the sea salty in the subtropics.

58489.q: What does the polar front separate?
a: Cold polar air and warm subtropical air
North-east trade wind and south-east trade wind
58489.e: The polar front is the boundary zone between cold air from high latitudes and warm air from the subtropics. Many weather events of the middle latitudes develop along it.
58489.m: The polar front separates cold polar air from warm subtropical air.

58490.q: Which group of meteorologists developed the polar front model around 1920?
58490.e: In Bergen (Norway), meteorologists around Vilhelm and Jacob Bjerknes explained fronts and how lows form. Their model is still taught today.
58490.m: The polar front model comes from the Bergen School.

58491.q: Where does the meteorological term “front” come from?
a: From a comparison with the battle fronts of the First World War
From the Latin word for cloud
From the name of a Norwegian ship
From the front side of a mountain range
58491.e: The Norwegian meteorologists compared the meeting of air masses with the front lines of the First World War. That is how the term caught on.
58491.m: The term front is a reminder of the battle lines of the First World War.

58492.q: What often forms at waves on the polar front?
58492.e: When the polar front is bent into a wave shape, the air begins to circle around the tip of the wave. This is how the travelling low-pressure systems of the middle latitudes form.
58492.m: The lows of the middle latitudes form on the polar front.

58493.q: In which range of latitudes does the polar front roughly lie?
58493.e: The polar front moves about a lot, but usually lies in the middle latitudes. It forms the boundary between the Ferrel cell and the polar cell.
58493.m: The polar front lies in the middle latitudes.

58494.q: Which clouds are often the first sign of an approaching warm front?
58494.e: At a warm front, warm air slides gently up over cold air. That is why high, wispy cirrus clouds appear first, well ahead of the front.
58494.m: High cirrus clouds are often the first messengers of a warm front.

58495.q: What weather is typical when a cold front passes?
a: Showers, thunderstorms and a sudden drop in temperature
58495.e: The cold air pushes under the warm air like a wedge and lifts it quickly. This forms heap clouds with showers, and afterwards it gets cooler.
58495.m: A cold front brings showers and cooler air.

a: The cold front catches up with the warm front
The warm front dissolves at altitude
58496.e: Cold fronts usually move faster than warm fronts. When the cold front catches up with the warm front, the warm air is lifted off the ground and an occlusion forms.
58496.m: In an occlusion, the cold front has caught up with the warm front.

58497.q: Where does the polar front shift in the northern hemisphere’s winter?
a: It stays exactly at the Arctic Circle
58497.e: In winter the Arctic cools down strongly and the cold air spreads out. As a result, the polar front and with it the tracks of the lows shift towards the equator.
58497.m: In winter the polar front moves south.

58498.q: Which language does the word “monsoon” originally come from?
58498.e: The word goes back to the Arabic “mausim”, which means season. Arab sailors used the winds that change with the seasons for trade.
58498.m: Monsoon comes from the Arabic word for season.

58499.q: What is the main cause of the monsoon?
a: Land and sea warm up differently
The Earth is thicker at the equator
Volcanoes in the Himalayas heat the air
58499.e: In summer, land warms up faster than the sea, and a heat low forms over the continent. In winter the land cools down more, and the wind direction reverses.
58499.m: Different warming of land and sea drives the monsoon.

58500.q: From which direction does the summer monsoon blow over India?
58500.e: In summer, moist air flows from the Indian Ocean to the heat low over Asia. After crossing the equator, the Earth’s rotation changes the deflection, so the wind over India comes from the south-west.
58500.m: In India the summer monsoon blows from the south-west.

58501.q: What is the winter monsoon like over most of India?
a: It brings snow down to the sea
58501.e: In winter, the north-east monsoon blows from the cool Asian continent towards the sea. The air comes from the land and therefore usually brings hardly any rain.
58501.m: In India the winter monsoon is usually dry.

58502.q: In which Indian state does the summer monsoon normally arrive first, around 1 June?
58502.e: The Indian weather service expects the monsoon to begin on the south-west coast in Kerala around 1 June. After that, the rain spreads over the whole country within a few weeks.
58502.m: The summer monsoon reaches India first in Kerala.

58503.q: In which region of Africa is there also a distinct monsoon system?
58503.e: In the northern summer, moist air flows from the Gulf of Guinea into West Africa and brings the rainy season. In winter, dry air blows from the Sahara, the harmattan.
58503.m: West Africa also has a monsoon with rain in summer.

58504.q: What role does the Tibetan Plateau play in the South Asian monsoon?
a: It heats up strongly and strengthens the heat low
It cools the monsoon air and stops it
It diverts the monsoon to Africa
58504.e: In summer, the high plateau heats the air at great height. This strengthens the low-pressure area over Asia and therefore the flow of moist sea air.
58504.m: The Tibetan Plateau strengthens the summer monsoon.

58505.q: Roughly what share of India’s annual rainfall falls during the summer monsoon from June to September?
58505.e: Most of India’s rain falls in the four monsoon months, about 75 per cent on average across the country. That is why farming depends heavily on the monsoon.
58505.m: India gets about three quarters of its rain in the summer monsoon.

58506.q: Which region of India gets much of its rain in autumn and winter from the north-east monsoon?
a: Tamil Nadu on the south-east coast
58506.e: The north-east monsoon picks up moisture over the Bay of Bengal. It rains out on the south-east coast in Tamil Nadu, which is why a lot of rain falls there from October to December.
58506.m: Tamil Nadu gets a lot of rain from the north-east monsoon.

58507.q: What is a stationary high called that forms the shape of a Greek letter in the high-altitude flow and blocks lows?
58507.e: In an omega pattern, the jet stream bends around a high so that it looks like the letter omega. Blocking highs like this can hold heat or drought in place for weeks.
58507.m: An omega block often blocks the track of the lows for a long time.

58508.q: What is the technical term for a high-pressure area?
58508.e: In technical language, a high is called an anticyclone. In the northern hemisphere, the air circles clockwise in it.
58508.m: A high-pressure area is also called an anticyclone.

58509.q: Which cold wind often blows in Switzerland when there is high air pressure to the north of Switzerland and low pressure over the Mediterranean?
58509.e: With this pressure pattern, cold, dry air flows from north-eastern Europe onto the Swiss Plateau. The bise there usually blows from the north-east to the east.
58509.m: A high to the north often brings the cold bise to Switzerland.

58510.q: What weather does a high often bring to the Swiss Plateau in winter?
58510.e: In a winter high, cold air collects in the lowlands beneath warmer air. In this inversion, high fog often forms for days, while it is sunny in the mountains.
58510.m: In a winter high, there is often high fog over the Swiss Plateau.

58511.q: Which powerful cold high forms over Central Asia in winter?
58511.e: In winter, the huge land mass of Asia cools down strongly, and the cold, heavy air creates a mighty high. It also drives the winter monsoon.
58511.m: In winter the Siberian High lies over Central Asia.

58512.q: What is a low called that often forms in the lee of the Alps over the Mediterranean and brings heavy rain to the southern side of the Alps?
58512.e: When cold air meets the Alps, a low often forms in the Gulf of Genoa. It carries moist Mediterranean air against the southern side of the Alps, for example into Ticino.
58512.m: A Genoa low often brings a lot of rain to Ticino.

58513.q: What is the technical term for a low-pressure area?
58513.e: The word cyclone comes from the Greek word for circle. It describes a vortex with low pressure at its centre.
58513.m: A low-pressure area is also called a cyclone.

58514.q: Why does a low-pressure area often bring clouds and rain?
a: The air rises and cools down
The air sinks and warms up
The sun shines more weakly there
The sea releases more salt there
58514.e: In a low, air flows together and has to rise. As it rises it cools down, water vapour condenses, and clouds and rain form.
58514.m: In a low, air rises, which is why clouds form.

58515.q: Which low over the North Atlantic often shapes the weather in Europe?
58515.e: The Icelandic Low is a low-pressure area that often occurs in the North Atlantic. Together with the Azores High it steers the westerlies towards Europe.
58515.m: The Icelandic Low often steers the weather in Europe.

58516.q: Why does the wind near the ground blow at an angle into a low instead of parallel to the isobars?
a: Friction with the ground slows the wind down
The Earth is warmer at the ground
The air is lighter at the ground
The Coriolis force is stronger at the ground
58516.e: At altitude, the wind blows almost parallel to the isobars. At the ground, friction slows the wind down, the deflection becomes weaker, and the air flows into the low at an angle.
58516.m: Friction with the ground makes the wind flow into a low at an angle.

58517.q: Why does a tropical cyclone usually weaken quickly over land?
a: It lacks a supply of warm, moist sea air
The Coriolis force does not work over land
The air pressure over land is too low
The sun is too weak over land
58517.e: Over land, the storm lacks a supply of warm, moist air from the sea. In addition, friction with the ground slows the winds down.
58517.m: Over land a cyclone loses its source of energy.

58518.q: What is a tropical cyclone in the north-western Pacific called?
58518.e: The names of tropical cyclones depend on the sea area. In the north-western Pacific, for example off Japan or the Philippines, they are called typhoons.
58518.m: In the north-western Pacific, tropical cyclones are called typhoons.

58519.q: What is a tropical cyclone in the northern Indian Ocean called?
58519.e: In the Bay of Bengal and the Arabian Sea, tropical storms are called cyclones. They often hit India, Bangladesh and Myanmar.
58519.m: In the Indian Ocean, tropical storms are called cyclones.

58520.q: Which organisation sets the lists of names for hurricanes in the Atlantic?
58520.e: The World Meteorological Organization (WMO) keeps lists of names that are reused regularly. The names of particularly destructive storms are removed.
58520.m: The WMO decides the names of Atlantic hurricanes.

58521.q: What is the weather like in the eye of a tropical cyclone?
a: Almost calm and often with few clouds
58521.e: In the centre, air sinks, which is why the eye is calm and often has few clouds. Around it is the eyewall with the strongest winds.
58521.m: In the eye of a cyclone it is almost calm.

58522.q: Where does a tropical cyclone get most of its energy from?
a: From the latent heat of evaporated seawater
From the jet stream at altitude
From the cold of the polar regions
58522.e: A lot of water evaporates over the warm sea. When the vapour condenses in the clouds, heat is released, which drives the storm.
58522.m: Evaporated warm seawater gives the cyclone its energy.

58523.q: In which direction do tropical cyclones turn in the southern hemisphere?
58523.e: Tropical cyclones are low-pressure vortices. Because the deflection works as a mirror image in the southern hemisphere, they turn the opposite way there from in the northern hemisphere.
58523.m: In the southern hemisphere, cyclones turn clockwise.

58524.q: When is the official hurricane season in the Atlantic?
58524.e: In these months the sea in the tropical Atlantic is warm enough. Most hurricanes occur from August to October.
58524.m: The Atlantic hurricane season lasts from June to November.

58525.q: Which danger from a tropical cyclone often claims the most lives on coasts?
58525.e: The storm pushes seawater against the coast and the water level rises sharply. This storm surge floods low-lying areas and is particularly dangerous.
58525.m: The storm surge is often the deadliest danger of a cyclone.

58526.q: Which climatologist developed the basis of today’s most widely used effective climate classification, later revised with Rudolf Geiger?
58526.e: Wladimir Köppen presented his climate classification around 1900 and refined it until 1936. Rudolf Geiger revised it in the 1950s and 1960s, hence the name Köppen-Geiger.
58526.m: The Köppen-Geiger climate classification is the best-known climate system in the world.

58527.q: In the Köppen-Geiger classification, which main letter stands for the dry climates?
58527.e: The main climates are called A (tropical), B (dry), C (warm temperate), D (boreal or snow climate) and E (polar). B is the only main group defined by the relationship between rainfall and temperature.
58527.m: In the Köppen-Geiger system, the letter B stands for the dry climates.

58528.q: Which condition must a climate meet to count as a tropical A climate in the Köppen-Geiger system?
a: The coldest month has an average of at least 18 °C.
The warmest month has an average of over 30 °C.
At least 2000 mm of rain falls each year.
The annual temperature range is less than 10 °C.
58528.e: For A climates, even the coldest month has an average temperature of at least 18 °C. This means there is no winter in terms of temperature.
58528.m: In A climates, even the coldest month averages at least 18 °C.

58529.q: What does the small letter “s” mean in a Köppen climate formula such as Csa?
58529.e: The second letter describes how the rain is spread over the year: f for wet all year, s for dry summer and w for dry winter. Cs therefore stands for a warm temperate climate with a dry summer.
58529.m: A small s in the Köppen formula means a dry summer.

58530.q: Which Köppen climate formula describes the climate of the Swiss Plateau, for example in Zurich?
58530.e: The Swiss Plateau has a warm temperate climate (C), is wet all year (f) and has warm but not hot summers (b). This gives Cfb.
58530.m: The Swiss Plateau has the warm temperate climate type Cfb, wet all year.

58531.q: Which type of climate is labelled BWh in the Köppen-Geiger system?
58531.e: B stands for dry, W for desert and h for hot. One example of BWh is the Sahara.
58531.m: The formula BWh stands for a hot desert climate like that of the Sahara.

58532.q: How does the ice cap climate EF differ from the tundra climate ET in the Köppen-Geiger system?
a: In EF, even the warmest month is below 0 °C.
In EF, more rain falls than in ET.
In EF, the summer is dry.
In EF, the coldest month is above 0 °C.
58532.e: In the ice cap climate (F for frost), no month reaches an average temperature above 0 °C. One example is the interior of Antarctica.
58532.m: In the ice cap climate EF, even the warmest month stays below freezing.

58533.q: In Köppen’s original version, which limit for the coldest month separates the C climates from the D climates?
58533.e: Köppen set the limit at an average temperature of -3 °C in the coldest month, because snow usually lies for a longer period then. Some newer versions use 0 °C instead.
58533.m: According to Köppen, the snow climate D begins when the coldest month is colder than -3 °C.

58534.q: Why is the Köppen-Geiger classification called an “effective” climate classification?
a: It sorts climates by measurable values and their effects, for example on vegetation.
It sorts climates by their causes, for example the distribution of air pressure.
It was created particularly quickly and cheaply.
It applies only to areas with farming.
58534.e: Effective classifications are based on temperature and rainfall and their effects; Köppen relied heavily on the boundaries of vegetation zones. Genetic classifications, by contrast, start from the causes, such as atmospheric circulation.
58534.m: An effective climate classification sorts climates by their effects, not by their causes.

58535.q: What does the small letter “f” mean in the Köppen formula Af?
a: The summer is wet, the winter dry.
58535.e: The f stands for wet all year, in other words without a distinct dry season. Af is the tropical rainforest climate.
58535.m: The code Af stands for the tropical rainforest climate that is always wet.

58536.q: In a Walter and Lieth climate diagram, in what ratio are temperature and rainfall scaled?
58536.e: The rainfall axis is labelled with values twice as large as the temperature axis. This ratio of 1 to 2 makes it possible to read off arid and humid months directly.
58536.m: In a Walter and Lieth climate diagram, 10 °C corresponds exactly to 20 mm of rainfall.

58537.q: In a Walter and Lieth climate diagram, how can you recognise an arid month?
a: The temperature curve lies above the rainfall curve.
The rainfall curve lies above the temperature curve.
The rainfall is more than 100 mm.
58537.e: If the temperature curve lies above the rainfall curve, more water evaporates than falls. This area is usually shown dotted or in yellow.
58537.m: When the temperature curve lies above the rainfall curve, the month is arid.

58538.q: A month has an average temperature of 15 °C and 25 mm of rainfall. How is it classified according to Walter and Lieth?
58538.e: According to the ratio of 1 to 2, the month would need at least 2 × 15 = 30 mm of rainfall to be humid. With 25 mm it is below that and is therefore arid.
58538.m: A month is humid if the rainfall in mm is more than twice the temperature in °C.

58539.q: In a Walter and Lieth climate diagram, how is rainfall above 100 mm per month shown?
a: Reduced to a scale of 1 to 10 and filled in black
On the same scale and dotted in yellow
As a dashed line below the axis
Not at all, it is cut off
58539.e: So that very wet months do not burst the diagram, the part above 100 mm is reduced to a tenth. This perhumid area is filled in black.
58539.m: Rainfall above 100 mm appears in the Walter-Lieth diagram reduced in scale as a black area.

58540.q: With which month does the time axis of a Walter and Lieth climate diagram begin for a station in the southern hemisphere?
58540.e: In the southern hemisphere, the diagram begins with July, so that summer lies in the middle, just as for stations in the northern hemisphere. This allows diagrams from both hemispheres to be compared directly.
58540.m: According to Walter and Lieth, climate diagrams for southern hemisphere stations begin with July.

58541.q: How is a humid period typically marked in a Walter and Lieth climate diagram?
58541.e: The area between the higher rainfall curve and the temperature curve is hatched with vertical lines, often in blue. The arid period, by contrast, is dotted.
58541.m: Humid periods are hatched vertically in the Walter-Lieth diagram.

58542.q: What information is usually given at the top of a Walter and Lieth climate diagram?
a: Station, altitude above sea level, mean annual temperature and annual rainfall
Station, population, area and capital city
Station, wind direction, air pressure and hours of sunshine
Station, soil type, vegetation and land use
58542.e: The top shows the name and altitude of the station as well as the mean annual temperature and the total annual rainfall. Sometimes the number of years of measurements is also given.
58542.m: The top of a climate diagram shows the station, altitude, mean annual temperature and annual rainfall.

58543.q: A month has an average temperature of 20 °C. From how many millimetres of rainfall does it count as humid according to Walter and Lieth?
58543.e: According to the ratio of 1 to 2, the limit is 2 × 20 = 40 mm. Only above that does the rainfall curve lie above the temperature curve.
58543.m: In a climate diagram, the boundary between arid and humid lies at twice the temperature value in millimetres.

58544.q: When is a climate described as arid?
a: When potential evaporation is greater than rainfall
When rainfall is greater than potential evaporation
When almost all precipitation falls as snow
When the temperature never falls below 0 °C
58544.e: In arid areas, more water could evaporate than falls as rain. The ground therefore dries out, and rivers often carry water only some of the time.
58544.m: An arid climate is one in which potential evaporation is greater than rainfall.

58545.q: Which geographer distinguished the climate types humid, arid and nival around 1910?
58545.e: Albrecht Penck classified climates according to what happens to the precipitation. In a nival climate it falls as snow and is carried away mainly by glaciers.
58545.m: Albrecht Penck divided climates into humid, arid and nival.

58546.q: De Martonne’s aridity index compares annual rainfall with annual temperature. What does a low value indicate?
58546.e: In de Martonne’s index, the annual rainfall is divided by the mean annual temperature plus 10. Little rainfall and high temperatures give a low value, in other words a dry climate.
58546.m: In de Martonne’s index, a low value means a dry climate.

58547.q: A station has 600 mm of annual rainfall and a mean annual temperature of 10 °C. What is its de Martonne aridity index?
58547.e: The calculation is 600 / (10 + 10) = 600 / 20 = 30. According to common classifications, this value lies at the border with the humid range; below 10 a climate counts as arid.
58547.m: De Martonne’s index is calculated as rainfall divided by temperature plus ten.

58548.q: An area receives as rainfall only a small fraction of the water that could evaporate there. What is such an extremely dry area called?
58548.e: According to the UNEP classification, an area is hyperarid if rainfall is less than a twentieth of potential evaporation. Semi-arid areas are less dry, humid areas are wet.
58548.m: An area is hyperarid if less than a twentieth of potential evaporation falls as rain.

58549.q: What do you call a river like the Nile that comes from a humid area and flows through an arid area without receiving any significant tributaries there?
58549.e: An exotic river gets its water from areas with plenty of rain and loses water in the desert through evaporation and seepage. The Nile gets its water mainly from East Africa and the Ethiopian Highlands.
58549.m: An exotic river carries water from wet areas through a desert.

a: A dry valley that carries water only after rare rainfall
A salt lake with no outlet
58550.e: Wadis are typical valleys of arid areas, through which water flows only occasionally after heavy rain. Dangerous flash floods can suddenly occur.
58550.m: A wadi is a dry valley that carries water only briefly after rain.

58551.q: Why is there a risk of soils becoming salty in arid areas when they are irrigated without enough drainage?
a: The water evaporates and the dissolved salts stay behind in the soil.
Rain washes salt from the air into the soil.
The plants release salt through their roots.
58551.e: Because of the high evaporation, soil water rises through capillary action and evaporates at the surface. The salts build up there because hardly any rain washes them out again.
58551.m: In dry areas, salts stay behind in the soil when water evaporates and can make it salty.

58552.q: What does the Latin word “humidus”, from which the term humid comes, mean?
58552.e: Humidus means wet or damp, while aridus means dry. In humid areas more rain falls than can evaporate, which is why rivers there flow all the time.
58552.m: The word humid comes from the Latin humidus and means wet.

58553.q: Why is the annual temperature range smaller near the coast than in the interior of a continent?
a: Water has a high heat capacity and warms up more slowly than land.
The sun shines for less time over the sea.
Coasts are always closer to the equator.
Seawater contains salt, which produces heat.
58553.e: Water stores a lot of heat and releases it slowly, and the heat is also spread into the depths by mixing. In this way the sea softens summer heat and winter cold on the coasts.
58553.m: The sea evens out temperatures because water stores heat well.

58554.q: Which city is a typical example of an extremely continental climate?
58554.e: Yakutsk in eastern Siberia has very cold winters with monthly averages of around -40 °C and warm summers. Its annual temperature range is one of the largest of any city in the world.
58554.m: In the interior of large continents, such as eastern Siberia, the climate is extremely continental.

58555.q: Which features are typical of a maritime climate?
a: Cool summers, mild winters and high humidity
Hot summers, very cold winters and dry air
A long dry season in summer and frost in winter
58555.e: The sea slows down warming in summer and cooling in winter. Frequent cloud and rain are also typical.
58555.m: In a maritime climate, summers are cool and winters mild.

58556.q: How does the climate in Europe typically change as you travel east from Ireland to the Urals?
a: It becomes more and more continental, and the annual range increases.
It becomes more and more maritime, and winters get milder.
It stays the same, because the latitude stays the same.
58556.e: The prevailing westerlies bring sea air from the Atlantic, whose influence decreases towards the east. That is why the winters become colder and the summers warmer.
58556.m: In Europe, continentality increases from west to east.

58557.q: Why is the warmest month in many very maritime coastal places not July but August?
a: The sea warms up slowly and reaches its highest temperature later.
The sun is highest in August.
In August there are more clouds that store heat.
The Earth is closest to the sun in August.
58557.e: Because water stores so much heat, the sea temperature lags behind the position of the sun. This delay carries over to the air temperature on the coast.
58557.m: In a maritime climate, the slow-to-warm sea delays the temperature peak.

58558.q: Why do west coasts in the middle latitudes usually have a more maritime climate than east coasts at the same latitude?
a: The prevailing westerly winds blow from the sea onto the land there.
There are no ocean currents on west coasts.
West coasts are always lower than east coasts.
The sun shines for longer on east coasts.
58558.e: In the middle latitudes, westerly winds dominate and bring moist, mild sea air onto the west coasts. On east coasts, by contrast, the air usually comes from the continent.
58558.m: In the westerly wind zone, west coasts are more strongly shaped by the sea than east coasts.

58559.q: Why does Valais have a drier and more continental climate than the Swiss Plateau?
a: High mountains shield it from moist air masses.
It is closer to the Mediterranean.
It lies higher than all the Alpine peaks.
It is warmed directly by the Gulf Stream.
58559.e: The Rhône valley lies in the rain shadow of the Bernese and Valais Alps, which make moist air rain out before it reaches the valley. That is why central Valais is one of the driest areas of Switzerland.
58559.m: Valais is dry because it lies in the rain shadow of high mountains.

58560.q: How does the daily temperature range in a continental climate differ from that in a maritime climate?
a: It is larger in a continental climate.
It is smaller in a continental climate.
It is exactly the same in both climates.
There is no daily range in a continental climate.
58560.e: Dry air and little cloud let the ground heat up strongly during the day and cool down strongly at night. Over the sea, water and moisture have an evening-out effect.
58560.m: In a continental climate, temperatures also vary greatly over the course of the day.

58561.q: How is Switzerland usually classified in terms of climate?
a: In a transition zone between maritime and continental climate
58561.e: Switzerland lies in the westerly wind zone and receives Atlantic sea air, but is also exposed to continental influences from the east. In addition, the Alps strongly shape the climate.
58561.m: Switzerland’s climate lies in the transition between maritime and continental climate.

58562.q: Which pattern of rainfall is typical of the Mediterranean climate?
a: Dry, hot summers and wet, mild winters
58562.e: Hardly any rain falls in summer; the rainfall is concentrated in the winter half of the year. In the Köppen-Geiger system, this climate belongs to type Cs.
58562.m: In the Mediterranean climate it rains mainly in winter.

58563.q: What causes the summer drought in the Mediterranean region?
a: The subtropical high-pressure area shifts towards the poles in summer.
The westerly wind zone shifts towards the equator in summer.
The Gulf Stream cools the Mediterranean in summer.
The Intertropical Convergence Zone lies over Italy in summer.
58563.e: In summer the region is under the influence of the subtropical high, such as the Azores High, which brings sinking, dry air. In winter the high moves south, and low-pressure areas of the westerlies bring rain.
58563.m: The subtropical high brings dry summers to the Mediterranean region.

58564.q: Which region does NOT have a Mediterranean climate?
a: The Cape region of South Africa
58564.e: Mediterranean climates are found on the western sides of continents at about 30 to 45 degrees latitude, for example in California, central Chile, the Cape region and south-western Australia. Florida lies on an east coast and has wet summers.
58564.m: Mediterranean climates exist on every continent except Antarctica, on the western sides of the subtropics.

58565.q: Which type of vegetation is particularly well adapted to the Mediterranean climate?
58565.e: Sclerophyll plants such as the holm oak or the olive tree have small, leathery leaves with a thick waxy layer. This means they lose little water in the dry summer.
58565.m: Sclerophyll plants protect themselves from drying out in summer with leathery leaves.

58566.q: Why does Ticino, despite its palm trees and mild climate, NOT have a Mediterranean climate according to Köppen-Geiger?
a: Because a lot of rain also falls in summer
Because it is too warm in winter
Because it is not by the sea
Because olive trees cannot grow there
58566.e: The climate on the southern side of the Alps is called Insubric and is sunny and mild, but has frequent heavy thunderstorms, especially in summer. It therefore lacks the summer drought needed for a Mediterranean climate.
58566.m: Ticino also gets a lot of rain in summer, so it does not count as a Mediterranean climate.

58567.q: Which city has a typical Mediterranean climate?
58567.e: Rome has hot, dry summers and mild, wet winters. London has rain all year, Moscow cold winters and Mumbai rain mainly during the summer monsoon.
58567.m: Rome is an example of a Mediterranean climate.

58569.q: In the northern hemisphere, which July isotherm roughly coincides with the polar tree line?
58569.e: Trees need a growing season that is long and warm enough. Where the average of the warmest month falls below about 10 °C, the treeless tundra begins.
58569.m: The polar tree line roughly follows the 10-degree isotherm of the warmest month.

58570.q: Which plants shape the vegetation in the tundra climate?
58570.e: The short, cool growing season and the frozen ground allow only low plants to grow. Dwarf shrubs such as the dwarf birch stay close to the ground, where it is warmer and more sheltered from the wind.
58570.m: In the tundra, mainly mosses, lichens and dwarf shrubs grow.

58574.q: Where in Switzerland can you find conditions similar to the tundra?
a: In the Alps above the tree line
On the Swiss Plateau by lake shores
In the valleys of the Jura
58574.e: Above the tree line, at about 1800 to 2400 m depending on the region, it is too cold for trees. Alpine grassland, dwarf shrubs, mosses and lichens grow there, and it is also called alpine tundra.
58574.m: Above the tree line in the Alps, conditions are similar to the tundra.

58575.q: Through which language did the word “tundra” come into English?
58575.e: English took the word from the Russian “тундра”. This probably comes from Finnish (tunturi) or Sami and describes a treeless upland.
58575.m: The word tundra came into English through Russian.

58576.q: Why does the tundra climate usually not count as arid, despite its low rainfall?
a: Evaporation is very low because of the low temperatures.
Over 2000 mm of rain falls there every year.
The sea constantly supplies water through high tides.
The wind brings lots of water from the tropics.
58576.e: Cold air can hold little water, and the sun provides little energy for evaporation. That is why even a little rainfall is enough for the climate to be humid.
58576.m: In the tundra so little water evaporates that even low rainfall is enough.

58577.q: What characterises the tropical wet and dry climate?
a: The change between rainy and dry seasons with high temperatures all year
The change between hot summers and icy winters
The daily change between rain and sunshine without seasons
The change between monsoon and snowfall
58577.e: Temperatures stay high all year, and the seasons are defined by rainfall. In the Köppen-Geiger system, this corresponds mainly to the savanna climate Aw.
58577.m: In the tropical wet and dry climate, rainy and dry seasons alternate.

58578.q: What causes the rainy season in the tropical wet and dry climate?
a: The Intertropical Convergence Zone moves with the overhead sun.
Cold ocean currents bring moist air.
Low-pressure areas from the westerly wind zone pass over the tropics.
The Earth is closest to the sun then.
58578.e: The Intertropical Convergence Zone follows the overhead sun with a delay. Where it lies, warm, moist air rises and brings heavy zenithal rains.
58578.m: The rainy season comes with the Intertropical Convergence Zone, which follows the highest position of the sun.

58579.q: Which vegetation zone is typical of the tropical wet and dry climate?
58579.e: In the savanna, grassland alternates with single trees or groups of trees. The plants are adapted to the yearly dry season.
58579.m: The typical vegetation of the tropical wet and dry climate is the savanna.

58580.q: How does the number of rainy seasons in the tropical wet and dry climate change with increasing distance from the equator?
a: The number always stays at two.
There is then no dry season at all.
58580.e: Near the equator, the sun is directly overhead twice a year, which can bring two rainy seasons. Towards the tropics, the two dates move closer together and only one rainy season is left.
58580.m: Towards the tropics, the two rainy seasons merge into one.

58581.q: Which type of savanna has the fewest humid months a year?
58581.e: The wet savanna has the most humid months, followed by the dry savanna and the thorn savanna. As the number of humid months decreases, the vegetation becomes sparser and thornier.
58581.m: The fewer humid months there are, the drier and sparser the savanna.

58582.q: Which city has a tropical wet and dry climate (Köppen Aw)?
58582.e: Brasília has a rainy season from about October to April and a distinct dry season in the southern winter. Singapore is wet all year, and Cairo and Lima have desert climates.
58582.m: Brasília has a tropical wet and dry climate with one rainy and one dry season.

58583.q: When is it often hottest in the tropical wet and dry climate?
a: Shortly before the rainy season begins
In the middle of the rainy season
At the end of the rainy season
In the middle of the cooler dry season
58583.e: Before the rainy season, the sun is already high, but the sky still has few clouds. When the rainy season begins, clouds and rain cool the air a little.
58583.m: In the tropical wet and dry climate, it is hottest shortly before the rainy season.

58584.q: In which season is the dry season in Köppen type Aw?
a: In the winter half of the year, when the sun is low
In the summer half of the year, when the sun is high
58584.e: The w in Aw stands for dry winter. When the sun is low, the Intertropical Convergence Zone lies in the other hemisphere, and trade winds bring dry air.
58584.m: In climate type Aw, the dry season falls in winter.

58585.q: Which naturalist, after whom the Humboldt Current is named, measured the water temperature off the coast of Peru around 1802?
58585.e: On his journey through the Americas, the naturalist Alexander von Humboldt studied the cold coastal water off Peru. The current is also called the Peru Current.
58585.m: The Humboldt Current bears the name of the naturalist Alexander von Humboldt.

58586.q: Which desert owes its extreme dryness partly to the Humboldt Current?
58586.e: The cold water cools the lowest layer of air, which creates stable layering so that hardly any rain clouds rise. The Atacama in Chile is one of the driest deserts on Earth.
58586.m: Cold ocean currents can cause very dry deserts on coasts.

58587.q: Why is it often grey and foggy in Lima in winter, but almost without rain?
a: Fog forms under an inversion over the cold Humboldt Current
The Andes hold all the rain clouds over the city
Smoke from volcanoes blocks the sun
The monsoon brings moist air from Asia
58587.e: The cold water cools the lowest layer of air. Above it lies warmer air, which stops the air from rising. This creates the coastal fog called garúa, with fine drizzle but hardly any measurable rainfall.
58587.m: The cold Humboldt Current brings Lima fog instead of rain.

58588.q: Which kind of fish is caught in particularly large quantities in the Humboldt Current off Peru?
58588.e: The nutrient-rich water feeds huge shoals of anchoveta. It is mainly processed into fishmeal and fish oil.
58588.m: Huge amounts of anchovies are caught in the Humboldt Current off Peru.

58589.q: Which raw material was mined in large quantities on the coast of Peru in the 19th century and is linked to the abundance of fish in the Humboldt Current?
58589.e: Guano consists of the droppings of seabirds that feed on the shoals of fish. In the dry climate it is hardly washed away and was very valuable as fertiliser.
58589.m: Guano is seabird droppings that were mined as a valuable fertiliser.

58590.q: Why can penguins live on the Galápagos Islands at the equator?
a: Cold water, partly from the Humboldt Current, reaches the islands.
The islands lie very high above sea level.
It snows on the islands every winter.
58590.e: Branches of the Humboldt Current and cold upwelling water keep the sea around the islands relatively cool and rich in nutrients. The Galápagos penguin is the only kind of penguin that also lives north of the equator.
58590.m: Cold water even allows penguins to live at the equator on the Galápagos Islands.

58591.q: What do the islands of plants on the coastal slopes of the desert in Peru and Chile live on?
a: The moisture of the coastal fog
58591.e: Fog forms over the cold Humboldt Current and clings to the coastal slopes. The plants of these fog oases, called lomas, take moisture directly from the fog.
58591.m: The lomas are fog oases on the desert coast of Peru and Chile.

58592.q: In which direction does the Humboldt Current flow along the coast of South America?
a: In a circle around the Galápagos Islands
58592.e: The Humboldt Current is part of the South Pacific gyre and carries cold water from higher latitudes towards the equator. Off Ecuador it turns west.
58592.m: The Humboldt Current carries cold water north towards the equator.

58593.q: Which Russian port north of the Arctic Circle stays free of ice all year thanks to branches of the North Atlantic Current?
58593.e: Murmansk lies on the Barents Sea, which is reached by branches of warm Atlantic water. Arkhangelsk and St Petersburg, by contrast, freeze over in winter.
58593.m: Warm Atlantic water keeps the port of Murmansk free of ice all year.

58594.q: Which Spanish explorer was one of the first to describe the Gulf Stream off Florida in 1513?
58594.e: Off Florida, Juan Ponce de León noticed that his ships were being pushed backwards despite a favourable wind. The current was later used for return journeys to Europe.
58594.m: Juan Ponce de León described the Gulf Stream off Florida in 1513.

58595.q: How much water does the Gulf Stream carry compared with all the rivers on Earth put together?
58595.e: The Gulf Stream carries tens of millions of cubic metres of water per second. All the rivers on Earth together bring only just over a million cubic metres per second into the sea.
58595.m: The Gulf Stream carries much more water than all the rivers on Earth together.

58596.q: Which ocean current in the Pacific is considered the counterpart to the Gulf Stream, because it carries warm water north along the western edge of the ocean?
58596.e: The Kuroshio flows north off Japan and brings warm water from the tropics. Like the Gulf Stream, it is a narrow, fast current on the western edge of an ocean.
58596.m: The Kuroshio is the Pacific counterpart to the Gulf Stream.

58597.q: Why is the climate in Bergen (Norway) much milder than on the coast of Labrador at a similar latitude?
a: Bergen is reached by warm Atlantic water, Labrador by a cold current.
Bergen lies much lower above sea level.
Labrador has more hours of sunshine.
There are no westerly winds in Bergen.
58597.e: Off Labrador, the cold Labrador Current flows south, while Norway is warmed by the North Atlantic Current. In addition, westerly winds in Europe blow from the sea, while in Labrador they blow from the cold continent.
58597.m: Ocean currents and westerly winds make north-western Europe warmer than north-eastern America.

58598.q: What happens to the water of the North Atlantic Current in the Greenland Sea and the Labrador Sea?
a: It cools down, becomes denser and sinks into the depths.
58598.e: In the north, the salty water gives off a lot of heat, becomes heavy and sinks. This forms North Atlantic Deep Water, which drives the overturning circulation in the Atlantic.
58598.m: In the North Atlantic, cooled, salty water sinks into the depths and drives the overturning circulation.

58599.q: What is the whole current system in the Atlantic called, to which the Gulf Stream belongs and which carries heat northwards?
58599.e: The AMOC carries warm water north near the surface and cold water south in the depths. Researchers are investigating whether it is weakening because of climate change.
58599.m: The Gulf Stream is part of the great overturning circulation in the Atlantic.

58600.q: What is the typical effect of a strong El Niño on the coast of Peru and Ecuador?
a: Heavy rain and floods in areas that are usually dry
58600.e: The warm water off the coast makes moist air rise, so that it can rain heavily in the coastal deserts. At the same time there is often drought in Indonesia and Australia.
58600.m: El Niño often brings heavy rain to Peru’s coastal deserts.

58601.q: What characterises La Niña in the tropical Pacific?
a: Stronger trade winds and unusually cold water in the eastern Pacific
Weak trade winds and warm water off Peru
A failure of the monsoon in Africa
58601.e: La Niña is the cold opposite phase to El Niño. Strong trade winds drive warm water westwards, and more cold deep water rises off South America.
58601.m: La Niña is the cold opposite phase of El Niño, with strong trade winds.

58602.q: Between which two measuring stations is the air pressure difference for the Southern Oscillation Index (SOI) traditionally calculated?
58602.e: The Southern Oscillation is a see-saw of air pressure between the eastern Pacific and the Indonesian-Australian region. A clearly negative SOI points to El Niño.
58602.m: The Southern Oscillation Index compares the air pressure in Tahiti and Darwin.

58603.q: Roughly how often do El Niño events occur?
58603.e: El Niño does not follow a fixed rhythm but occurs irregularly at intervals of about 2 to 7 years. In between there are neutral years and La Niña phases.
58603.m: El Niño comes irregularly, about every two to seven years.

58604.q: What is the west-east air circulation over the tropical Pacific called, which weakens during an El Niño?
58604.e: In normal years, warm air rises over Indonesia, flows east at altitude and sinks over the cool eastern Pacific. During El Niño, the rising air moves east and the circulation becomes weaker.
58604.m: The Walker circulation links the western and eastern Pacific and weakens during El Niño.

58605.q: Which sea area is often used as the main measuring area to identify El Niño and La Niña events from the water temperature?
a: The Niño 3.4 region in the central equatorial Pacific
58605.e: The US weather agency NOAA speaks of El Niño conditions when the temperature in the Niño 3.4 region stays at least 0.5 °C above average. If it is at least 0.5 °C below, it is called La Niña.
58605.m: El Niño is measured mainly by the water temperature in the central equatorial Pacific.

58606.q: How do strong El Niño years affect the global average temperature?
a: They lower it sharply for decades.
They have no influence at all.
They make it fall only in the southern hemisphere.
58606.e: During El Niño, the Pacific releases a lot of heat into the atmosphere. That is why 1998 and 2016, which followed strong El Niños, were each among the warmest years measured up to then.
58606.m: A strong El Niño makes the Earth temporarily warmer.

58607.q: What is meant by upwelling water in the sea?
a: Cold, nutrient-rich deep water that rises to the surface
Warm surface water that sinks into the depths
Fresh water that flows from rivers into the sea
Water that is pushed onto land at high tide
58607.e: In upwelling, water from the depths replaces surface water that has been driven away. It is cold and rich in nutrients such as nitrate and phosphate.
58607.m: Upwelling water is cold, nutrient-rich water from the depths.

58608.q: Which process leads to upwelling on coasts such as those of Peru or Namibia?
a: Offshore Ekman transport pushes the surface water away from the coast.
Tides push water down into the depths.
Undersea volcanoes heat the deep water.
58608.e: Wind blowing parallel to the coast moves the surface water away from the land at an angle to the wind direction because of the Coriolis force. Cold water flows up from below to replace it.
58608.m: When the wind drives surface water away from the coast, deep water rises.

58609.q: In the northern hemisphere, in which direction relative to the wind is the water near the surface moved on average by Ekman transport?
a: Exactly in the direction of the wind
58609.e: Because of the Coriolis force, water movement in the northern hemisphere is deflected to the right. Averaged over the whole moving layer, this gives a transport at 90 degrees to the wind direction.
58609.m: In the northern hemisphere, Ekman transport deflects the water to the right.

58610.q: Off which country is the upwelling area of the Benguela Current?
58610.e: The cold Benguela Current flows north off the south-west coast of Africa. Strong coastal upwelling makes the waters off Namibia very rich in fish.
58610.m: Off Namibia, cold water rises in the Benguela Current.

58611.q: Which coastal desert is closely linked to the upwelling of cold water in the Benguela Current?
58611.e: The cold water cools the air from below, prevents rain clouds and often creates coastal fog. Some beetles in the Namib collect water from this fog.
58611.m: The Namib is a fog desert above cold upwelling water.

58612.q: Why are upwelling areas particularly rich in fish?
a: The nutrients help phytoplankton, the basis of the food chain, to grow.
The warm water attracts tropical fish.
There are no predatory fish there.
The water contains a particularly large amount of salt.
58612.e: Nutrients such as nitrate and phosphate from the depths make phytoplankton grow strongly. Zooplankton feeds on it, and large shoals of fish in turn feed on the zooplankton.
58612.m: Upwelling areas are fertile because nutrients make the plankton grow.

58613.q: Why does upwelling also occur along the equator in the Pacific?
a: Ekman transport deflects the water towards the poles on both sides of the equator.
The Coriolis force is strongest at the equator.
There are no winds at the equator.
Most rivers flow into the sea at the equator.
58613.e: The trade winds blow west there, and the water is deflected north on the northern side and south on the southern side. The surface water spreads apart, and cold water rises in between.
58613.m: At the equator the surface water moves away to both sides, so deep water rises.

58614.q: What is the opposite process to upwelling, in which surface water sinks into the depths, called?
58614.e: In downwelling, surface water is pushed together against a coast or in a convergence zone and sinks. Such areas are usually poor in nutrients.
58614.m: In downwelling, surface water sinks into the depths.

58615.q: Which ocean current with strong upwelling lies off the north-west coast of Africa?
58615.e: The cold Canary Current flows south off Morocco, Western Sahara and Mauritania. The coastal upwelling there contributes to rich fishing grounds.
58615.m: Off north-west Africa, the Canary Current causes strong upwelling.

58616.q: Why do fish catches off Peru often collapse during an El Niño?
a: Warm surface water suppresses the upwelling of nutrient-rich deep water.
The sea freezes over at the coast.
Storms stop boats from going out for months.
The fish migrate into the rivers.
58616.e: A thick layer of warm water lies above the cold deep water, so hardly any nutrients reach the surface. The plankton decreases, and the shoals of anchovies decline.
58616.m: During El Niño, the nutrients from the depths are missing off Peru.

58617.q: Which light conditions shape the tundra climate north of the Arctic Circle?
a: Polar day in summer and polar night in winter
Twelve hours of day and night all year
Polar night in summer and polar day in winter
58617.e: North of the Arctic Circle, the sun does not set for a time in summer and does not rise for a time in winter. Despite constant light, the summer stays cool because the sun is low in the sky.
58617.m: North of the Arctic Circle there is polar day in summer and polar night in winter.

58618.q: What do you call an area with no outflow to the sea, whose rivers end in inland lakes or salt pans?
58618.e: In arid areas, the water evaporates before it reaches the sea, and the rivers end in basins. Examples are the Caspian Sea or the Dead Sea.
58618.m: Endorheic areas have no outflow to the sea.

58619.q: In a Walter and Lieth climate diagram, what does the area drawn in black below the month axis stand for?
a: Months with an average daily minimum below 0 °C
Months with over 100 mm of rainfall
58619.e: Bars below the axis show frost conditions: black for months with regular frost, diagonally hatched for months with possible frost. This shows the frost-free period for farming.
58619.m: Below the month axis, the Walter-Lieth diagram shows the frost months.

58620.q: What delay does the zenithal rain show compared with the highest position of the sun?
a: It usually starts a few weeks after the sun is overhead.
It always falls exactly on the day the sun is overhead.
It always falls a few weeks before the sun is overhead.
It falls exactly half a year later.
58620.e: The warming of ground and air and the shift of the convergence zone take time. That is why the heaviest rains follow the overhead sun by a few weeks.
58620.m: Zenithal rains follow the highest position of the sun with a delay.

58621.q: From which sea area does the Gulf Stream get much of its warm water?
a: From the Gulf of Mexico and the Caribbean
58621.e: The trade wind drives warm water into the Caribbean and the Gulf of Mexico. It flows out through the Straits of Florida as the Florida Current and feeds the Gulf Stream.
58621.m: The Gulf Stream brings warm water from the Gulf of Mexico into the Atlantic.

58622.q: On which side of the continents do areas with a Mediterranean climate typically lie?
a: On the western side in the subtropics
On the eastern side in the tropics
In the centre of the continents
On the northern side in the polar regions
58622.e: The western sides lie under the subtropical high in summer and under the influence of the westerlies in winter. This combination results in winter rain and summer drought.
58622.m: Mediterranean climates lie on the subtropical western sides of the continents.

58623.q: Which quantity are continentality indices mainly based on?
58623.e: Continentality indices, for example Gorczyński’s, are based mainly on the difference between the warmest and the coldest month and take the latitude into account. High values mean a continental climate.
58623.m: The larger the annual range, the more continental the climate.

58624.q: Why is the seawater in the Humboldt Current off Peru colder than its position in the tropics would suggest?
a: Cold water from the south and rising deep water cool it.
Andean glaciers calve directly into the sea.
58624.e: The current brings water from higher southern latitudes, and in addition cold deep water rises off the coast. This means water temperatures off Lima are often well below 20 °C.
58624.m: The Humboldt Current is cold because its water comes from the south and from the depths.

58625.q: Which Köppen-Geiger climate group hardly occurs at all in the southern hemisphere outside mountains, because large land masses are missing at the right latitudes?
58625.e: D climates need large continents in middle to high latitudes, where severe cold develops in winter. In the southern hemisphere, there is almost only sea at these latitudes.
58625.m: Boreal D climates exist almost only in the northern hemisphere.

58626.q: Roughly what average surface temperature would the Earth have without the natural greenhouse effect?
58626.e: Without greenhouse gases, the Earth would hold only enough heat to reach about -18 °C. In fact the global average is about +15 °C, which is about 33 degrees higher.
58626.m: The natural greenhouse effect is what makes the Earth habitable.

58627.q: Since when has the warming effect of the atmosphere, today’s greenhouse effect, been described scientifically?
58627.e: As early as 1824, the Frenchman Joseph Fourier realised that the Earth would be much colder without an atmosphere. Later, researchers such as John Tyndall and Svante Arrhenius demonstrated the effect of CO2 and water vapour.
58627.m: The greenhouse effect has been known for almost 200 years.

58628.q: Which radiation do greenhouse gases mainly absorb?
58628.e: The Earth’s surface gives off energy as long-wave infrared radiation. Greenhouse gases absorb this radiation and send some of it back to the Earth.
58628.m: Greenhouse gases hold back the Earth’s heat radiation.

58629.q: Why are nitrogen (N2) and oxygen (O2) not greenhouse gases, even though they make up most of the air?
a: They hardly absorb any heat radiation
They only occur at great heights
They dissolve straight away in seawater
They are heavier than carbon dioxide
58629.e: Greenhouse gases such as CO2 and water vapour absorb the Earth’s heat radiation. The simple molecules N2 and O2, on the other hand, let this radiation through almost unhindered.
58629.m: Only gases that absorb heat radiation act as greenhouse gases.

58630.q: Which Swedish chemist was the first to calculate, in 1896, how much a change in CO2 content changes the Earth’s temperature?
58630.e: In 1896 Svante Arrhenius estimated how the temperature changes with more or less CO2 in the air. He later received the Nobel Prize in Chemistry, but for other work.
58630.m: In 1896 Svante Arrhenius laid the foundation for climate sensitivity.

58631.q: Which gases were shown in the laboratory in the 19th century to be important absorbers of heat radiation?
58631.e: From 1859 the physicist John Tyndall used an apparatus of his own to show that trace gases in particular, such as water vapour and CO2, strongly absorb heat radiation. The main gases of the air hardly do this.
58631.m: Water vapour and CO2 hold back heat radiation.

58632.q: Calculated over 100 years, how strong is the effect of methane compared with the same mass of CO2 (global warming potential)?
58632.e: The IPCC gives methane a global warming potential of about 28 to 30 over 100 years. Methane is very powerful but is broken down in the atmosphere after about twelve years.
58632.m: Methane is a short-lived but very powerful greenhouse gas.

58633.q: Which greenhouse gas contributes most to human-caused warming worldwide?
58633.e: Per kilogram, methane, nitrous oxide or sulphur hexafluoride are more powerful. But because huge amounts of CO2 are released from coal, oil and natural gas, CO2 causes most of the warming.
58633.m: Because of its large quantity, CO2 is the most important human-made greenhouse gas.

58634.q: For every degree of warming, the air can hold about 7 per cent more water vapour. What is the resulting amplification called?
58634.e: Warmer air holds more water vapour, and this water vapour strengthens the greenhouse effect further. This positive feedback roughly doubles the warming caused by CO2 alone.
58634.m: Water vapour feedback amplifies any warming.

58635.q: On which volcano is the famous series of measurements known as the Keeling Curve recorded?
a: Mount St. Helens in the USA
58635.e: The measuring station is at about 3400 m on Mauna Loa, far away from large sources of emissions. The air there is well mixed and representative of the northern hemisphere.
58635.m: The Keeling Curve comes from Mauna Loa in Hawaii.

58636.q: In which year did the continuous CO2 measurements of the Keeling Curve begin?
58636.e: Charles David Keeling started the measurements in 1958. Since then it has been the longest unbroken series of direct measurements of the CO2 content of the air.
58636.m: The Keeling Curve has run without a break since 1958.

58637.q: Why does the Keeling Curve show a regular rise and fall every year?
a: Plants in the northern hemisphere grow and decay
Heating is used in winter in the southern hemisphere
The volcanoes in Hawaii are only active in certain seasons
Solar activity varies over the year
58637.e: In the northern hemisphere’s summer, the many plants there take up CO2, and in autumn and winter it is released again as they decompose. Because the northern hemisphere has much more land, it shapes the curve.
58637.m: The yearly zigzags of the Keeling Curve are the breathing of the plant world.

58638.q: In which month does the CO2 content at Mauna Loa reach its highest value each year?
58638.e: Until spring, decomposition outweighs growth, so the CO2 content rises until about May. After that, the growing plants take up a lot of CO2 and the value falls until autumn.
58638.m: At Mauna Loa, CO2 reaches its peak every year in May.

58639.q: Roughly what CO2 content did Keeling measure at the start of his series of measurements?
58639.e: The first measurements in 1958 gave about 315 ppm. Today the value is well above 420 ppm.
58639.m: Since the Keeling measurements began, the CO2 content has risen by more than 100 ppm.

58640.q: In which year was the daily average at Mauna Loa above 400 ppm CO2 for the first time?
58640.e: In May 2013 a daily average above 400 ppm was measured at Mauna Loa for the first time. A few years later the annual average was also permanently above that.
58640.m: Since 2013 the CO2 content has at times been above 400 ppm.

58641.q: By how much did the CO2 content at Mauna Loa rise in the calendar year 2024, the largest rise since measurements began?
58641.e: Over the course of 2024 the value rose by about 3.6 ppm, more than ever before in a calendar year of the series (as of 2025). The reasons were high fossil fuel emissions as well as wildfires and El Niño.
58641.m: 2024 brought the largest CO2 rise in the Keeling Curve so far.

58642.q: A CO2 content of 420 ppm corresponds to what share of the volume of air?
58642.e: ppm means “parts per million”, in other words millionths. 420 millionths are 420 ÷ 1,000,000 = 0.00042, which is 0.042 per cent.
58642.m: One ppm is a millionth, in other words a ten-thousandth of a per cent.

58643.q: Which US researcher started the CO2 measurements at Mauna Loa?
58643.e: The chemist Charles David Keeling from the Scripps Institution in California started the measurements. After his death in 2005, his son Ralph Keeling continued the work.
58643.m: The Keeling Curve bears the name of its founder, Charles David Keeling.

58644.q: In which year was the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change (IPCC) founded?
58644.e: The IPCC was set up in 1988. Its First Assessment Report appeared in 1990.

58645.q: Which two UN organisations founded the IPCC?
58645.e: The World Meteorological Organization (WMO) and the United Nations Environment Programme (UNEP) founded the IPCC together. The UN General Assembly confirmed its founding.
58645.m: The IPCC was created by the WMO and UNEP.

58646.q: In which city is the secretariat of the IPCC based?
58646.e: The IPCC secretariat is based at the World Meteorological Organization in Geneva. Bonn, on the other hand, is home to the secretariat of the UN Framework Convention on Climate Change.
58646.m: The IPCC has its secretariat in Geneva.

58647.q: Which organisation received the Nobel Peace Prize in 2007 together with Al Gore for its work on climate change?
58647.e: The IPCC and the former US Vice President Al Gore were honoured in 2007. They had spread knowledge about human-made climate change.
58647.m: The IPCC received the Nobel Peace Prize in 2007.

58648.q: How are the IPCC’s assessment reports produced?
a: The IPCC runs its own measuring stations
A UN computing centre creates new models
58648.e: The IPCC does not do research itself. Hundreds of scientists summarise and assess the state of the published scientific literature.
58648.m: The IPCC summarises existing research instead of doing research itself.

58649.q: What happens to the “Summary for Policymakers” of an IPCC report before it is published?
a: Governments approve it line by line
A court checks it for accuracy
It is kept secret until the next COP
It is written by a single person
58649.e: The delegates of the member states approve the summary sentence by sentence together with the authors. Its content must match the scientific report.
58649.m: The summary of an IPCC report is approved jointly by all governments.

58650.q: What do ice cores from Antarctica show, which researchers at the University of Bern also analyse for the IPCC reports?
a: What the air was made of in earlier times
How old the Earth is altogether
Where volcanoes used to be in Europe
How much oil lies beneath the ice
58650.e: Tiny bubbles of air are trapped in the ice. From them, the CO2 content of the atmosphere can be determined over hundreds of thousands of years. Bern is a centre of this research.
58650.m: Ice cores are an archive of the air of past times.

58651.q: According to the Sixth Assessment Report, how much warmer was the global surface temperature in 2011 to 2020 than in 1850 to 1900?
58651.e: The Sixth Assessment Report gives a warming of about 1.1 °C for the decade 2011 to 2020 compared with 1850 to 1900. It describes the human influence as unequivocal.
58651.m: In the decade up to 2020, the Earth was about 1.1 degrees warmer than before industrialisation.

58652.q: Why does the IPCC use fixed terms such as “likely” or “very likely” in its reports?
a: To express how certain a statement is in a consistent way
To make the reports easier to read
To hide errors in the measurements
Because numbers are banned in UN reports
58652.e: Each term stands for a fixed range of probability, “very likely”, for example, for 90 to 100 per cent. This means the words mean the same thing in every chapter.
58652.m: The IPCC expresses uncertainty with fixed terms.

58653.q: Which long-term climate target did Swiss voters approve in 2023 with the Climate and Innovation Act?
58653.e: In June 2023 the people approved the law. By 2050 Switzerland should no longer emit more greenhouse gases than are stored naturally or technically.
58653.m: Switzerland wants to be climate-neutral by 2050.

58654.q: In which year did the Paris Agreement come into force?
58654.e: The agreement came into force on 4 November 2016, less than a year after it was adopted. That was unusually fast for a UN treaty.
58654.m: The Paris Agreement has applied since November 2016.

58655.q: Why did the Paris Agreement not come into force as soon as it was adopted in 2015?
a: Enough countries first had to ratify it
The UN General Assembly first rejected it
The USA first had to sign it
It first had to be translated into all languages
58655.e: At least 55 countries accounting for 55 per cent of emissions had to ratify it. This threshold was reached in October 2016.
58655.m: An agreement only applies once enough countries have ratified it.

58656.q: What are the national climate targets that each country submits under the Paris Agreement called?
58656.e: The countries set their contributions themselves, the so-called NDCs. These nationally determined contributions are the heart of the agreement.
58656.m: Under the Paris Agreement, each country sets its own climate targets.

58657.q: How often do countries have to present new climate targets under the Paris Agreement?
58657.e: Every five years, each country has to submit a new target that is as ambitious as possible. This is called the ambition mechanism.
58657.m: The Paris climate targets are tightened every five years.

58658.q: Before the Paris Agreement, which treaty from 1997 committed only industrialised countries to binding emission targets?
58658.e: In the 1997 Kyoto Protocol, only industrialised countries had fixed reduction targets. The Paris Agreement, by contrast, includes all countries.
58658.m: The Kyoto Protocol was the forerunner of the Paris Agreement.

58659.q: In which city was the first Global Stocktake of the Paris Agreement completed in 2023?
58659.e: The first Global Stocktake was completed at COP28 in Dubai. It found that the world is not on track and called for a transition away from fossil fuels in energy systems.
58659.m: At COP28 in Dubai, the world officially took stock of the Paris Agreement for the first time.

58660.q: According to its Paris climate target, by how much does Switzerland want to cut its greenhouse gas emissions by 2030 compared with 1990?
58660.e: Switzerland has committed to halving its emissions by 2030 compared with 1990. Part of this may be achieved through projects abroad.
58660.m: Switzerland wants to halve its emissions by 2030 compared with 1990.

58661.q: What does Article 6 of the Paris Agreement allow Switzerland to do?
a: Count climate protection abroad towards its own target
Emit more CO2 than other countries
58661.e: Switzerland funds projects, for example in Peru or Ghana, and counts the emissions saved towards its target. It signed the first such agreement with Peru in 2020.
58661.m: Through Article 6, Switzerland counts climate projects abroad.

58662.q: In which year did the IPCC publish its special report on global warming of 1.5 °C?
58662.e: The Paris climate conference had asked the IPCC for this report. It appeared in October 2018 and showed the large differences between 1.5 and 2 degrees.
58662.m: The IPCC special report on the 1.5-degree target appeared in 2018.

58663.q: According to the IPCC special report, by how much would global CO2 emissions have to fall by 2030 compared with 2010 to reach 1.5 °C?
58663.e: In the pathways with no or only a small overshoot, CO2 emissions fall by about 45 per cent by 2030 compared with 2010. After that they have to keep falling to zero.
58663.m: For 1.5 degrees, CO2 emissions would have to almost halve by 2030.

58664.q: According to the IPCC special report, around when do global CO2 emissions have to reach net zero to limit warming to 1.5 °C?
58664.e: The 1.5-degree pathways reach net zero CO2 around the middle of the century. For 2 degrees, this point is only reached around 2070.
58664.m: The 1.5-degree target requires net zero CO2 by the middle of the century.

59611.q: A woman borrows 200 francs at 20 per cent interest a year. How much does she pay back after one year?
59611.e: Interest: 200 × 0.20 = 40 francs; she has to pay back 200 + 40 = 240 francs.
59611.m: Interest is calculated as a percentage of the amount borrowed.

60412.q: Which plate tectonic process formed the Pyrenees?
a: Collision of the Iberian plate with the Eurasian plate
Collision of the African plate with the Arabian plate
Drifting apart of the American and Eurasian plates
Rise of a hotspot under the Bay of Biscay
60412.e: The Iberian plate rotated towards Europe and collided with the Eurasian plate. The rocks were folded up in the course of the Alpine mountain building.
60412.m: The Pyrenees formed when Iberia was pushed against Europe.

60413.q: Which mountain is the highest peak of the Pyrenees?
60413.e: Aneto is about 3404 metres high and lies in the Maladeta massif in the Spanish province of Huesca. The largest glacier in the Pyrenees lies on its north side.
60413.m: Aneto is the highest mountain in the Pyrenees.

60414.q: Which small state in the Pyrenees has two heads of state, the French president and a Spanish bishop?
60414.e: Andorra is represented by two co-princes: the President of France and the Bishop of Urgell in Spain. This arrangement goes back to the Middle Ages.
60414.m: Andorra has two co-princes from France and Spain.

60415.q: What is the name of the glacial cirque in the French Pyrenees with one of the highest waterfalls in Europe?
60415.e: The Cirque de Gavarnie is a huge corrie carved out by Ice Age glaciers. The Grande Cascade there plunges over 400 metres.
60415.m: In the Cirque de Gavarnie a waterfall plunges over a huge rock face.

60416.q: Which pass in the French Pyrenees has been climbed most often in the Tour de France?
60416.e: The Col du Tourmalet lies at about 2115 metres and has been part of the Tour de France again and again since 1910. No other pass has been ridden more often.
60416.m: The Tourmalet is the classic Tour de France pass.

60417.q: Which language is spoken in the western Pyrenees on both sides of the border and is unrelated to any other language in Europe?
60417.e: Basque is an isolated language that is older than the Indo-European languages of the region. It is spoken in the Basque Country in Spain and France.
60417.m: Basque is unrelated to any other language in Europe.

60418.q: Which French river rises on the Spanish side of the Pyrenees in the Val d'Aran?
60418.e: The Garonne rises in the Val d'Aran and then flows into France, past Toulouse and Bordeaux. It flows into the Gironde.
60418.m: The Garonne begins its journey in the Spanish Pyrenees.

60419.q: Which treaty in 1659 largely set the border between France and Spain along the Pyrenees?
60419.e: The Treaty of the Pyrenees ended a long war between France and Spain. Among other things, France received Roussillon north of the main ridge.
60419.m: The Treaty of the Pyrenees in 1659 largely made the mountain ridge the national border.

60420.q: On which Pyrenean peak is there a well-known astronomical observatory?
60420.e: Weather and sky research has been carried out on the Pic du Midi de Bigorre since the 19th century. The clear, calm mountain air is well suited to observations.
60420.m: Researchers watch the sky from the Pic du Midi de Bigorre.

60421.q: What is the name of the gorge where the Danube breaks through between the Southern Carpathians and the Balkan Mountains?
60421.e: At the Iron Gates the Danube has cut a narrow valley through the mountains. Today large power stations dam the river there.
60421.m: At the Iron Gates the Danube breaks through the Carpathians.

60422.q: Which mountain in the Eastern Carpathians is the highest mountain in Ukraine?
60422.e: Hoverla is about 2061 metres high and belongs to the Chornohora range. Roman-Kosh, on the other hand, is the highest mountain in Crimea.
60422.m: Hoverla is the roof of Ukraine.

60423.q: Which historical region is enclosed by the arc of the Eastern and Southern Carpathians?
60423.e: Transylvania is an upland region inside the Carpathian arc. Wallachia, on the other hand, lies to the south outside it.
60423.m: Transylvania lies sheltered inside the Carpathian arc.

60424.q: Why were areas of the Carpathians declared a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 2007?
60424.e: The primeval beech forests of the Carpathians in Slovakia and Ukraine were added in 2007. Later, old beech forests from other countries were added, including from Ticino since 2021.
60424.m: The Carpathians preserve some of Europe's last primeval beech forests.

60425.q: Which large lowland lies inside the Carpathian arc?
60425.e: The Pannonian Basin covers large parts of Hungary and neighbouring countries. The Carpathians frame it to the north and east.
60425.m: The Pannonian Basin is framed by the Carpathians.

60426.q: What else are the Southern Carpathians called?
60426.e: The Southern Carpathians are the highest part of the Romanian Carpathians and, with their corries and ridges, are reminiscent of the Alps. That is where the name Transylvanian Alps comes from.
60426.m: Because of their high-mountain character, the Southern Carpathians are also called the Transylvanian Alps.

60427.q: Geologically, which mountain belt do the Carpathians belong to?
60427.e: Like the Alps, the Carpathians were folded up in the Cenozoic era. That makes them young fold mountains.
60427.m: The Carpathians are young fold mountains like the Alps.

60428.q: Which large river rises in the Silesian Beskids of the Western Carpathians?
60428.e: The Vistula rises on the mountain Barania Góra in southern Poland. It flows through Kraków and Warsaw and into the Baltic Sea.
60428.m: The Vistula comes from the Beskids of the Western Carpathians.

60429.q: Which Carpathian range in south-eastern Poland is known for its thinly populated wilderness?
60429.e: The Bieszczady lie where Poland, Slovakia and Ukraine meet. After the Second World War many villages were abandoned; today there are wolves, bears and bison there.
60429.m: The Bieszczady are among the wildest areas of Poland.

60430.q: What does the name of the Norwegian mountain area Jotunheimen mean?
60430.e: Jotunheimen comes from the Jötunn, the giants of Norse mythology. Norway's highest peaks lie in Jotunheimen.
60430.m: Jotunheimen is named after the giants of the Norse sagas.

60431.q: Where is the highest point in Finland?
a: On Halti on the border with Norway
