60431.e: Finland's highest point lies at about 1324 metres on the slope of Halti. The summit itself belongs to Norway.
60431.m: Finland's highest point is on Halti in the far north-west.

60432.q: Which two ancient continents collided when the rocks of the Scandinavian Mountains were formed?
60432.e: About 430 to 390 million years ago Laurentia and Baltica collided. This created a mountain range that was later almost completely worn away.
60432.m: The Scandinavian Mountains go back to the collision of Laurentia and Baltica.

60433.q: Why has Scandinavia been rising since the end of the last Ice Age?
a: Because the weight of the ice sheet has gone
Because volcanoes are pushing up magma
Because glaciers are piling up rock
60433.e: The huge ice sheet pressed the Earth's crust down. Since it melted, the crust has been slowly springing back, which is called isostatic or post-glacial rebound.
60433.m: Scandinavia is rising because the heavy ice has gone.

60434.q: What is special about the small Calderone glacier in the Gran Sasso massif?
a: It was long regarded as Europe's southernmost glacier
It is the largest glacier in Italy
It lies on an active volcano
It grows every year despite global warming
60434.e: The Calderone lies in a shady hollow below the Corno Grande in the Abruzzo. Because of warming it has shrunk a lot and split into two ice fields.
60434.m: The Calderone is the remains of a glacier in the Abruzzo.

60435.q: Which town at the foot of the Gran Sasso was hit by a severe earthquake in 2009?
60435.e: The earthquake in April 2009 destroyed large parts of the old town of L'Aquila. More than 300 people died.
60435.m: L'Aquila was shaken by a devastating earthquake in 2009.

60436.q: Which stone is quarried in the Apuan Alps on the north-western edge of the Apennines?
60436.e: White marble has been quarried near Carrara since Roman times. Michelangelo had blocks brought from there for his sculptures.
60436.m: The famous Carrara marble comes from the Apuan Alps.

60437.q: Which mountain range do the Apennines join near Savona in Liguria?
60437.e: The low Colle di Cadibona near Savona is usually seen as the boundary between the Alps and the Apennines. From there the Apennines curve all the way to Calabria.
60437.m: Near Savona the Alps turn into the Apennines.

60438.q: Where do the Dinaric Alps run?
a: Along the Adriatic from Slovenia to Albania
60438.e: The Dinarides run along the eastern coast of the Adriatic through Croatia, Bosnia and Herzegovina and Montenegro to Albania. The highest peak is Maja Jezercë in Albania.
60438.m: The Dinaric Alps stretch from Slovenia to Albania.

60439.q: Which mountain are the Dinaric Alps named after?
60439.e: Dinara lies on the border between Croatia and Bosnia and Herzegovina. At about 1831 metres it is the highest mountain in Croatia.
60439.m: The Dinarides take their name from the mountain Dinara.

60440.q: Which landscape does the technical term “karst” come from?
a: The Kras between Slovenia and Trieste
The Jura between Switzerland and France
60440.e: The Kras is a limestone plateau in the border area of Slovenia and Italy. Its German name, Karst, became the technical term for limestone landscapes with caves and sinkholes.
60440.m: The term karst comes from a landscape near Trieste.

60441.q: What is a large, flat basin in karst that is often flooded from time to time called?
60441.e: A polje has a level, fertile floor and steep edges. Many of these technical terms come from the South Slavic languages of the Dinarides.
60441.m: A polje is a flat karst basin with fertile soil.

60442.q: What is an opening in karst where a river disappears underground called?
60442.e: Through a ponor, water drains away into cave systems. It often comes out again elsewhere as a strong karst spring.
60442.m: In a ponor a river sinks into the limestone.

60443.q: Which river has carved one of the deepest gorges in Europe in Montenegro?
60443.e: The Tara gorge is up to about 1300 metres deep and lies in the Durmitor area. The Tara is a headwater of the Drina.
60443.m: The Tara gorge is one of the deepest gorges in Europe.

60444.q: Which cold downslope wind rushes down from the Dinarides to the Adriatic in winter?
60444.e: The bora forms when cold air from inland falls over the coastal mountains. It reaches hurricane force and can close bridges and roads.
60444.m: The bora is an icy downslope wind on the Adriatic coast.

60445.q: What separates the Plitvice Lakes in Croatia from one another like steps?
60445.e: Mosses and algae help limestone to settle out of the water. This makes tufa barriers grow, and the water flows over them in waterfalls from lake to lake.
60445.m: The Plitvice Lakes are dammed by growing tufa barriers.

60446.q: Which coastal mountain range is the largest mountain range in Croatia?
60446.e: Velebit stretches about 145 kilometres along the Adriatic coast. It is a UNESCO biosphere reserve.
60446.m: Velebit is Croatia's longest coastal mountain range.

60447.q: Which depression separates the Greater Caucasus from the Lesser Caucasus?
60447.e: Between the two mountain ranges lies a low zone with the River Rioni in the west and the Kura in the east. Large parts of Georgia and Azerbaijan lie in it.
60447.m: The Transcaucasian Depression lies between the Greater and Lesser Caucasus.

60448.q: Which high mountain region of Georgia is known for its medieval defensive towers?
60448.e: Hundreds of stone tower houses stand in the villages of Upper Svaneti. The region has been a UNESCO World Heritage Site since 1996.
60448.m: Svaneti is famous for its old defensive towers.

60449.q: What did Arab geographers call the Caucasus because of its many languages?
60449.e: Dozens of peoples with their own languages live close together in the Caucasus. Many of these languages belong to language families found only there.
60449.m: The Caucasus is one of the regions with the most languages in the world.

60450.q: In which place in the western Caucasus were the Alpine events of the 2014 Sochi Winter Olympics held?
60450.e: Krasnaya Polyana lies in the mountains about 40 kilometres from the Black Sea coast. Ski areas and lifts were built there for the Games.
60450.m: The Sochi 2014 ski races took place in Krasnaya Polyana.

60451.q: Which extinct volcano, at about 5642 metres, is the highest mountain in the Caucasus?
60451.e: Elbrus lies in the west of the Greater Caucasus in Russia. If you count the Caucasus as part of Europe, it is the highest mountain in Europe. Ararat, on the other hand, lies in Turkey, outside the Caucasus.
60451.m: Elbrus is the highest mountain in the Caucasus.

60452.q: Through which countries does the Lesser Caucasus mainly run?
60452.e: The Lesser Caucasus lies south of the Transcaucasian Depression. In the south it merges into the Armenian Highlands.
60452.m: The Lesser Caucasus links Georgia, Armenia and Azerbaijan.

60453.q: Which Russian republic on the north-eastern edge of the Caucasus is considered especially multilingual?
60453.e: Avars, Dargins, Lezgins and many other peoples live in Dagestan. The name means roughly “land of mountains”.
60453.m: Dagestan is a mountainous land with very many peoples and languages.

60454.q: Roughly how long is the Greater Caucasus?
60454.e: The Greater Caucasus stretches from the Taman Peninsula on the Black Sea to the Absheron Peninsula on the Caspian Sea. That is about 1100 kilometres.
60454.m: The Greater Caucasus is about as long as the Alps.

60455.q: What type of volcano is Elbrus?
60455.e: Elbrus is built up from many layers of lava and ash. Such stratovolcanoes are usually steep and cone-shaped.

60456.q: How long ago did Elbrus last erupt?
60456.e: The last eruption is dated to around AD 50. That is why Elbrus is regarded not as extinct but as a dormant volcano.
60456.m: Elbrus is dormant, but not extinct.

60457.q: What Swiss connection is there to the first ascent of the western summit of Elbrus in 1874?
a: A mountain guide from Valais was there
The Federal Council paid for the expedition
The summit was named after a Swiss person
60457.e: Peter Knubel from St. Niklaus guided the British climbers Gardiner, Grove and Walker to the highest summit. So the first ascent has a Swiss connection.
60457.m: A mountain guide from St. Niklaus was one of the first on top of Elbrus.

60459.q: Why is Elbrus often regarded as the highest mountain in Europe?
a: It lies north of the main Caucasus ridge, which is often taken as the border
It lies in the middle of the Alps
It belongs to the Scandinavian Mountains
The EU has officially declared it so
60459.e: Where the border between Europe and Asia runs in the Caucasus is disputed. If you draw it along the main ridge, the 5642-metre Elbrus lies on the European side and is clearly higher than Mont Blanc.
60459.m: Elbrus is often regarded as Europe's highest mountain.

60460.q: Roughly how many glaciers flow down from Elbrus into the valleys?
a: None, it is free of ice
60460.e: 22 glaciers flow down from Elbrus, together covering about 145 square kilometres. They feed rivers such as the Kuban, Baksan and Malka.
60460.m: Elbrus carries a large ice cap with more than twenty glaciers.

60461.q: Why is climbing Elbrus dangerous for many people, despite the cable car?
a: Because of thin air, cold and sudden changes in the weather
Because of poisonous plants on the summit
Because of avalanches of hot sand
60461.e: Above about 4000 metres there is a risk of altitude sickness, icy wind and thick fog. Climbers die on Elbrus again and again, often because they underestimate the mountain.
60461.m: Elbrus is often underestimated because of height, cold and weather.

60462.q: In which geological feature did the present summit structure of Elbrus form?
60462.e: The present double summit grew up in a caldera measuring about 14 by 17 kilometres. A caldera forms when a volcano collapses after an eruption.
60462.m: Elbrus grew up inside a collapsed volcanic basin.

60463.q: Roughly up to what height does the cable car on Elbrus go?
60463.e: The cable car starts at Polyana Azau at about 2300 metres. The top station, Garabashi, lies at about 3850 metres.
60463.m: On Elbrus a cable car takes climbers up to almost 4000 metres.

60464.e: The name goes back to Muley Hacén, a ruler of the Emirate of Granada in the 15th century. According to legend he was buried on the mountain.
60464.m: Mulhacén recalls a Moorish ruler of Granada.

60465.q: Which peak is the second highest in the Sierra Nevada?
60465.e: Pico del Veleta is just under 3400 metres high and lies near the ski area. Alcazaba follows only a few metres lower.
60465.m: Veleta is the second highest mountain in the Sierra Nevada.

60466.q: Which larger mountain system does the Sierra Nevada in Spain belong to?
60466.e: The Baetic Cordillera runs through southern Spain and formed during the Alpine mountain building. The Sierra Nevada is its highest part.
60466.m: The Sierra Nevada is the highest part of the Baetic Cordillera.

60467.q: What is the area with white mountain villages on the southern slope of the Sierra Nevada called?
60467.e: The Alpujarras were long inhabited by Moors, who built terraces and irrigation channels there. The villages with flat roofs are reminiscent of North Africa.
60467.m: The Alpujarras lie on the sunny southern side of the Sierra Nevada.

60468.q: Why is it remarkable that you can ski in the Sierra Nevada?
a: The ski area is in southern Spain close to the Mediterranean
It has artificial snow in halls all year round
It lies on a Mediterranean island
60468.e: The Sierra Nevada has one of the southernmost ski areas in Europe. In clear weather you can see from the slopes to the Mediterranean and sometimes as far as Africa.
60468.m: In the Sierra Nevada you ski with a view of the Mediterranean.

60469.q: Which rock is dominant in the high areas of the Sierra Nevada?
60469.e: Mica schist is a metamorphic rock formed from other rocks under high pressure and temperature. It weathers into dark, flaky scree.
60469.m: The peaks of the Sierra Nevada are mainly mica schist.

60470.q: Roughly what share of France's area does the Massif Central cover?
60470.e: The Massif Central covers about 85,000 square kilometres. That is about twice the area of Switzerland.
60470.m: The Massif Central covers about a seventh of France.

60471.q: Which volcano of the Chaîne des Puys can be reached by a rack railway?
60471.e: Puy de Dôme is about 1465 metres high and the landmark of Clermont-Ferrand. Since 2012 the “Panoramique des Dômes” has run to the summit.
60471.m: A rack railway goes up Puy de Dôme.

60472.q: What kind of mountain is the Cantal in the Auvergne?
60472.e: The Cantal volcano had a diameter of about 70 kilometres and is regarded as the largest volcano in Europe by area. Today it is heavily eroded, and valleys run outwards from its centre like the points of a star.
60472.m: The Cantal is a huge, eroded volcano in the Auvergne.

60473.q: During which mountain building did the old rock base of the Massif Central form?
60473.e: In the Palaeozoic a large fold mountain range formed there, which was later worn down to a stump. Only in the Cenozoic was the base raised again.
60473.m: The Massif Central is the remains of an ancient mountain range.

60474.q: What are the Causses in the south of the Massif Central?
60474.e: The Causses are made of Jurassic limestone and are dry and barren. Rivers such as the Tarn have cut deep gorges into them.
60474.m: The Causses are dry limestone plateaus in southern France.

A narrow valley with a river
60475.e: 3000 feet is about 914 metres. The term goes back to Sir Hugh Munro, who published a list of these mountains in 1891.
60475.m: A Munro is a Scottish mountain more than 3000 feet high.

60476.q: What do mountaineers in Scotland mean by “Munro bagging”?
a: Climbing and ticking off as many Munros as possible
60476.e: Munros are Scottish mountains over 3000 feet. Many walkers collect them like trophies and try to climb all the peaks on the official list.
60476.m: Munro bagging means collecting Scottish summits.

60477.q: Geologically, what did Ben Nevis develop from?
60477.e: Ben Nevis is the remains of a Devonian volcanic complex. Its inside sank down, and glaciers later shaped today's mountain.
60477.m: Ben Nevis is what remains of an ancient volcano.

60478.q: Where does the Caledonian orogeny get its name from?
a: From the Latin name for Scotland
60478.e: The Romans called northern Britain Caledonia. The mountain building was named after this region because its traces are clearly visible there.
60478.m: Caledonia is the old Latin name for Scotland.

60479.q: In which Highland glen were members of the MacDonald clan murdered in 1692?
60479.e: In the Massacre of Glencoe, soldiers killed their hosts because the clan chief had sworn loyalty to King William III too late. The event is seen as a serious breach of the duty of hospitality.
60479.m: Glen Coe recalls a massacre in 1692.

60480.q: Which Celtic language is still spoken in parts of the Highlands?
60480.e: Scottish Gaelic is spoken mainly in the Hebrides and on the west coast. It is closely related to Irish.
60480.m: Scottish Gaelic lives on in the Highlands.

60481.q: Which jagged mountain range made of gabbro lies on the Isle of Skye?
60481.e: The Black Cuillin are made of rough, dark gabbro, a plutonic rock. Their sharp ridges are regarded as the most demanding mountains in Great Britain.
60481.m: The Cuillin on Skye are Scotland's wildest mountains.

60482.q: What is the mountain range called that forms a large part of the Highlands south of the Great Glen?
60482.e: The Grampian Mountains stretch right across Scotland. They include Ben Nevis and the Cairngorms.
60482.m: The Grampians form the backbone of the central Highlands.

60483.q: Which largest national park in Great Britain protects a harsh, almost Arctic high plateau in the Highlands?
60483.e: Cairngorms National Park includes a high granite plateau with long, cold winters. Species such as ptarmigan and reindeer live there, which are otherwise found more in the far north.
60483.m: The Cairngorms are the Arctic heart of the Highlands.

60484.q: What is the highest peak in the Carpathians called?
60484.e: Gerlachovský štít is about 2655 metres high and lies in Slovakia. Since no marked footpath leads to the top, most visitors climb it with a mountain guide.
60484.m: Gerlachovský štít is the highest mountain in the Carpathians.

60485.q: On which Tatra peak is the highest point in Poland?
60485.e: Poland's highest point lies at about 2499 metres on the north-western summit of Rysy. The main summit belongs to Slovakia.
60485.m: Poland's highest point is on Rysy.

60486.q: How is the area of the High Tatras divided between the two countries?
a: Two thirds Slovakia, one third Poland
Two thirds Poland, one third Slovakia
60486.e: The High Tatras cover about 340 square kilometres. The larger and higher part lies on the Slovak side.
60486.m: Most of the High Tatras belong to Slovakia.

60487.q: What do the Slovak national park TANAP and the Polish national park TPN protect together?
a: The High Tatras on both sides of the border
60487.e: TANAP was founded in 1949 and the Polish TPN in 1954. Together they protect the high mountains of the Tatras with bears, chamois and marmots.
60487.m: The High Tatras are a national park on both sides of the border.

60488.q: What destroyed large parts of the forest in the Slovak Tatras in November 2004?
60488.e: On 19 November 2004 a storm swept over the southern side of the Tatras. It blew down almost half the trees over about 12,000 hectares.
60488.m: A violent storm devastated the forests of the High Tatras in 2004.

60489.q: What rock is most of the High Tatras made of?
60489.e: The granite solidified deep in the Earth in the Carboniferous, about 315 million years ago. It was raised much later and shaped by glaciers.
60489.m: The peaks of the High Tatras are mainly granite.

60490.q: What is the well-known mountain lake on the Polish side below Rysy called?
60490.e: Morskie Oko means “eye of the sea” and is one of the largest lakes in the Tatras. It is a popular destination near Zakopane.
60490.m: Morskie Oko is the most famous lake in the Polish Tatras.

60491.q: How were most of the mountain lakes of the High Tatras formed?
a: In hollows carved out by Ice Age glaciers
60491.e: During the Ice Ages glaciers carved hollows and corries out of the granite. When the ice melted, they filled with water. In Slovak these lakes are usually called “pleso”, in Polish “staw”.
60491.m: The Tatra lakes lie in glacial hollows from the Ice Age.

60492.q: Which Tatra peak does a cable car reach at over 2600 metres?
60492.e: Lomnický štít is about 2632 metres high. A weather station and an observatory stand on the summit.
60492.m: You can take a cable car up Lomnický štít.

60493.q: Which country has used the euro since 2009 and shows a Tatra peak on its coins?
60493.e: Slovakia introduced the euro in 2009. The 1, 2 and 5 cent coins show Kriváň, a national symbol. Poland, the Czech Republic and Hungary have their own currencies.
60493.m: Slovakia has paid with the euro since 2009.

60494.q: Which large Norwegian glacier lies just north of the Arctic Circle?
60494.e: At about 370 square kilometres, Svartisen is Norway's second largest glacier. It lies in Saltfjellet-Svartisen National Park in the county of Nordland.
60494.m: Svartisen is a large glacier on the Arctic Circle.

60495.q: What does “Kjølen”, the Norwegian name of the Scandinavian Mountains, mean?
60495.e: The mountains run across the Scandinavian Peninsula like the keel of an upturned ship. That is where the name comes from.
60495.m: The Norwegian name Kjølen compares the mountains to a ship's keel.

60496.q: In which geological period were the heavily eroded Scandinavian Mountains raised to their present height?
60496.e: The old mountains had long been worn down to a stump. Only in the Tertiary did the crust rise again, probably in connection with the opening of the North Atlantic.
60496.m: The present height of the Scandinavian Mountains comes from a recent uplift in the Tertiary.

60497.q: Which mountain in Jotunheimen is the second highest in Norway?
60497.e: Glittertind is only a few metres lower than Norway's highest mountain. In the past, with its ice cap, it was at times even higher.
60497.m: Glittertind is only just behind Norway's highest peak.

60498.q: What shape do the Scandinavian Mountains have in cross-section?
a: Steep towards the Atlantic, gentle towards the east
Gentle towards the Atlantic, steep towards the east
A flat hollow in the middle
60498.e: In the west the mountains drop steeply to the Norwegian coast. To the east they slope gently down to the plateaus and lakes of Sweden.
60498.m: The Scandinavian Mountains drop steeply in the west and gently in the east.

60499.q: Which Umbrian town lost its Basilica of San Benedetto in the earthquake of October 2016?
60499.e: The earthquake of 30 October 2016 was the strongest in Italy for decades. In Norcia, the birthplace of Saint Benedict, the basilica collapsed almost completely.
60499.m: Norcia in the Apennines was hit by a severe earthquake in 2016.

60500.q: Who was held in a hotel on Campo Imperatore on the Gran Sasso in 1943 and freed by German paratroopers?
60500.e: After he was removed from power, Mussolini was held prisoner on Campo Imperatore. German paratroopers freed him in September 1943 using gliders.
60500.m: Mussolini was freed on the Gran Sasso in 1943.

60501.q: Which research facility lies deep in the rock beneath the Gran Sasso?
a: A final repository for nuclear waste
60501.e: The Laboratori Nazionali del Gran Sasso lie next to a motorway tunnel. About 1400 metres of rock shield the experiments from cosmic radiation.
60501.m: Under the Gran Sasso, researchers search for rare particles.

60502.q: What rocks are the Apennines mainly made of?
a: Sedimentary rocks such as limestone and sandstone
60502.e: The rocks were once deposited in the sea and later folded up. That is why there are many limestone massifs and fossils in the Apennines.
60502.m: The Apennines are built mainly from former sea deposits.

60503.q: Roughly how high are the highest peaks of the Apennines?
60503.e: The highest peak is Corno Grande in the Gran Sasso at about 2912 metres, followed by Monte Amaro in the Majella at about 2793 metres. The Alps are considerably higher.
60503.m: The Apennines reach just under 3000 metres.

60504.q: Which double peak in Svaneti is often called the “Matterhorn of the Caucasus”?
60504.e: Ushba is about 4700 metres high and has two steep summits. It is regarded as one of the most difficult mountains in the Caucasus.
60504.m: With its steep faces, Ushba is reminiscent of the Matterhorn.

60505.q: What is the plant life of the Sierra Nevada particularly known for?
60505.e: In the isolated high areas dozens of plant species have developed that grow nowhere else. They survived the warm phases after the Ice Age there.
60505.m: The Sierra Nevada is home to many plants found only there.

60506.q: Which traces show that the Sierra Nevada was covered by glaciers in the last Ice Age?
60506.e: Glaciers shaped wide trough valleys in the high areas and left behind moraine ridges. Today the mountains are free of ice.
60506.m: U-shaped valleys in the Sierra Nevada recall Ice Age glaciers.

60507.q: Roughly how long is the Sierra Nevada in Spain?
60507.e: The Sierra Nevada stretches from west to east through the provinces of Granada and Almería. It is about 100 kilometres long.
60507.m: The Sierra Nevada is a high mountain range about 100 kilometres long.

60508.q: Which mountain range on the south-eastern edge of the Massif Central is protected as a national park?
60508.e: Cévennes National Park was founded in 1970. Its highest peak is the granite Mont Lozère at about 1699 metres. The Vosges and Ardennes lie in north-eastern France, the Pyrenees on the border with Spain.
60508.m: The Cévennes on the edge of the Massif Central are a national park.

60509.q: What kind of landform is the Limagne, where Clermont-Ferrand lies?
60509.e: The Limagne sank when the Earth's crust was pulled apart, similar to the Upper Rhine Graben. Young volcanoes line its western edge.
60509.m: Clermont-Ferrand lies in the Limagne rift.

60510.q: Which river forms at Puy de Sancy from the streams Dore and Dogne?
60510.e: The Dordogne forms at Puy de Sancy where the two streams Dore and Dogne meet. North of Bordeaux it joins the Garonne and flows into the Gironde.
60510.m: The Dordogne rises at Puy de Sancy from the streams Dore and Dogne.

60511.q: What is the circular maar lake in the Auvergne called, which formed in one of the most recent volcanic eruptions in France?
60511.e: Lac Pavin formed about 7000 years ago in an explosion. It is almost perfectly round and over 90 metres deep.
60511.m: Lac Pavin fills the crater of a young volcano.

60512.q: In which mountains does the Elbe rise?
60512.e: The Elbe rises on the Czech side of the Giant Mountains near the Polish border. From there it flows through Bohemia into Germany.
60512.m: The Elbe has its source in the Giant Mountains.

60513.q: Which river that flows through Prague joins the Elbe?
60513.e: The Vltava flows through Prague and joins the Elbe north of it at Mělník. At the confluence it even carries more water than the Elbe.
60513.m: The Vltava joins the Elbe at Mělník.

60514.q: Which rock landscape on the Elbe has a name that goes back to the Swiss painters Adrian Zingg and Anton Graff?
60514.e: The two Swiss artists worked in Dresden in the 18th century and felt the sandstone rocks reminded them of their homeland. That gave rise to the name Saxon Switzerland.
60514.m: Saxon Switzerland owes its name to two Swiss painters in Dresden.

60515.q: In which year did the Elbe in Dresden reach its record level of 9.40 m?
60515.e: During the so-called flood of the century in August 2002, the level in Dresden rose to 9.40 m. It was the highest level ever measured.
60515.m: The Elbe flood of 2002 brought Dresden its highest recorded level.

60516.q: Why did the Dresden Elbe Valley lose its UNESCO World Heritage status in 2009?
a: Because of the building of the Waldschlösschen Bridge
Because the Elbe was deepened for container ships
Because of a new harbour in the old town
Because the river's course was straightened
60516.e: UNESCO considered the cultural landscape to be harmed by the four-lane Waldschlösschen Bridge. The Dresden Elbe Valley was only the second site ever removed from the World Heritage List.
60516.m: Because of the Waldschlösschen Bridge, the Dresden Elbe Valley is no longer World Heritage.

60517.q: How does the Mittelland Canal cross the Elbe near Magdeburg?
a: In a tunnel under the river
Via a flight of locks in the river
By a ferry for cargo ships
60517.e: Since 2003 an aqueduct about 918 m long has carried the canal over the Elbe. This means ships no longer have to go down into the river.
60517.m: Near Magdeburg, ships travel over the Elbe on a bridge.

60518.q: What does it mean that the Elbe at Hamburg is a tidal river?
a: The ebb and flow of the North Sea reach that far
The river freezes over every winter
The river is fed only by glaciers
The river carries only salt water
60518.e: The influence of the tides reaches as far as the weir at Geesthacht above Hamburg. That is why the water level in the port of Hamburg rises and falls twice a day.
60518.m: The tidal Elbe reaches Geesthacht above Hamburg.

60519.q: In which town on the Elbe did Martin Luther publish his 95 Theses in 1517?
60519.e: Luther taught at the University of Wittenberg, which lies on the middle Elbe. Today the town has the extra name Lutherstadt (Luther town).
60519.m: Wittenberg on the Elbe is the town of the Reformation.

60520.q: Which animal survived in Germany in the 20th century almost only on the middle Elbe?
60520.e: The Elbe beaver, a subspecies of the Eurasian beaver, held on in the floodplain forests of the middle Elbe. From there, other areas were later recolonised.
60520.m: The Elbe beaver survived on the middle Elbe.

60521.q: Why is the Loire regarded as one of the last largely natural big rivers in Western Europe?
a: It is only slightly dammed and canalised.
It flows almost only through protected areas.
It is completely closed to ships.
It has no towns on its banks.
60521.e: Unlike the Rhine or Rhône, the Loire was hardly built up with dams. Sandbanks and changing water levels still shape its course today.
60521.m: The Loire is little built up and therefore still fairly wild.

60522.q: What do several French nuclear power stations such as Chinon use the water of the Loire for?
60522.e: Thermal power stations need a lot of cooling water to condense the steam. In hot summers output has to be reduced when the river gets too warm.
60522.m: Nuclear power stations on the Loire use the river as cooling water.

60523.q: Which city, once the residence of the Dukes of Brittany, is the largest city on the Loire?
60523.e: Nantes lies in the Loire estuary and has over 300,000 inhabitants. The castle of the Dukes of Brittany now houses a city museum.
60523.m: Nantes is the largest city on the Loire.

60524.q: What is special about the canal bridge at Briare on the Loire?
a: Ships travel across the river on it
It can be raised for ships
It is the oldest stone bridge in France
60524.e: The canal bridge, opened in 1896 and over 600 metres long, links two canals and spares ships the dangerous crossing of the river. For a long time it was the longest canal bridge in the world.
60524.m: At Briare, ships cross the Loire on a bridge.

60525.q: Why is the English king Richard the Lionheart buried in an abbey on the Loire?
a: England's kings owned large areas of western France
He died on a pilgrimage to Rome
England had no monasteries at the time
60525.e: Richard the Lionheart came from the House of Plantagenet, which also owned Anjou and Aquitaine. He, his father Henry II and his mother Eleanor of Aquitaine lie in Fontevraud Abbey.
60525.m: Richard the Lionheart rests in Fontevraud Abbey.

60526.q: What are the “levées”, built up along the Loire since the Middle Ages, for?
60526.e: Since the Middle Ages, embankments have been built along the Loire to protect the fertile valley from flooding. Many of them now carry roads.
60526.m: The levées protect the Loire Valley from flooding.

60527.q: Which town near the Loire was the capital of the County of Anjou in the Middle Ages?
60527.e: Angers lies on the Maine shortly before it flows into the Loire. The famous Apocalypse Tapestry now hangs in the mighty castle of the Counts of Anjou.
60527.m: Angers was the capital of Anjou.

60528.q: What nickname does the Loire Valley have because of its mild climate and its gardens and orchards?
60528.e: A mild climate and fertile soils made the valley a centre for vegetables, fruit and flowers. That is also why the French kings loved the area.
60528.m: The Loire Valley is called the Garden of France.

60529.q: Where does the Vistula flow into the sea?
60529.e: The Vistula flows into the Bay of Gdańsk near Gdańsk. The Oder, on the other hand, flows into the Pomeranian Bay.
60529.m: The Vistula ends in the Bay of Gdańsk.

60530.q: Which river is the last glaciation in northern Germany named after?
60530.e: The most recent cold period in northern Germany is called the Weichselian glaciation, after the German name of the Vistula, because its glaciers advanced into that area. Elster and Saale stand for older cold periods; in the Alps it is called the Würm glaciation.
60530.m: The last Ice Age is called the Weichselian in the north and the Würm in the Alps.

60531.q: What is special about the lowland in the Vistula delta near Gdańsk, similar to parts of the Netherlands?
a: Parts of it lie below sea level
It is an active volcanic area
It is permanently covered with ice
60531.e: The Żuławy were diked and drained over centuries, partly by Dutch Mennonites. Poland's lowest point is there, at about 2 m below sea level.
60531.m: In the Vistula delta there is land below sea level.

60532.q: On which hill on the Vistula does the royal castle of Kraków stand?
60532.e: Wawel was the residence of the Polish kings for centuries. They were also crowned and buried in the cathedral on the hill.
60532.m: Kraków's royal castle stands on Wawel Hill.

60533.q: Why is the lower Vistula regarded as one of the most natural large rivers in Europe?
a: It is hardly dammed or straightened
It flows only through national parks
It carries water only in spring
It is closed to all ships
60533.e: Only one large dam was built on the lower Vistula, in 1970 at Włocławek. Other planned dams were never built, so there are still many sandbanks and floodplains.
60533.m: The lower Vistula is hardly dammed and therefore very natural.

a: An artificial outlet channel straight to the Baltic Sea
A bridge over the mouth of the Vistula
A tunnel under the Vistula in Gdańsk
A canal between the Vistula and the Oder
60534.e: After severe floods caused by ice jams, a new short route to the sea was dug near Świbno. Since then the main stream has flowed into the sea there.
60534.m: The Vistula cut takes the river to the sea by a short route.

60535.q: Which place at the mouth of the Vistula in Gdańsk is known because the Second World War began there on 1 September 1939?
60535.e: On the morning of 1 September 1939 the German training ship Schleswig-Holstein fired on the Polish ammunition depot at Westerplatte. It lies on the Dead Vistula, an old branch of the river mouth.
60535.m: The Second World War began at Westerplatte in 1939.

60536.q: Which two large Polish cities both lie on the Vistula?
60536.e: The Vistula flows from the Beskids via Kraków and Warsaw to Gdańsk. Wrocław and Szczecin lie on the Oder, Poznań on the Warta.
60536.m: Kraków, Warsaw and Gdańsk lie on the Vistula.

60537.e: The Dnieper rises in the Valdai Hills west of Moscow. The sources of the Volga are also there.
60537.m: The Dnieper begins in the Valdai Hills.

60538.q: What does the city name Zaporizhzhia originally mean?
60538.e: The Zaporozhian Cossacks lived below the former Dnieper rapids. The rapids disappeared into a reservoir in the 20th century.

60539.q: Which sea does the Dnieper flow into?
60539.e: Together with the Southern Bug, the Dnieper flows into the Black Sea through a wide, lagoon-like estuary called a liman.
60539.m: The Dnieper flows into the Black Sea.

60540.q: Which community lived on the rapids of the lower Dnieper from the 16th century?
60540.e: On the island of Khortytsia and nearby, the Zaporozhian Cossacks built their fortified camps, the Sich. They are seen as an important root of Ukrainian history.
60540.m: The Zaporozhian Cossacks lived on the lower Dnieper.

60542.q: On which tributary of the Dnieper did Napoleon's army suffer heavy losses during the retreat in 1812?
60542.e: Tens of thousands of soldiers died crossing the Berezina in November 1812. Swiss regiments also fought there, which the Beresinalied (Berezina song) recalls.
60542.m: At the Berezina, Napoleon's Russian campaign ended in disaster.

60543.q: Which Russian city lies on the upper Dnieper?
60543.e: Smolensk is one of the oldest cities in Russia and lies on the still young Dnieper. Tver, on the other hand, lies on the Volga.
60543.m: Smolensk lies on the upper Dnieper.

60544.q: What happened to the Dnieper in Ukraine in the 20th century?
a: It was dammed into a chain of reservoirs
It was moved into an underground canal
It was diverted to the Volga
60544.e: Large dams turned the Dnieper into a chain of reservoirs, the largest being the Kremenchuk Reservoir. They provide electricity and water for irrigation.
60544.m: The Dnieper in Ukraine is dammed almost all the way.

60545.q: Which canal carried water from the lower Dnieper to the Crimean peninsula?
60545.e: The canal was built from 1961 and supplied the dry Crimea with water for farming and towns. It branched off at Nova Kakhovka.
60545.m: The North Crimean Canal brought Dnieper water to Crimea.

60546.q: On which mountain does the Po rise?
60546.e: The Po rises on Monte Viso in the Cottian Alps near the French border. At about 650 km it is the longest river in Italy.
60546.m: The Po begins on Monte Viso.

60547.q: How was the Po Valley formed?
a: An arm of the sea was filled with debris from the Alps and Apennines.
A volcano collapsed and left a hollow.
A huge glacial lake drained completely.
Sea level fell sharply in Roman times.
60547.e: Between the Alps and the Apennines lay a hollow that was once covered by the sea. Over millions of years rivers deposited thick sediments and filled it up.
60547.m: The Po Valley is a sea basin filled with river debris.

60548.q: Why does the Po Valley often have some of the worst air quality in Europe in winter?
a: Temperature inversions trap exhaust fumes between the Alps and the Apennines.
The foehn blows Saharan dust into the plain.
The many rice fields release soot.
Sea winds bring salt from the coast.
60548.e: The plain is surrounded by mountains on three sides, and in winter cold air often lies under warmer air. Pollutants from traffic, industry and heating then cannot escape.
60548.m: During an inversion, exhaust fumes collect in the Po Valley.

60549.q: Which city is the largest in the Po Valley?
60549.e: With over 1.3 million inhabitants, Milan is the largest city in the plain and the centre of a huge built-up area. The Po Valley is the economic heart of Italy.
60549.m: Milan is the largest city in the Po Valley.

60550.q: Why does the Po in its lower course partly lie higher than the surrounding land?
a: It deposits debris and is enclosed by high embankments
The sea pushes its water upwards
Glaciers fill its bed with ice
60550.e: The Po deposits a lot of sediment in its embanked riverbed, which therefore gets higher and higher. If the embankments break, as in 1951 in the Polesine, large areas are flooded.
60550.m: The embanked Po partly flows above the level of the land around it.

60551.q: What is the area called where the Po splits into many branches as it flows into the sea, which is a nature park?
60551.e: The Po Delta keeps growing out into the sea through sediment. Its lagoons and reed beds are important habitats for water birds.
60551.m: Before reaching the sea, the Po splits into a large delta.

60552.q: Which crop is grown on irrigated fields in the western Po Valley, more than anywhere else in Europe?
60552.e: In Piedmont and Lombardy the fields are flooded through canals such as the Canale Cavour with water from the Po and Alpine rivers. Italy is the largest rice producer in Europe.
60552.m: The Po Valley is the largest rice-growing area in Europe.

60553.q: Which river flows through Lake Como and then into the Po?
60553.e: The Adda comes from the Valtellina, flows through Lake Como and joins the Po near Cremona. The Mincio, on the other hand, drains Lake Garda.
60553.m: The Adda links Lake Como with the Po.

60554.q: Which river links Lake Ladoga with the Baltic Sea?
60554.e: The Neva is only about 74 kilometres long but carries a great deal of water. St Petersburg lies at its mouth on the Baltic Sea.
60554.m: The Neva flows from Lake Ladoga through St Petersburg into the Baltic.

60555.q: What was the supply route across frozen Lake Ladoga during the siege of Leningrad called?
60555.e: In winter lorries drove across the ice, and in summer ships sailed. During the siege from 1941 to 1944 this route was the only link into the city.
60555.m: The Road of Life led across Lake Ladoga to Leningrad.

60556.q: On which island in Lake Ladoga is there a famous Russian Orthodox monastery?
60556.e: Valaam Monastery lies on the island of the same name in the north of Lake Ladoga. In the Winter War in 1940 the monks were evacuated to Finland.
60556.m: A famous monastery stands on the island of Valaam.

60557.q: Which mammal lives as a subspecies of its own only in the fresh water of Lake Ladoga?
60557.e: The Ladoga ringed seal is a leftover from the time after the Ice Age when the lake was connected to the sea. It is endemic and endangered.
60557.m: A subspecies of ringed seal of its own lives in Lake Ladoga.

60558.q: Roughly how deep is Lake Ladoga at its deepest point?
60558.e: The greatest depth of about 230 m is in the rocky north-west. The south of the lake is much shallower.
60558.m: Lake Ladoga is over two hundred metres deep in the north.

60559.q: What makes Lake Ladoga special among Europe's lakes?
a: It is the largest lake in Europe
It is the deepest lake in Europe
It is the saltiest lake in Europe
It is the highest lake in Europe
60559.e: At about 17,700 square kilometres, Lake Ladoga is the largest lake entirely in Europe. It is almost half the size of Switzerland.
60559.m: Lake Ladoga is the largest lake in Europe.

60560.q: Why was the Shlisselburg fortress at the outflow of the Neva from Lake Ladoga so important?
a: It controlled the waterway between the lake and the Baltic Sea
It protected gold mines on the lakeshore
It was the tsars' summer residence
It guarded the border with China
60560.e: The fortress (Oreshek) lies on a small island at the outflow of the Neva. Peter the Great captured it from the Swedes in 1702 and so secured the route to the Baltic.
60560.m: Shlisselburg was the key to the route from Lake Ladoga to the Baltic.

60561.q: Roughly how large is the area of Lake Ladoga?
60561.e: Without islands, the lake covers about 17,700 to 17,900 km², depending on the source. That is more than 40 per cent of the area of Switzerland.
60561.m: Lake Ladoga is almost half the size of Switzerland.

60562.q: Why does the Baltic Sea have a much lower salt content than the Atlantic?
a: Many rivers supply fresh water, and exchange with the North Sea is small.
Ice in winter removes all the salt from the water.
Underground springs wash the salt into the ground.
60562.e: The Baltic is a brackish sea, as it receives a lot of fresh water from rivers and rainfall. Salty North Sea water only gets in through shallow, narrow passages.
60562.m: The Baltic is a brackish sea with little salt.

60563.q: Which straits link the Baltic Sea with the Kattegat?
a: Øresund, Great Belt and Little Belt
Skagerrak, Pentland Firth and the Minch
Bothnian Sea, Sea of Åland and Archipelago Sea
60563.e: The three Danish straits lie between Jutland, the Danish islands and Sweden. All the water exchange with the North Sea passes through them.
60563.m: The Øresund and the Belts are the Baltic's gateway to the North Sea.

60564.q: What is the main cause of the oxygen-poor dead zones on the floor of the Baltic Sea?
a: Oil drilling in the central Baltic
Too strong a current on the seabed
60564.e: Nitrogen and phosphorus encourage algal blooms, and breaking these down on the seabed uses up a lot of oxygen. On top of this, the stable layering of the water prevents mixing.
60564.m: Too many nutrients make the Baltic suffocate on its floor.

60565.q: What do the rare major inflows of salt water from the North Sea do in the Baltic Sea?
a: They bring oxygen into the deep basins.
They make the Baltic freeze in winter.
They raise the water level permanently by metres.
They wash all the brackish water out.
60565.e: In certain storm conditions, a lot of salty, oxygen-rich water flows over the sills into the Baltic. Because it is heavy, it sinks and supplies the deep basins with oxygen.
60565.m: Saltwater inflows supply the depths of the Baltic with oxygen.

60566.q: What did the area of today's Baltic Sea look like during the last Ice Age?
a: It was covered by a thick ice sheet
It was a warm inland sea
It was a dry lowland without ice
It was part of the Mediterranean
60566.e: During the last Ice Age a huge ice sheet lay over Scandinavia and the Baltic. Only after it melted did the Baltic Sea form, switching several times between fresh and salt water.
60566.m: The Baltic is a young sea that formed after the Ice Age.

60567.q: Why does the land on the Gulf of Bothnia rise by up to almost 1 cm every year?
a: The Earth's crust is springing back after the ice sheet melted.
Volcanoes are slowly pushing the rock upwards.
The Baltic is evaporating and the level is falling.
Rivers deposit so much sand there.
60567.e: The weight of the Ice Age ice sheet had pressed the crust down. Since it melted, the crust has been slowly rising again, which is called post-glacial rebound.
60567.m: Scandinavia has been slowly rising again since the Ice Age.

60568.q: What is the typical coastal form of Western Pomerania called, with shallow, bay-like waters behind islands and peninsulas?
60568.e: Bodden are shallow, often brackish bays separated from the open sea by spits and islands. One example is the area around Fischland-Darss-Zingst.
60568.m: Bodden shape the landscape on the coast of Western Pomerania.

60570.q: Which intergovernmental commission has worked to protect the Baltic Sea since the 1970s?
60570.e: It is based on the Helsinki Convention of 1974, to which all the coastal states and the EU belong. The OSPAR Commission, on the other hand, is responsible for the north-east Atlantic.
60570.m: HELCOM protects the marine environment of the Baltic.

60571.q: Why are many of the East Frisian Islands slowly moving east?
a: The current removes sand in the west and deposits it in the east.
The Earth's crust is shifting under the North Sea.
The tides push the islands as a whole.
The wind blows dunes out to sea.
60571.e: The East Frisian Islands are sandy barrier islands. Without protective structures their western ends would break away while their eastern ends grew.
60571.m: The East Frisian Islands move east with the sand.

60572.q: Which salt-loving plant is one of the first to colonise the mud at the edge of the salt marshes?
60572.e: Glasswort holds the mud in place and so slowly raises the ground. Marram grass, on the other hand, grows on dry sand dunes.
60572.m: Glasswort is a pioneer plant on the mudflats.

60573.q: What are the brushwood groynes (Lahnungen) off the coast in the Wadden Sea for?
a: They calm the water so that mud settles.
They lead the water into the tidal channels.
They mark safe routes for mudflat walkers.
They serve as resting places for seals.
60573.e: Lahnungen are double rows of wooden posts filled with brushwood. Mud settles in the calm fields between them, and new foreshore is created.
60573.m: Brushwood groynes help create new land on the coast.

60574.q: Which sunken settlement in the North Frisian Wadden Sea is still a well-known legend today?
60574.e: Rungholt was lost in 1362 in a huge storm surge, the Grote Mandrenke. Vineta is a legendary town on the Baltic, Ys one in Brittany.
60574.m: Rungholt sank into the Wadden Sea in 1362.

60575.q: Which introduced shellfish species now forms large reefs in the Wadden Sea?
60575.e: The Pacific oyster was introduced for farming and spread widely from the 1990s. It often pushes out the native blue mussel.
60575.m: The Pacific oyster has spread widely in the Wadden Sea.

60576.q: Why are many shelducks unable to fly for a few weeks in the Wadden Sea in late summer?
a: They are too heavy from eating so much.
They are nesting on the sandbanks.
Their wings are stuck together by salt water.
60576.e: During the moult, shelducks lose their flight feathers and cannot fly for a few weeks. Tens of thousands then gather on remote sandbanks in the Wadden Sea, where they find shelter and food.
60576.m: Many shelducks moult in the Wadden Sea.

60577.q: How has the island of Sylt been linked to the mainland since 1927?
a: By the Hindenburg Dam with the railway
By a tunnel under the mudflats
By a footpath at low tide
60577.e: The dam, about 11 km long, carries only railway tracks. Cars are taken to Sylt on trains.
60577.m: You reach Sylt by train over the Hindenburg Dam.

60578.q: Which wild animal, which also lives in the Wadden Sea, is the largest predator in Germany?
60578.e: Grey seal bulls can grow over 2 m long and weigh about 300 kg. There are large colonies on Heligoland and near Amrum, for example.
60578.m: The grey seal is Germany's largest predator.

60579.q: Which river brings the most water into the Black Sea?
60579.e: The Danube flows into the sea through a large delta in Romania and Ukraine. It drains large parts of Central Europe, including the Grisons via the Inn.
60579.m: The Danube is the largest river flowing into the Black Sea.

60580.q: What does the disputed “flood hypothesis” about the Black Sea say?
a: A freshwater lake was suddenly flooded by the Mediterranean after the Ice Age.
The sea was created by a meteorite impact.
The sea once dried up completely in ancient times.
A flood wave from the Caspian Sea filled the basin.
60580.e: The researchers Ryan and Pitman suggested a rapid flooding about 7500 years ago. Other experts think a gradual rise is more likely.
60580.m: According to one hypothesis, the Black Sea was once suddenly flooded.

60581.q: Roughly how salty is the surface water of the Black Sea?
60581.e: The salt content is about half that of the world's oceans, which have about 35 g per litre. Deeper down the water is a little saltier.
60581.m: The Black Sea is about half as salty as the ocean.

60582.q: Which mountain range runs along Turkey's Black Sea coast?
60582.e: The Pontic Mountains rise steeply behind the northern coast of Anatolia. They catch a lot of rain, so the coast is very green.
60582.m: The Pontic Mountains line Turkey's Black Sea coast.

60583.q: Which ancient region on the eastern coast of the Black Sea was, according to legend, the destination of the Argonauts?
60583.e: The Argonauts searched for the Golden Fleece in Colchis, in today's western Georgia. Taurica, on the other hand, was the name for Crimea.
60583.m: The Argonauts sailed to Colchis on the Black Sea.

60584.q: Roughly how big is the Black Sea compared with Switzerland?
a: A good ten times as big
About a hundred times as big
60584.e: The Black Sea covers about 436,000 km², Switzerland about 41,000 km². That makes a little more than ten times as much.
60584.m: The Black Sea is a good ten times as big as Switzerland.

60585.q: Which introduced animal caused the anchovy fishery in the Black Sea to collapse in the 1980s?
60585.e: The comb jelly Mnemiopsis leidyi probably arrived in ships' ballast water. It ate huge amounts of plankton and fish larvae.
60585.m: An introduced comb jelly harmed fishing in the Black Sea.

60586.q: Which canal has shortened the shipping route from the Danube to the Black Sea since 1984?
60586.e: The canal runs from Cernavodă straight to the coast near Constanța. This means ships do not have to take the long detour through the delta.
60586.m: The Danube-Black Sea Canal provides a shortcut to the coast.

60587.q: In which year was the first bridge over the Bosphorus opened?
60587.e: The first Bosphorus Bridge was opened for the 50th anniversary of the Republic of Turkey. Today there are three suspension bridges.
60587.m: Since 1973 a bridge has linked Europe and Asia in Istanbul.

60589.q: Why was a third bridge opened far to the north of the Bosphorus in 2016?
a: To keep heavy traffic out of central Istanbul
To stop shipping on the Bosphorus
To link Istanbul with Asia for the first time
Because the old bridges had collapsed
60589.e: The Yavuz Sultan Selim Bridge carries a motorway and railway tracks. It is meant to route lorries around the overloaded city centre.
60589.m: The northernmost Bosphorus bridge takes heavy traffic away from the city centre.

60590.q: What is the planned artificial waterway west of the Bosphorus called?
60590.e: The canal is meant to link the Black Sea with the Sea of Marmara and relieve the Bosphorus. The project is disputed because of environmental and cost issues.
60590.m: Kanal Istanbul is meant to relieve the Bosphorus.

60591.q: What is the small tower on a rocky islet in the Bosphorus off Üsküdar called?
60591.e: The Maiden's Tower (Kız Kulesi) has stood on a tiny island for centuries. It served as a lighthouse and customs station.
60591.m: The Maiden's Tower stands in the middle of the Bosphorus.

60592.q: Why did the Ottomans build fortresses on both banks at the narrowest point of the Bosphorus?
a: To control the passage of ships
To get salt from the sea
To protect their sultan's palace there
To build a bridge over the strait
60592.e: With Anadolu Hisarı on the Asian side and Rumeli Hisarı on the European side, the Ottomans could close the strait. This helped them in the siege of Constantinople in 1453.
60592.m: The fortresses on the Bosphorus controlled shipping through the strait.

60593.q: According to the common view, how was the Bosphorus formed?
a: As a river valley flooded by the sea
As the crater of a volcano
60593.e: Its winding shape is reminiscent of a river valley that was flooded when sea level rose. Tectonic fault lines also played a part.
60593.m: The Bosphorus is regarded as a drowned river valley.

60594.q: Which famous luxury train ran to Istanbul on the Bosphorus from 1889?
60594.e: The Orient Express ran from Paris to Constantinople, today's Istanbul, and ended at Sirkeci station. On the Asian side, the Baghdad Railway began at Haydarpaşa station.
60594.m: The Orient Express ended in Istanbul on the Bosphorus.

60595.q: Which strait was called the “Cimmerian Bosphorus” in ancient times?
60595.e: As well as the Thracian Bosphorus near Byzantion, there was the Cimmerian Bosphorus between Crimea and Taman. The ancient Bosporan Kingdom lay there.
60595.m: The Cimmerian Bosphorus is today's Kerch Strait.

60596.q: What is the Strait of Dover called in French?
60596.e: The French name the strait after the town of Calais. A département is also named after it.
60596.m: In French the Strait of Dover is called the Pas de Calais.

60597.q: Where on the English Channel has one of the world's first large tidal power stations stood since 1966?
a: On the Seine near Le Havre
60597.e: The power station uses the very high tidal range in Brittany. A dam across the mouth of the Rance contains the turbines.
60597.m: Electricity has been generated from the tides on the Rance since 1966.

60598.q: Which peninsula in Normandy, with the port of Cherbourg, juts far out into the English Channel?
60598.e: The Cotentin Peninsula separates the Bay of the Seine from the Bay of Mont-Saint-Michel. Cherbourg at its tip is an important ferry port.
60598.m: Cherbourg lies at the tip of the Cotentin Peninsula.

60599.q: On which Channel Island are cars banned?
60599.e: On Sark only tractors, bicycles and horse-drawn carriages are used. Until 2008 the island was regarded as the last feudal state in Europe.
60599.m: There are no cars on Sark.

60600.q: In which year did the Spanish Armada sail through the English Channel and fail?
60600.e: The fleet was meant to make an invasion of England possible, but it was defeated off Gravelines and scattered by storms. In 1066, on the other hand, William the Conqueror crossed over.
60600.m: The Spanish Armada failed in the English Channel in 1588.

60601.q: What was the evacuation of over 300,000 Allied soldiers from Dunkirk in 1940 called?
60601.e: Many ships and boats carried the trapped troops across the Channel to England. Overlord, on the other hand, was the landing in Normandy in 1944.
60601.m: Operation Dynamo rescued soldiers from Dunkirk in 1940.

60602.q: How is the heavy shipping traffic in the Strait of Dover regulated?
a: By a traffic separation scheme with separate lanes
By traffic lights on each coast
By allowing passage only by day
By a lock in the middle
60602.e: Ships heading south-west use the English side, and those heading north-east the French side. This avoids collisions.
60602.m: In the Strait of Dover there are separate lanes for ships.

60603.q: Which British territories in the English Channel were occupied by German troops in the Second World War?
60603.e: The Channel Islands were occupied from 1940 to 1945. They were the only British Crown territory in Europe to be occupied.
60603.m: The Channel Islands were under German occupation from 1940 to 1945.

60604.q: Why does the town of Adria, which gave the sea its name, now lie about 20 km from the sea?
a: The Po and Adige have pushed the coast out with sediments.
Sea level has fallen sharply since Roman times.
An earthquake moved the town inland.
The town was rebuilt further inland in the Middle Ages.
60604.e: In ancient times Adria was an important port. Since then the rivers have deposited so much material that the coast has moved far to the east.
60604.m: River sediments have cut the town of Adria off from the sea.

60605.q: Which strait links the Adriatic with the Ionian Sea?
60605.e: The Strait of Otranto lies between Apulia and Albania and is about 70 km wide. Water is exchanged with the Mediterranean through it.
60605.m: The Strait of Otranto is the gateway to the Adriatic.

60606.q: Why is the northern Adriatic particularly shallow and warm in summer?
a: It is a flooded part of the Po Valley, mostly less than 50 m deep.
Warm water flows in from the Red Sea there.
It is separated from the open sea by dams.
60606.e: The northern part lies on the continental shelf and therefore warms up quickly. In the south, by contrast, the Adriatic is over 1200 m deep.
60606.m: The northern Adriatic is shallow and therefore warms up quickly.

60607.q: How were the long chains of islands parallel to the coast off Dalmatia formed?
a: Parallel mountain ridges were partly flooded after the Ice Age
Volcanoes formed a chain of islands
Glaciers pushed moraines out to sea
60607.e: Mountain ridges there run parallel to the coast and were partly flooded after the Ice Age. The ridges now stick out of the sea as long islands. This is called the Dalmatian type of coast.
60607.m: On the Dalmatian coast the islands lie parallel to the mainland.

60608.q: What is the bay between Istria and the Croatian mainland, with the islands of Krk and Cres, called?
60608.e: The port city of Rijeka also lies on the Kvarner Gulf. Krk is linked to the mainland by a bridge.
60608.m: The islands of Krk and Cres lie in the Kvarner Gulf.

60609.q: What is the natural sloshing of the Adriatic's water level called, which together with the sirocco can make floods in Venice worse?
60609.e: In a seiche the water sloshes back and forth in the long Adriatic basin, rather like in a bathtub. If this coincides with high tide and a south wind, the water in Venice rises especially high.
60609.m: A seiche makes the water of the Adriatic slosh back and forth.

60610.q: The Adriatic port of Ancona has a Greek name. What does that tell us about its history?
a: It was founded by Greek settlers
It was the capital of the Byzantine Empire
The Greek alphabet was invented there
60610.e: Greek settlers named the place after the curved headland Ankon, which means “elbow”. Today Ancona is an important ferry port for Croatia and Greece.
60610.m: Ancona was founded by the Greeks.

60611.q: Which Adriatic port was the end point of the Roman Via Appia?
60611.e: The Via Appia ran from Rome via Capua to Brindisi. From there people crossed over to Greece.
60611.m: The Via Appia ended in Brindisi.

60612.q: What is the continuation of the North Atlantic Current that flows north along the Norwegian coast called?
60612.e: Off Scandinavia the North Atlantic Current continues as the Norwegian Current. It carries warm Atlantic water far into the Arctic.
60612.m: The Norwegian Current carries Atlantic warmth north along the coast of Norway.

60613.q: Which ocean current branches south from the North Atlantic Current and flows along Portugal and north-west Africa?
60613.e: Part of the water turns south off Europe and flows as the relatively cool Canary Current off north-west Africa. This closes the subtropical gyre of the North Atlantic.
60613.m: The Canary Current is the cool southern branch that closes the North Atlantic circuit.

60614.q: What mainly drives the North Atlantic Current?
a: Westerly winds and differences in temperature and salt content
The water of Europe's large rivers
60614.e: Westerly winds push the surface water north-east. In addition, cold, salty water sinks in the north and draws warm water after it.
60614.m: Wind and differences in temperature and salt keep the North Atlantic Current going.

60615.q: Why does the west coast of Svalbard stay free of ice longer in winter than the east coast?
a: An offshoot of warm Atlantic water flows north there
Hot volcanic springs warm the sea there
The sun shines longer there in winter
Strong storms prevent any ice forming there
60615.e: The West Spitsbergen Current is the northernmost offshoot of the North Atlantic Current. It brings warmth to the west coast, while the east side is shaped by cold polar water.
60615.m: Warm Atlantic water keeps the west coast of Svalbard free of ice for longer.

60616.q: Why are winters in Reykjavík milder than in Helsinki, even though Reykjavík lies further north?
a: A branch of the North Atlantic Current brings warm water to Iceland's coast
The long summer days store heat into the winter
Greenland protects Iceland from all cold winds
Iceland lies higher above sea level than Finland
60616.e: The Irminger Current, a branch of the North Atlantic Current, flows around the south and west of Iceland. Helsinki, on the other hand, is influenced by the cold continental climate.
60616.m: Warm Atlantic water makes the winters on Iceland's coast mild.

60617.q: What is the cold, salty water mass called that forms when the water of the North Atlantic Current sinks in the far north?
60617.e: In the Nordic Seas and the Labrador Sea the salty water cools, becomes denser and sinks. This forms North Atlantic Deep Water, which flows south at depth.
60617.m: North Atlantic Deep Water is cooled surface water that sinks in the north.

60618.q: Why is it especially often foggy off Newfoundland, where the warm Gulf Stream meets the cold Labrador Current?
a: Warm, moist air cools over cold water
Volcanoes release a lot of steam there
The sea is especially low in salt there
60618.e: When moist air moves from the warm water over the cold water of the Labrador Current, it cools below the dew point. This creates advection fog, for which the Grand Banks of Newfoundland are notorious.
60618.m: Fog often forms over the Grand Banks because warm sea air cools over cold water.

60619.q: Why can even palm trees grow outdoors on the north-west coast of Scotland?
a: The North Atlantic Current gives mild, almost frost-free winters
The summers there are hotter than on the Mediterranean
Warm winds from the Sahara reach the coast
The ground is warmed by volcanoes
60619.e: The warm water of the North Atlantic Current greatly softens the winters on Scotland's west coast. That is why plants from all over the world grow in gardens such as Inverewe, even though the coast lies at almost 58 degrees north.
60619.m: The North Atlantic Current makes Scotland's coast surprisingly mild.

60620.q: What is the striking zone south of Greenland called, where the sea has hardly warmed or has even cooled, against the worldwide trend?
60620.e: Many researchers interpret the “Cold Blob” in the subpolar North Atlantic as a possible sign that the Atlantic overturning circulation is weakening. Less warm water then reaches the north.
60620.m: The Cold Blob south of Greenland is seen as a possible warning sign of a weaker Atlantic circulation.

60621.q: Between which mountain ranges is the mistral speeded up in the Rhône Valley as if through a nozzle?
60621.e: The mistral flows through the gap between the foothills of the Alps and the Cévennes on the edge of the Massif Central. The narrowing speeds up the air as if through a nozzle.
60621.m: In the Rhône Valley the mistral is speeded up between the Alps and the Cévennes as if through a nozzle.

60622.q: Which pattern of air pressure typically sets off a mistral?
a: High over the Bay of Biscay, low over the Gulf of Genoa
Low over the Bay of Biscay, high over the Gulf of Genoa
High over Russia, low over Iceland
Low over the Sahara, high over Scandinavia
60622.e: When there is a high over the Bay of Biscay and a low around the Gulf of Genoa, cold air flows from the north to the Mediterranean. A passing cold front often strengthens the mistral further.
60622.m: A high over Biscay and a low near Genoa set the mistral going.

60623.q: In which seasons does the mistral occur most often?
60623.e: The mistral is most frequent and strongest in winter and spring, but it can blow in any season. It often lasts from one to several days.
60623.m: The mistral blows mainly in winter and spring.

60624.q: What does the name “mistral” originally mean in Occitan?
60624.e: The name comes from the Languedoc dialect of Occitan and means “masterly”. It goes back to the Latin “magistralis”.
60624.m: The mistral is named the “masterly” wind.

60625.q: What effect does a strong mistral have on the water temperature in the Gulf of Lion?
a: It falls because cold deep water rises
It rises because warm air heats the sea
It stays the same because the wind blows only over land
It rises because river water is added
60625.e: The offshore wind pushes the warm surface water out to sea. Colder water rises from the depths to replace it, and the sea near the coast cools noticeably.
60625.m: The mistral drives warm surface water away, so cold deep water rises.

60626.q: Because of the mistral, which way do traditional Provençal farmhouses (mas) usually face?
a: With the gable towards the wind
60626.e: The mas turn their backs to the north wind and open towards the south. The north side usually has only a few small windows.
60626.m: Provençal farmhouses face south and turn their backs on the mistral.

60627.q: Which trees did farmers in the Rhône Valley plant in long rows as protection against the mistral?
60627.e: Dense rows of cypresses slow down the wind and protect fields and gardens. They still shape the landscape of Provence today.
60627.m: Cypress hedges protect the fields in the Rhône Valley from the mistral.

60628.q: Why do many church towers in Provence have open wrought-iron frames instead of closed belfries?
a: So that the mistral can blow through freely
So that the bells can be stolen more easily
Because there is no stone in Provence
Because iron has a cooling effect in summer
60628.e: The open wrought-iron frames give the wind little surface to push against. So the tower is put under less strain in a strong mistral.
60628.m: Open iron frames on Provençal towers let the mistral blow through.

60629.q: Which painter complained in letters from Arles that the mistral made painting outdoors difficult?
60629.e: Van Gogh lived in Provence in 1888 and 1889 and often painted outdoors. In his letters he described how the mistral shook his easel.
60629.m: Van Gogh had to battle the mistral while painting in Provence.

60630.q: Why does the bora arrive cold at the coast despite descending, while the foehn becomes warm as it descends?
a: The starting air is so cold that the warming is not enough
The bora keeps rising as it blows
The sea cools the air beforehand
The bora blows only at night without sun
60630.e: The bora also warms up dry-adiabatically as it descends. But the cold air from inland is so cold that it still reaches the Adriatic as a cold wind.
60630.m: The bora stays cold because its starting air is very cold, despite warming as it descends.

60631.q: In which port city are ropes or chains put up along some steep streets to hold on to during a strong bora?
60631.e: In Trieste gusts of the bora often exceed 120 km/h, and in extreme cases reach almost 200 km/h. That is why chains are sometimes put up along the pavements.
60631.m: In Trieste pedestrians hold on to chains during a strong bora.

60832.q: Roughly how long is the Afsluitdijk?
60832.e: The dam is about 32 kilometres long and 90 metres wide. It separates the IJsselmeer from the Wadden Sea.
60832.m: The Afsluitdijk is just over 30 kilometres long.

60833.q: In which period was the Afsluitdijk built in the Netherlands?
a: After the fall of the Berlin Wall
60833.e: Construction began in 1927, and the last gap was closed on 28 May 1932. The official opening followed in 1933.
60833.m: The Afsluitdijk was built between the World Wars.

60834.q: Which two aims did the Netherlands pursue with the Zuiderzee Works and the Afsluitdijk?
a: Protection from storm floods and gaining new land
Building a naval port and an airport
Creating salt pans and fish farms
60834.e: The dam shortened the coastline and protects the land from storm floods. Behind it, large polders were drained, where there are farms and towns today.
60834.m: The Zuiderzee Works brought protection and new land.

60835.q: What did the Afsluitdijk turn the salty Zuiderzee into?
60835.e: Cut off from the sea, the basin gradually became fresh thanks to the inflow of the IJssel. Today the IJsselmeer is an important store of drinking water.
60835.m: The Afsluitdijk turned the Zuiderzee into the IJsselmeer.

60836.q: At the Frisian end of the Afsluitdijk lies a hamlet with the same name as a Swiss city, spelt without the umlaut. Which one?
60836.e: The small hamlet of Zurich lies near Harlingen in the municipality of Súdwest-Fryslân. That is where the Afsluitdijk ends on the Frisian side.
60836.m: At the end of the Afsluitdijk lies the Frisian Zurich.

60837.q: What gave the decisive push in the Netherlands in 1916 to dam the Zuiderzee?
a: A severe storm flood with major flooding
A strong earthquake on the coast
A long drought on the Rhine
60837.e: In January 1916 the Zuiderzee flooded large areas, and there was also a food shortage during the First World War. Two years later the Zuiderzee Act was passed.
60837.m: The storm flood of 1916 paved the way for the Afsluitdijk.

60838.q: Apart from shipping, what job do the Stevin and Lorentz locks in the Afsluitdijk have?
a: At low tide they release surplus water into the Wadden Sea
At high tide they let salt water into the lake
They generate the electricity for all of Friesland
They pump water into the polders
60838.e: At low tide the IJsselmeer lies higher than the Wadden Sea. Then the sluices open and the water of the IJssel flows down into the sea by gravity.
60838.m: The sluices in the Afsluitdijk drain the IJsselmeer at low tide.

60839.q: What was the dam between Enkhuizen and Lelystad in the IJsselmeer, completed in 1975, originally intended for?
a: As the edge of a planned new polder
As a harbour pier for ocean-going ships
As a pipeline to bring salt water into the lake
60839.e: The Houtribdijk was meant to prepare for a Markerwaard polder, which was never drained. Today it separates the Markermeer from the rest of the IJsselmeer.
60839.m: The Houtribdijk separates the Markermeer from the IJsselmeer.

60840.q: Roughly how long is the Sognefjord?
60840.e: The Sognefjord stretches from the coast near Solund to Skjolden. It is the longest and deepest fjord in Norway.
60840.m: At about 205 kilometres, the Sognefjord is Norway's longest fjord.

60841.q: Which glacier, the largest on the European mainland, lies north of the Sognefjord?
60841.e: Jostedalsbreen is a plateau glacier whose tongues reach into side valleys of the Sognefjord. It lies in a national park.
60841.m: Jostedalsbreen is the largest glacier on the European mainland.

60842.q: How did a fjord like the Sognefjord form?
a: A glacier carved out a valley that the sea later flooded
A river cut a valley that was later drowned
A tectonic rift sank below sea level
Karst caves collapsed and filled with water
60842.e: Ice Age glaciers deepened existing valleys far below today's sea level. After the ice melted, the sea flowed into these troughs.
60842.m: A fjord is a valley carved by a glacier and flooded by the sea.

60843.q: Which cross-section shape is typical of a fjord valley?
60843.e: Glaciers grind down the valley floor and sides evenly, creating steep walls with a wide floor. Rivers, on the other hand, leave V-shaped valleys.
60843.m: Fjords have the U-shaped cross-section of a glacial trough.

60844.q: Why is a fjord usually much shallower at its mouth than further inland?
a: There is a rock sill there, because the glacier eroded less deeply
The river deposits sand in a delta there
The tides have washed out the inner part
The land has sunk more there
60844.e: Towards the open sea the glacier lost thickness and carving power. It left behind a sill of rock or moraine, behind which the basin is deep.
60844.m: A sill typically lies at the mouth of a fjord.

60845.q: Which narrow branch of the Sognefjord is part of the UNESCO World Heritage Site “West Norwegian Fjords”?
60845.e: The Nærøyfjord was added to the World Heritage list in 2005 together with the Geirangerfjord. At its narrowest point it is only about 250 metres wide.
60845.m: The Nærøyfjord is a World Heritage branch of the Sognefjord.

60846.q: Which fjord is considered longer than the Sognefjord and therefore the longest in the world?
60846.e: Kangertittivaq on the east coast of Greenland is about 350 kilometres long. At about 205 kilometres, the Sognefjord is clearly shorter.
60846.m: The world's longest fjord is in Greenland.

60847.q: Which Norwegian fylke (county) does the Sognefjord belong to (as of 2025)?
60847.e: Since 2020 the former Sogn og Fjordane and Hordaland have together formed the county of Vestland. Its main town is Bergen.
60847.m: The Sognefjord lies in the county of Vestland.

60848.q: What is the Flåm Railway on the Sognefjord known for?
a: It is one of the steepest standard-gauge railways in the world
It is the longest undersea railway in Europe
It is the only railway that runs over a glacier
It is the northernmost railway in the world
60848.e: Between Flåm on the fjord and Myrdal, the Flåm Railway climbs about 860 metres in about 20 kilometres. It is one of the steepest standard-gauge railways and a major tourist attraction.
60848.m: The Flåm Railway climbs steeply from the fjord into the mountains.

60849.q: What characterises the Dalmatian type of coast?
a: Long chains of islands parallel to the coast, separated by sea channels
Deeply cut glacial troughs at right angles to the coast
Flat sand spits in front of calm lagoons
Countless small rocky islands smoothed by ice
60849.e: On the Dalmatian coast, mountain ridges, islands and straits run in the same direction as the coastline. This is called a longitudinal or concordant coast.
60849.m: The Dalmatian coast is a longitudinal coast with parallel islands.

60850.q: Geologically, what are the long, narrow islands off the Dalmatian coast?
a: The ridges of flooded mountain ranges
60850.e: After the last Ice Age, the level of the Adriatic rose. The water filled the long valleys, and only the mountain ridges stick out as islands.
60850.m: The Dalmatian islands are the crests of a drowned mountain range.

60851.q: Which mountain system do the coastal mountains and islands of Dalmatia belong to?
60851.e: The Dinarides run along the eastern coast of the Adriatic from the Slovenian Karst to Albania. Their direction determines the shape of the coast.
60851.m: Dalmatia's coast is shaped by the Dinarides.

60852.q: In which direction do the islands and ridges of Dalmatia run?
60852.e: The islands follow the direction of the Dinarides from north-west to south-east. That is why they lie like barriers parallel to the mainland.
60852.m: The Dalmatian islands are aligned from north-west to south-east.

60853.q: Which bridge, opened in 2022, connects the Croatian mainland with the Pelješac peninsula?
60853.e: The bridge bypasses the short Bosnian stretch of coast near Neum. This links Dubrovnik to the rest of Croatia without crossing a border.
60853.m: The Pelješac Bridge links southern Dalmatia directly with the rest of Croatia.

60854.q: Which rock shapes the mountains and islands of Dalmatia and leads to typical karst landforms?
60854.e: Limestone is dissolved by water containing carbonic acid, which creates sinkholes, caves and underground rivers. The bare, pale slopes are typical of the Dinaric Karst.
60854.m: Limestone forms the karst of Dalmatia.

60855.q: Which river near Šibenik forms limestone terraces and waterfalls in a national park?
60855.e: The Krka flows through the Dalmatian karst and deposits lime on mosses, so that travertine barriers grow. It flows into a bay of the Adriatic near Šibenik.
60855.m: The Krka forms waterfalls made of travertine.

60856.q: Which steep limestone mountain range rises directly behind the Makarska Riviera?
60856.e: Biokovo is a steep limestone range between Makarska and the hinterland. Its highest peak, Sveti Jure, is about 1,760 metres high.
60856.m: Biokovo rises behind the Makarska Riviera.

60857.q: Which town on the Dalmatian coast grew out of the palace of a Roman emperor?
60857.e: Emperor Diocletian had a large retirement residence built around AD 300. In the Middle Ages people settled inside the palace walls, and this became the old town of Split.
60857.m: Split's old town sits inside Diocletian's Palace.

60858.q: How does the western Algarve differ from the eastern Algarve?
a: Cliffs in the west, flat sandy coasts with lagoons in the east
Flat lagoons in the west, high cliffs in the east
Volcanoes in the west, glaciers in the east
Desert in the west, rainforest in the east
60858.e: The western Barlavento between Faro and Cabo de São Vicente is also called the rocky Algarve. East of Faro comes the flat Sotavento with sandy beaches and lagoons.
60858.m: The rocky Algarve lies in the west.

60859.q: Which rocks make up the yellow and reddish-brown cliffs of the rocky Algarve?
60859.e: The waves easily wash out these fairly soft sedimentary rocks. This creates many coves, grottoes and rock towers.
60859.m: The Algarve's cliffs are made of limestone and sandstone.

60860.q: How high are the cliffs of the Barlavento in the Algarve usually?
60860.e: The cliffs between Lagos and Sagres are usually a few dozen metres high, and about 75 metres at Cabo de São Vicente. Below them are small coves with sandy beaches.
60860.m: The Algarve cliffs are usually a few dozen metres high.

60861.q: Which cape in the Algarve is considered the south-westernmost point of mainland Europe?
60861.e: Cabo de São Vicente near Sagres was once thought of as the “end of the world”. Cabo da Roca near Lisbon, on the other hand, is the westernmost point.
60861.m: Cabo de São Vicente is the south-western tip of Europe.

60862.q: What are the rock towers standing freely in the sea, like those at Ponta da Piedade near Lagos, called?
60862.e: Sea stacks are the remains of a cliff that the waves have worn away all around. They are also simply called stacks.
60862.m: Sea stacks are the remains of a cliff that has retreated.

60863.q: In which order do the erosion features typically form on a limestone cliff coast?
60863.e: The waves widen cracks into caves, which join up to form an arch through a headland. If the roof of the arch collapses, a stack is left standing.
60863.m: A cave becomes an arch, and the arch becomes a stack.

60864.q: How does an active cliff like those in the Algarve retreat?
a: The waves hollow out its foot until the overhang breaks off
The rain washes the cliff down evenly from above
The whole cliff slowly sinks into the sea
The wind removes the rock face grain by grain
60864.e: Waves create a wave-cut notch at the foot of the cliff. When the overhang becomes too big, it collapses, and the process starts again.
60864.m: A cliff retreats because the waves undercut its foot.

60865.q: What is the flat rock surface called that forms in the surf zone in front of a retreating cliff?
60865.e: The waves grind the rock in front of the cliff into a surface that slopes gently towards the sea. It often becomes visible at low tide.
60865.m: In front of a cliff lies the wave-cut platform.
