60866.q: Which famous sea cave with a hole in its roof is on the rocky Algarve?
60866.e: The Benagil cave lies east of Carvoeiro and can only be reached from the sea. The Höllgrotten near Baar in the canton of Zug, by contrast, are inland caves with stalactites.
60866.m: The Benagil cave is a sea cave on the Algarve.

60867.q: Roughly how long is the Curonian Spit?
60867.e: The spit stretches from Zelenogradsk in the south to opposite Klaipėda in the north. The northern part belongs to Lithuania, the southern part to Russia.
60867.m: The Curonian Spit is almost 100 kilometres long.

60868.q: Roughly how high are the tallest shifting dunes on the Curonian Spit?
60868.e: The large dunes near Nida and Pervalka rise over 50 metres, and the highest reaches almost 70 metres above sea level. They are among the highest shifting dunes in Europe.
60868.m: The shifting dunes of the Curonian Spit are over 50 metres high.

60869.q: Which body of water lies between the Curonian Spit and the mainland?
60869.e: The Curonian Lagoon is a large, shallow lagoon. Near Klaipėda it is connected to the Baltic Sea by a narrow opening.
60869.m: Behind the Curonian Spit lies the Curonian Lagoon.

60870.q: Which process brought the sand for the Curonian Spit?
a: Longshore drift caused by waves arriving at an angle
The uplift of the sea floor
60870.e: Waves that hit the beach at an angle move sand step by step along the coast. Where the coast bends, the sand is deposited as a spit, which keeps growing.
60870.m: Spits form through sand being moved along the coast.

60871.q: In the 19th century, how were the shifting dunes of the Curonian Spit stopped after they had buried several villages?
a: With concrete walls across the dune
By digging them away with excavators
60871.e: After the forests were cut down, the dunes moved inland unhindered. Marram grass, pine trees and a foredune fixed the sand in place again.
60871.m: Plants hold the sand of shifting dunes in place.

60872.q: Which two countries share the Curonian Spit today?
60872.e: The northern part with Nida belongs to Lithuania, the southern part to the Russian exclave of Kaliningrad. The whole spit is a UNESCO World Heritage Site.
60872.m: The Curonian Spit belongs to Lithuania and Russia.

60873.q: Which institution in the village of Rossitten (today Rybachy) on the Curonian Spit is world-famous?
a: The oldest bird observatory in the world
The largest astronomical observatory in Europe
60873.e: An important migratory bird route crosses the spit. From 1901, birds were ringed systematically in Rossitten, much as was later done at the Swiss Ornithological Institute in Sempach.
60873.m: The world's oldest bird observatory is in Rossitten.

60874.q: Which writer had a summer house built in Nidden (Nida) on the Curonian Spit in 1930?
60874.e: Thomas Mann spent the summers from 1930 to 1932 in Nidden. Today the house is a cultural centre.
60874.m: Thomas Mann had a summer house on the Curonian Spit.

a: A river valley flooded by the sea
A sea valley deepened by a glacier
A strip of sand in front of a lagoon
60875.e: A ria is a former river valley that the sea has flowed into. It is often funnel-shaped and branched.
60875.m: A ria is a drowned river valley.

60876.q: What fundamentally distinguishes a ria from a fjord?
a: It was never carved out by glaciers
It is always deeper than a fjord
It is always in tropical regions
60876.e: Rias are river valleys with a V-shaped cross-section that were flooded only by rising sea levels. Fjords, by contrast, are troughs deepened by glaciers.
60876.m: Rias come from rivers, fjords from glaciers.

60877.q: Which process turned the river valleys of Galicia into rias?
a: The rise in sea level after the last Ice Age
The uplift of the land after the Ice Age
60877.e: When the ice sheets melted, sea level rose worldwide by over 100 metres. The sea pushed far into the lower courses of the rivers.
60877.m: Rias formed through the rise in sea level after the Ice Age.

60878.q: What is the southern group of Galician rias, which includes the Ría de Vigo, called?
60878.e: “Baixas” means “lower” in Galician. The Rías Altas lie in the north, for example near A Coruña and Ferrol.
60878.m: The Ría de Vigo is one of the Rías Baixas.

60879.q: Where does the word “ria” come from?
a: From the Galician word for river
From the Latin word for bay
From the Arabic word for harbour
From the Basque word for sea
60879.e: The Galician “ría” is related to “río” (river). The term was taken into geography from the coast of Galicia.
60879.m: The word ria comes from Galicia and refers to rivers.

60880.q: Which use is especially typical of the calm waters of the Rías Baixas?
a: Tidal power stations in the bays
Sea salt production in salt pans
60880.e: In the sheltered, nutrient-rich rias, mussels hang on ropes under wooden rafts called “bateas”. Galicia is one of the largest mussel producers in the world.
60880.m: The Rías Baixas are a centre of mussel farming.

60881.q: Apart from Galicia, which coast is a well-known example of a ria coast?
a: The North Sea coast of the Netherlands
60881.e: In Brittany, drowned river valleys called “abers” reach deep inland. Norway, by contrast, has fjords, Western Pomerania has bodden lagoons and the Netherlands has a smooth, straightened coast.
60881.m: Brittany also has a ria coast.

60882.q: Why are rias often good natural harbours?
a: They are sheltered, fairly deep and reach far inland
They never freeze because glaciers warm them
They are always filled with fresh water
60882.e: The drowned river valleys offer shelter from waves and enough depth for ships. That is why ports such as Vigo and Ferrol lie in rias.
60882.m: Rias provide sheltered, deep natural harbours.

60883.q: Why are ria coasts counted as transverse (discordant) coasts?
a: Because the valleys reach inland at right angles to the coastline
Because the islands lie parallel to the coast
Because the coast runs at right angles to the wind
Because glaciers flowed across the valley
60883.e: On a transverse coast, valleys and ridges meet the sea roughly at right angles. This creates bays reaching deep inland with peninsulas in between.
60883.m: Ria coasts are transverse coasts with deep bays.

a: Small rocky islands smoothed by ice
Sandbanks that disappear at high tide
Long chains of dunes off the coast
60884.e: Skerries are mostly flat, rounded humps of granite or gneiss. Huge numbers of them lie off the coasts of Sweden and Finland.
60884.m: Skerries are rocky islands smoothed by glaciers.

60885.q: Which glacial landform, when flooded by the sea, makes a typical skerry?
60885.e: Glaciers ground the rock smooth on the side facing the ice flow and plucked it away on the sheltered side. After the ice melted, these roches moutonnées stick out of the water as islands.
60885.m: A skerry is a roche moutonnée in the sea.

60886.q: Roughly how many islands make up the Stockholm archipelago?
60886.e: The archipelago stretches about 60 kilometres east of Stockholm. It is the largest group of islands in Sweden.
60886.m: The Stockholm archipelago has about 24,000 islands.

60887.q: Why do new islands keep appearing on Sweden's skerry coasts?
a: The land is rising after the ice melted
The Baltic Sea is evaporating more and more
60887.e: The heavy ice sheet had pressed the Earth's crust down. Since it melted, the crust has been slowly springing back, which is called isostatic uplift.
60887.m: Post-glacial uplift creates new skerries in Sweden.

60888.q: By how much has the land on the High Coast (Höga Kusten) in Sweden risen since the last Ice Age?
60888.e: At about 285 metres, the High Coast shows the greatest post-glacial uplift in the world. It has been a World Natural Heritage Site since 2000.
60888.m: The High Coast has risen by about 285 metres since the Ice Age.

60889.q: Roughly how fast is the land on the High Coast rising today?
60889.e: The uplift today is about 8 millimetres per year. In a hundred years that adds up to almost a metre.
60889.m: The High Coast rises by about eight millimetres a year.

60890.q: Which island group in the Baltic Sea is even larger than the Stockholm archipelago?
60890.e: The Archipelago Sea between Turku and Åland is considered the largest archipelago in the Baltic. The Stockholm archipelago comes second.
60890.m: The largest skerry archipelago in the Baltic lies off Finland.

60891.q: In which Swedish province on the west coast do reddish granite skerries shape the coastline?
60891.e: Bohuslän lies north of Gothenburg on the Skagerrak. The ice ground the reddish Bohus granite into smooth skerries.
60891.m: The skerries of Bohuslän are made of reddish granite.

60892.q: How many chemical elements are named after the village of Ytterby in the Stockholm archipelago?
60892.e: The names yttrium, ytterbium, terbium and erbium come from minerals found in the Ytterby mine on Resarö. No other place has given its name to so many elements.
60892.m: Four chemical elements are named after Ytterby.

60893.q: What does the name “Côte d'Azur” refer to?
a: The blue in the French flag
60893.e: Azur means sky blue. The poet Stéphen Liégeard coined the name in 1887 with his book “La Côte d'Azur”.
60893.m: The name Côte d'Azur means “sky-blue coast”.

60894.q: At which border does the Côte d'Azur end in the east?
a: At the border with Italy near Menton
At the border with Spain near Cerbère
At the mouth of the Rhône near Marseille
At the border with Monaco near Nice
60894.e: Menton is the last French town before Ventimiglia. In the west, the coast is counted as far as Toulon or Cassis, depending on the source.
60894.m: In the east, the Côte d'Azur reaches Menton on the Italian border.

60895.q: What is the origin of the red rocks of the Esterel massif on the Côte d'Azur?
a: They are made of present-day desert sand
60895.e: The rocks are made of rhyolite, a volcanic rock from the Palaeozoic era. Iron compounds colour it red.
60895.m: The red rocks of the Esterel are volcanic in origin.

60896.q: Why are winters on the Côte d'Azur especially mild?
a: The Maritime Alps shelter it from cold north winds
The Gulf Stream flows right along the coast
The sun is directly overhead there in winter
Warm springs heat the coastal water
60896.e: The mountains behind hold back cold air masses, and the Mediterranean stores heat. That is why the coast became a winter destination for wealthy travellers in the 19th century.
60896.m: The Alps behind it make the Côte d'Azur mild in winter.

60897.q: Which independent microstate lies on the Côte d'Azur?
60897.e: The Principality of Monaco is surrounded by French territory on all sides except the sea. After the Vatican, it is the second smallest country in the world.
60897.m: Monaco lies in the middle of the Côte d'Azur.

60898.q: Who is the Promenade des Anglais in Nice named after?
a: English winter visitors who started its construction
An English king who lived there
60898.e: In the 19th century, many English people spent the winter in Nice. In the 1820s they paid for a first path along the shore, which was later turned into a grand boulevard.
60898.m: The Promenade des Anglais recalls the English winter visitors in Nice.

60899.q: Which seafront promenade is the landmark of Cannes?
60899.e: The Boulevard de la Croisette runs along the bay of Cannes. The Festival Palace of the film festival stands on it.
60899.m: La Croisette is the famous seafront road of Cannes.

60900.q: Apart from the island itself, what does the Port-Cros National Park off Hyères protect?
a: The surrounding sea with its seagrass meadows
The castles of the Maritime Alps
A glacier in the Maritime Alps
The marshes of the Rhône delta
60900.e: Port-Cros was founded in 1963 and was one of the first national parks in Europe to include a marine area. The seagrass meadows are a nursery for many fish.
60900.m: Port-Cros is a marine national park on the Côte d'Azur.

60901.q: In which French department are Nice, Cannes and Antibes?
60901.e: The Alpes-Maritimes department stretches from the Maritime Alps to the sea, and its main town is Nice. Saint-Tropez, by contrast, is in the Var department.
60901.m: Nice, Cannes and Antibes are in the Alpes-Maritimes.

60902.q: What happens on a cliff coast when the waves hollow out the foot of the cliff?
a: The cliff collapses and the coast retreats
The coast grows out towards the sea
A delta forms in front of the cliff
The salt hardens the cliff permanently
60902.e: The waves cut a notch into the foot of the cliff. When the overhang becomes too heavy, it breaks off, and the coast moves back inland. On the Holderness coast in England this is up to 2 metres per year.
60902.m: Waves undercut cliffs until they collapse.

60903.q: Why is the Holderness coast eroding so quickly?
a: It is made of soft glacial till
It is made of hard but cracked granite
A volcano is pushing the coast down
60903.e: The cliffs are made of loose boulder clay, which glaciers deposited in the last Ice Age. Waves and rain wear it away easily.
60903.m: Soft glacial material makes Holderness vulnerable to erosion.

60904.q: What is the “Sand Engine” (Zandmotor) on the Dutch coast near The Hague?
a: An artificial sand peninsula whose sand is spread by nature
A pumping station that removes sand from polders
A machine that shapes dunes with wind
A power station that makes electricity from sand
60904.e: In 2011 a hook-shaped area of sand was pumped up off Ter Heijde. Currents and wind gradually spread the sand onto the neighbouring beaches.
60904.m: With the Sand Engine, nature spreads deposited sand along the coast.

60905.q: What is the biggest advantage of the Sand Engine near The Hague compared with yearly beach nourishment?
a: Sand only has to be pumped once instead of every year
The sand stays in the same place for ever
It needs no sand from the sea at all
It keeps the wind away from the dunes
60905.e: In 2011 about 21.5 million cubic metres of sand were pumped up in one go. Waves and currents spread it along the coast over about 20 years, so fewer operations are needed and nature on the beach is disturbed less often.
60905.m: The Sand Engine replaces many small nourishments with one big one.

60906.q: What are groynes, built into the sea at right angles to the beach, for?
a: They slow down the movement of sand along the coast
They break the waves far out at sea
They carry river water into the sea
They stop salt water getting in
60906.e: Groynes trap the sand that the current carries parallel to the beach. On the side facing away from the current, however, more sand may be lost.
60906.m: Groynes hold sand on the beach.

60907.q: Which method has mainly been used since the 1970s to make up for sand loss on the west coast of Sylt?
60907.e: Special ships pump about one million cubic metres of sand onto the beach every year. This soft coastal protection replaces the sand that storms carry away.
60907.m: Sylt is protected by beach nourishment.

60908.q: What is the free-standing red rock tower on Heligoland, threatened by the waves, called?
60908.e: Lange Anna (“Tall Anna”) is a sea stack about 47 metres high made of red sandstone. Without protective structures, its foot would quickly wear away further.
60908.m: Lange Anna is the landmark of Heligoland.

60909.q: Why do rocks keep breaking off the chalk coast of Rügen?
a: Frost, rain and waves undermine the soft chalk
The level of the Baltic Sea is falling fast
Glaciers push the rocks into the sea
60909.e: Chalk is a soft rock. Freezing water forces cracks open, rain softens the slope and the waves gnaw at the foot. In 2005 the well-known Wissower Klinken mostly fell into the sea in this way.
60909.m: Frost, rain and waves wear away the chalk cliffs of Rügen.

60910.q: Why can a sea wall even increase erosion on neighbouring stretches of coast?
a: It cuts off the supply of sand along the coast
It attracts the tides more strongly
It warms the water off the coast
It makes the sea level rise locally
60910.e: Behind the wall, no more material is worn away that the current could carry onwards. The neighbouring beaches lack this sand and are eroded more strongly.
60910.m: Hard coastal defences can starve neighbouring beaches.

60911.q: In countries with low mortality, roughly how high must the total fertility rate be for a population to stay the same size in the long run without immigration?
60911.e: This so-called replacement level is about 2.1, because on average each woman has to replace herself and a partner. The value is slightly above 2 because not all girls reach childbearing age and slightly more boys are born.
60911.m: Without immigration, a stable population needs about 2.1 children per woman.

60912.q: What effect does a permanently low birth rate have on pension systems such as the AHV (old-age insurance)?
a: Fewer workers have to pay for more pensioners
60912.e: If few children are born over decades, there will later be fewer people in work. At the same time, people live longer. As a result, there are fewer and fewer contributors for each person of retirement age.
60912.m: Few births put a strain on pensions later on.

60913.q: According to Eurostat, how many children did a woman in Spain have on average in 2023?
60913.e: In 2023 Spain had a total fertility rate of about 1.12, making it one of the countries with the lowest figures in the EU.
60913.m: With about 1.1 children per woman, Spain is one of Europe's countries with the fewest births.

60914.q: What does a fertility rate of about 1.2 children per woman mean for a population without immigration?
a: Each generation is much smaller than the one before
The population stays the same size in the long run
60914.e: A stable population needs about 2.1 children per woman. With about 1.2 children, each new generation is almost half the size of the parents' generation. Countries such as Spain and Italy are close to such figures.
60914.m: At about 1.2 children per woman, each new generation shrinks sharply.

60915.q: Which factor is considered an important cause of the falling birth rate in southern Europe?
a: Young adults move out of home late
There are a great many nurseries
60915.e: In Italy, Spain and Greece, young people leave their parents' home at around 30 on average. Insecure jobs, high youth unemployment and expensive housing delay starting a family.
60915.m: People who move out late and have insecure work often start a family late.

60916.q: How does the shape of the population pyramid change when births fall sharply over decades?
a: It becomes narrower at the bottom and looks like an urn
It becomes wider at the bottom like a triangle
It becomes narrower at the top like a tower
It stays unchanged like a bell
60916.e: When fewer children are born, the lower age groups become narrower than the middle ones. This creates the typical urn shape of ageing societies.
60916.m: An urn-shaped population pyramid shows a shrinking, ageing population.

60917.q: How did the number of births in the EU in 2023 compare with the year before?
a: It fell more sharply than ever since 1961
It rose to a new record
It stayed practically exactly the same
It rose clearly because of immigration
60917.e: In 2023 about 3.67 million children were born in the EU, around 5 per cent fewer than the year before. According to Eurostat, that was the biggest drop since records began in 1961.
60917.m: In 2023 births in the EU fell more sharply than at any time since 1961.

60918.q: According to Eurostat, what was the total fertility rate of the whole EU in 2023?
60918.e: In 2023 the EU reached a figure of 1.38 children per woman. That is well below the replacement level that would keep a population stable without immigration.
60918.m: At about 1.4 children per woman, the EU is clearly below replacement level.

60919.q: What does the total fertility rate measure?
a: The number of children a woman would have at current age-specific birth rates
The number of births per 1,000 inhabitants
The number of children per household
The share of children in the population
60919.e: The figure adds up the birth rates of all ages from about 15 to 49. It shows how many children a woman would have if today's rates applied throughout her life.
60919.m: The total fertility rate gives the average number of children per woman.

60920.q: According to Eurostat, which EU country had the highest median age of its population in 2024?
60920.e: Italy's median age in 2024 was about 48.7 years, well above the EU figure of about 44.7 years. Ireland had the youngest population.
60920.m: Italy has the oldest population in the EU.

60921.q: How has the number of births in Italy changed since the 1960s?
a: It has fallen to about a third
It has stayed about the same
It has fallen to about a hundredth
60921.e: In the 1960s about one million children were born each year; in 2024, according to ISTAT, it was just under 370,000. That is a historic low.
60921.m: Only about a third as many children are born in Italy today as in the 1960s.

60922.q: According to ISTAT, what was Italy's total fertility rate in 2024?
60922.e: ISTAT reported about 1.18 children per woman for 2024, one of the lowest figures ever recorded in the country.
60922.m: Italian women have only about 1.2 children on average.

60923.q: What does it mean that Italy has had a negative natural balance for years?
a: More people die than are born
More boys than girls are born
60923.e: The natural balance is the difference between births and deaths. In Italy deaths clearly outnumber births, so without immigration the population shrinks.
60923.m: A negative natural balance means deaths outnumber births.

60924.q: Which problem caused by Italy's ageing population is especially serious for the state budget?
a: Rising pension spending with fewer people in work
60924.e: Italy spends one of the largest shares of its economic output in the EU on pensions. At the same time, fewer and fewer workers are paying for pensions in a pay-as-you-go system.
60924.m: When fewer young people pay for more old people, the pension system comes under pressure.

60925.q: Which figure compares the number of people over 64 with the number of people of working age?
60925.e: The old-age dependency ratio shows how many older people there are for every 100 people of working age. Italy has one of the highest old-age dependency ratios in the EU.
60925.m: The old-age dependency ratio measures the burden of the older generation on people in work.

60926.q: Which measure do some depopulated villages in Italy use to attract new residents?
a: Selling empty houses for a symbolic one euro
Banning people from moving to the cities
Abolishing all local taxes for pensioners
Building new motorways through the villages
60926.e: Municipalities such as Salemi and Sambuca in Sicily offered empty houses for 1 euro. Buyers must promise to renovate the buildings within a few years.
60926.m: Italian villages fight depopulation with one-euro houses.

60927.q: Which region of Italy is considered a “Blue Zone” because of its many centenarians?
60927.e: In the mountains of Sardinia, especially in the province of Ogliastra, an unusually large number of very old people live, above all men. Researchers study their diet, exercise and social ties there.
60927.m: Sardinia is one of the well-known Blue Zones with many centenarians.

60928.q: What does “fuga dei cervelli” mean in Italy?
a: The emigration of well-educated young people
The arrival of pensioners from northern Europe
The flight from the countryside to the cities in the 19th century
The return of emigrants from America
60928.e: The expression means “brain drain” (literally “flight of brains”). Many young graduates go abroad, which makes the ageing of the country even worse.
60928.m: In Italy the emigration of young skilled people is called “fuga dei cervelli”.

60929.q: How many inhabitants did Bulgaria have in the 2021 census?
60929.e: The 2021 census counted about 6.52 million inhabitants. That was around 840,000 fewer than in the 2011 census.
60929.m: In 2021 Bulgaria had only about 6.5 million inhabitants.

60930.q: Roughly how many inhabitants did Bulgaria have at its peak at the end of the 1980s?
60930.e: At the end of the 1980s almost 9 million people lived in Bulgaria. Since then the country has lost about a quarter of its population.
60930.m: Bulgaria has lost about a quarter of its population since the end of communism.

60931.q: Which two causes mainly explain Bulgaria's sharp population decline?
a: Emigration and more deaths than births
Border changes and loss of territory
60931.e: Since 1989, hundreds of thousands of mostly young people have moved abroad. In addition, far more people have died in Bulgaria than have been born for years.
60931.m: Emigration and more deaths than births are shrinking Bulgaria's population.

60932.q: According to Eurostat, which region of Bulgaria was long considered the poorest region in the EU?
60932.e: The North-West region around towns such as Vidin and Vratsa has the lowest income per head in the EU. It is losing especially many inhabitants through emigration.
60932.m: North-western Bulgaria is one of the poorest and fastest-shrinking regions in the EU.

60933.q: Which event of 1989 is known as the “Big Excursion”?
a: The departure of about 360,000 Bulgarian Turks to Turkey
The opening of the border with Greece for tourists
The mass departure of students to West Germany
The resettlement of farmers to Sofia
60933.e: After forced measures against the Turkish minority, about 360,000 people left Bulgaria for Turkey in 1989. Some of them later returned.
60933.m: The “Big Excursion” of 1989 was the emigration of many Bulgarian Turks.

60934.q: According to Eurostat, which EU country had the highest total fertility rate in 2023 despite a shrinking population?
60934.e: With about 1.81 children per woman, Bulgaria was top of the EU in 2023, ahead of France. The population loss comes mainly from emigration and high mortality.
60934.m: High fertility rates alone do not stop a population falling if many people emigrate.

60935.q: Which sector in Bulgaria suffers especially from the emigration of skilled workers?
a: Tourism on the Black Sea coast
Rose oil production in the Rose Valley
60935.e: Many Bulgarian doctors and nurses work in Germany or other EU countries, where wages are much higher. Rural hospitals struggle to fill posts.
60935.m: The emigration of medical staff weakens Bulgarian healthcare.

60936.q: Within Bulgaria, where do especially many people from rural areas move to?
60936.e: Sofia is the economic centre and one of the few regions with a growing population. Many villages, by contrast, are ageing or almost abandoned.
60936.m: While villages empty, it is mainly Sofia that is growing in Bulgaria.

60937.q: What increased emigration from Bulgaria to other European countries from 2007 onwards?
a: Joining the EU, with access to the European labour market
60937.e: When Bulgaria joined the EU, its citizens gradually gained the right to work in other EU countries. The last transitional restrictions ended in 2014 at the latest.
60937.m: Joining the EU made labour migration from Bulgaria much easier.

60938.q: Which four fundamental freedoms of the EU single market include the free movement of workers?
60938.e: The single market is based on the free movement of goods, persons, services and capital. The free movement of workers is part of the free movement of persons.
60938.m: The EU single market rests on four fundamental freedoms.

60939.q: Since when has the Agreement on the Free Movement of Persons between Switzerland and the EU been in force?
60939.e: The agreement is part of the Bilateral Agreements I, which were signed in 1999. It came into force on 1 June 2002.
60939.m: Free movement of persons with the EU has applied in Switzerland since 2002.

60940.q: What does the so-called guillotine clause of the Bilateral Agreements I do?
a: If one agreement is terminated, all seven lapse
New EU members are automatically included
Switzerland must adopt EU law immediately
Cross-border commuters must pay a tax
60940.e: The seven agreements of the Bilaterals I are legally linked. If Switzerland terminated free movement of persons, for example, the other six agreements would also cease to apply.
60940.m: Because of the guillotine clause, the Bilaterals I hang together.

60941.q: How did Swiss voters decide on the limitation initiative in September 2020?
a: They rejected it with about 62 per cent voting no
They narrowly accepted it with 50.3 per cent
They rejected it with over 80 per cent
They accepted it with about 58 per cent
60941.e: The initiative wanted to end free movement of persons with the EU. On 27 September 2020 about 61.7 per cent of voters said no.
60941.m: The limitation initiative was clearly rejected in 2020.

60942.q: What are Switzerland's measures against wage and social dumping in connection with the free movement of persons called?
60942.e: Since 2004 the cantons and the social partners have checked whether foreign companies and posted workers comply with Swiss wage and working conditions. This is meant to stop wages coming under pressure.
60942.m: The accompanying measures protect wages in Switzerland from dumping.

60943.q: Which group of foreign nationals is the largest in Switzerland (as of 2024)?
60943.e: According to the Federal Statistical Office, people with Italian nationality form the largest foreign group, just ahead of Germans and Portuguese. Many came as guest workers after the Second World War.
60943.m: Italians are the largest foreign population group in Switzerland.

60944.q: What were the old EU member states allowed to do for a few years after the eastern enlargement of 2004?
a: Restrict access to their labour market
Charge customs duties on goods from the new states
Deny the new states the right to vote
60944.e: Transitional rules allowed them to restrict the free movement of workers for up to seven years. Germany and Austria used the full period until 2011.
60944.m: After the eastern enlargement, old EU states could protect their labour markets for a while.

60945.q: Which permit do cross-border commuters from EU countries receive in Switzerland?
60945.e: The G cross-border commuter permit is for people who live abroad and work in Switzerland. As a rule they must return to their place of residence at least once a week.
60945.m: Cross-border commuters work in Switzerland with a G permit.

60946.q: Which country ended free movement of persons with the EU at the end of 2020?
60946.e: With Brexit and the end of the transition period on 31 December 2020, free movement between the United Kingdom and the EU ended. Since then a points-based immigration system has applied.
60946.m: Brexit ended free movement of persons between the UK and the EU.

60947.q: On which body of water near Schengen was the first Schengen Agreement signed?
a: On a boat on the Moselle
On a boat on the Rhine
On a ferry on the Saar
On a boat on the Meuse
60947.e: Representatives of five countries signed it on the pleasure boat “Princesse Marie-Astrid” on the Moselle. Luxembourg, Germany and France meet there.
60947.m: The Schengen Agreement was signed on a boat on the Moselle.

60948.q: Which five countries signed the first Schengen Agreement?
a: Germany, France and the three Benelux countries
France, Italy and the three Benelux countries
60948.e: The Federal Republic of Germany, France, Belgium, the Netherlands and Luxembourg began removing border controls. Other countries joined later.
60948.m: Five founding states laid the foundations of the Schengen Area.

60949.q: What does the abbreviation SIS stand for in the Schengen Area?
60949.e: The SIS is a shared search database in which police and border authorities post alerts for wanted people and stolen objects. It makes up for the removal of internal border controls.
60949.m: The Schengen Information System links the member states' police searches.

60950.q: How did Switzerland vote on joining Schengen and Dublin in June 2005?
60950.e: On 5 June 2005, 54.6 per cent of voters accepted the association agreements. The agreements are part of the Bilateral Agreements II.
60950.m: In 2005 Switzerland narrowly said yes to Schengen and Dublin.

60951.q: What changed for travellers at Swiss airports when Schengen was introduced?
a: Passport checks no longer apply on flights within the Schengen Area
All flights now need a visa
60951.e: Since 2009 flights within the Schengen Area have been treated like domestic flights, with no passport control. Customs checks remain, however, because Switzerland is not in the EU customs union.
60951.m: Schengen flights from Switzerland no longer have passport control.

60952.q: Which non-EU country joined the Schengen Area in 2011 as the last of today's associated states?
60952.e: Liechtenstein brought Schengen into force in December 2011. Together with Switzerland, Norway and Iceland, it is an associated state.
60952.m: Liechtenstein has been part of the Schengen Area since 2011.

60953.q: Which EU member does not yet fully apply the Schengen rules because the island is divided (as of 2025)?
60953.e: Cyprus is obliged to introduce Schengen, but the unresolved division of the island makes it hard to control the external border. That is why there are still passport checks.
60953.m: Cyprus is an EU member but not yet a full Schengen member.

60954.q: Since when has Croatia been fully part of the Schengen Area?
60954.e: Croatia joined the EU in 2013. On 1 January 2023 the checks at its borders with Slovenia and Hungary ended, and at the same time it introduced the euro.
60954.m: Croatia has been a member of the Schengen Area since 2023.

60955.q: What may Schengen countries do in exceptional cases despite open internal borders?
a: Permanently expel citizens of other Schengen countries
Require their own visas for EU citizens
Charge customs duties on goods at the border
60955.e: The Schengen Borders Code allows temporary internal border controls if there is a serious threat to public order. Several countries did this, for example during the 2015 migration crisis and the Covid pandemic.
60955.m: In emergencies, Schengen countries may carry out checks at internal borders for a limited time.

60956.q: Which EU agency helps member states monitor the Schengen external borders?
60956.e: Frontex is the European Border and Coast Guard Agency, based in Warsaw. As a Schengen country, Switzerland takes part in it.
60956.m: Frontex helps protect the Schengen external borders.

60957.q: Which language family does Hungarian belong to?
60957.e: Like Finnish and Estonian, Hungarian is a Uralic language. The ancestors of the Hungarians came from the east into the Carpathian Basin in the 9th century.
60957.m: Hungarian is distantly related to Finnish.

60958.q: Which ancient language of India turned out to be closely related to Greek and Latin?
60958.e: At the end of the 18th century, scholars realised that Sanskrit, Greek and Latin go back to a common ancestor language. This is how the Indo-European language family was discovered, which German and English also belong to.
60958.m: Like English and German, Sanskrit belongs to the Indo-European language family.

60959.q: Which language of Europe belongs to the Turkic languages?
60959.e: Turkish is the most widely spoken Turkic language and is spoken in the European part of Turkey and parts of the Balkans. It is not Indo-European.
60959.m: Turkish belongs to the Turkic language family.

60960.q: Which language is a North Germanic language?
60960.e: Icelandic, Faroese, Norwegian, Swedish and Danish make up the North Germanic languages. Icelandic has changed particularly little since Old Norse.
60960.m: Icelandic is the closest to Old Norse.

60961.q: Which language with its own script belongs to the Kartvelian language family?
60961.e: Georgian is the most important Kartvelian language and is written in its own script. This small language family is found almost only in the South Caucasus.
60961.m: Georgian is one of the Kartvelian languages of the Caucasus.

60962.q: How many official languages does the European Union have (as of 2025)?
60962.e: The EU has 24 official languages for 27 member states, because some countries share the same language. Irish has had full equal status since 2022.
60962.m: The EU works with 24 official languages.

60963.q: According to estimates, which European language has the most native speakers in Europe?
60963.e: If the European part of Russia is included, Russian is the native language of the most people in Europe. Within the EU, German has the most native speakers.
60963.m: Russian has the most native speakers in Europe.

60964.q: Which sound shift describes the change from Indo-European to Germanic, for example from Latin “pater” to English “father”?
a: Second or High German sound shift
60964.e: In the first sound shift, p became f, t became th and k became h, among other changes. It was described by Rasmus Rask and Jacob Grimm and is therefore also called Grimm's law.
60964.m: The first sound shift separates Germanic from the rest of Indo-European.

60965.q: In which Russian republic in Europe is a Mongolic language widely spoken?
60965.e: The Kalmyks speak a Mongolic language and are mostly Buddhists. Their republic lies on the lower Volga, north-west of the Caspian Sea.
60965.m: Kalmykia is the only region of Europe with a mainly Buddhist tradition.

60966.q: Which language family provides three of Switzerland's four national languages?
60966.e: French, Italian and Romansh are Romance languages that developed from Latin. Only German belongs to the Germanic languages.
60966.m: Three of Switzerland's four national languages are Romance languages.

60967.q: What do the Basques call their own language?
60967.e: The Basques call their language Euskara and their country Euskal Herria. The language is spoken on both sides of the western Pyrenees.
60967.m: In Basque, the Basque language is called Euskara.

60968.q: Which Basque town was bombed by German and Italian aircraft on 26 April 1937 during the Spanish Civil War?
60968.e: The Condor Legion largely destroyed the symbolic town. Pablo Picasso portrayed the attack in his famous painting “Guernica”.
60968.m: The bombing of Gernika became world-famous through Picasso's painting.

60969.q: Which city is the seat of the government and parliament of the Basque Autonomous Community?
60969.e: Bilbao is the largest city, but the government and parliament are based in Vitoria-Gasteiz in the province of Álava.
60969.m: Vitoria-Gasteiz is the seat of the Basque government.

60970.q: In which year did the Basque underground organisation ETA announce its dissolution?
60970.e: ETA had declared a definitive end to violence in 2011. In 2018 it announced its complete dissolution.

60971.q: What is special about the finances of the Spanish Basque Country?
a: It pays no taxes to Spain
It receives its money directly from the EU
60971.e: Thanks to the historic economic agreement (“Concierto Económico”), the Basque provinces collect most taxes themselves. They pay Spain a contribution for shared tasks.
60971.m: The Basque Country has extensive powers over taxation.

60972.q: On which day did the disputed independence referendum take place in Catalonia?
60972.e: The Spanish Constitutional Court had banned the vote. It went ahead despite police operations, after which Madrid temporarily took control of the regional government.
60972.m: The Catalan independence referendum took place on 1 October 2017.

60973.q: Which event does the Diada, Catalonia's national day on 11 September, commemorate?
a: The fall of Barcelona in 1714 in the War of the Spanish Succession
The founding of the Generalitat in 1977
The end of the Franco dictatorship in 1975
60973.e: On 11 September 1714 Bourbon troops captured Barcelona. Afterwards Catalonia lost its own institutions.
60973.m: The Diada commemorates the fall of Barcelona in 1714.

60974.q: In which town on Sardinia is a form of Catalan still spoken today?
60974.e: Alghero was conquered by the Crown of Aragon in the 14th century and settled with Catalans. Part of the population still speaks Catalan today.
60974.m: Catalan lives on in Alghero on Sardinia.

60975.q: Which Catalan tradition has been part of UNESCO's Intangible Cultural Heritage since 2010?
60975.e: In castells, teams climb on top of each other and build towers up to ten storeys high. The motto is strength, balance, courage and good sense.
60975.m: Catalan human towers are UNESCO cultural heritage.

60976.q: What is the Catalan regional government called?
60976.e: The Generalitat goes back to a medieval institution and was restored after the end of the Franco dictatorship. It is based in the Palau de la Generalitat in Barcelona.
60976.m: Catalonia's government is called the Generalitat.

60977.q: Which language family do the Sámi languages belong to?
60977.e: The Sámi languages are related to Finnish and Estonian. This makes them fundamentally different from Norwegian and Swedish.
60977.m: The Sámi languages are Uralic languages.

60978.q: Which Sámi language has the most speakers?
60978.e: Northern Sámi is spoken in Norway, Sweden and Finland and accounts for the great majority of speakers. Several other Sámi languages are seriously endangered.
60978.m: Northern Sámi is the most widely spoken Sámi language.

60979.q: What status of the Sámi is unique in the EU?
a: They are the only recognised indigenous people in the EU
They have their own EU member state
They are exempt from all EU laws
They have their own official EU language
60979.e: The Sámi in Sweden and Finland are considered the only indigenous people within the EU. Norway is not part of the EU.
60979.m: The Sámi are the only indigenous people in the EU.

60980.q: Which country was the first to ratify ILO Convention 169 on the rights of indigenous peoples, in 1990?
60980.e: Norway ratified the convention in 1990, the first country in the world to do so. Sweden and Finland have still not ratified it.
60980.m: Norway was the first country to ratify ILO Convention 169.

60981.q: What is the elected assembly of the Sámi in Norway, Sweden and Finland called?
60981.e: In each of the three countries the Sámi elect their own Sámi Parliament. The Storting, Riksdag and Eduskunta, by contrast, are the national parliaments of Norway, Sweden and Finland.
60981.m: The parliament of the Sámi is called the Sameting.

60982.q: What is the traditional dress of the Sámi called?
60982.e: The cut and patterns of the colourful gákti often show which region the wearer comes from. It is worn at celebrations and in everyday life.
60982.m: The Sámi traditional dress is called gákti.

60983.q: Which way of making a living is still especially important culturally for many Sámi?
60983.e: In Norway and Sweden, reindeer herding is partly reserved by law for the Sámi. Today, however, only a minority of Sámi live mainly from it.
60983.m: Reindeer herding still shapes Sámi culture today.

60984.q: Which conflict particularly affects Sámi reindeer herders in Norway, for example on the Fosen peninsula?
a: Wind farms being built on grazing land
Ski resorts being built in the Alps
60984.e: In 2021 Norway's Supreme Court ruled that wind farms on Fosen violated the rights of Sámi reindeer herders. The case led to large protests.
60984.m: Wind farms on grazing land lead to conflicts with Sámi reindeer herders.

60985.q: What was the policy called with which Norway long pressured the Sámi to give up their language and culture?
60985.e: From about the middle of the 19th century until well into the 20th century, Sámi was suppressed in schools. A Truth and Reconciliation Commission presented its report on this in 2023.
60985.m: Norwegianisation long suppressed the Sámi language.

60986.q: According to current knowledge, which region did the ancestors of the Roma come from?
60986.e: Language comparisons and genetic studies show that the ancestors of the Roma moved west from northern India about 1,000 years ago. The old belief that they came from Egypt was wrong.
60986.m: The ancestors of the Roma came from northern India.

60987.q: Which language group does Romani, the language of the Roma, belong to?
60987.e: Romani is related to languages such as Hindi but contains many loanwords from Persian, Greek and the languages of Europe. Despite the similar name, it has nothing to do with the Romance languages.

60988.q: According to Council of Europe estimates, roughly how many Roma live in Europe?
60988.e: The Council of Europe estimates their number at 10 to 12 million. This makes the Roma Europe's largest ethnic minority.
60988.m: The Roma are the largest minority in Europe.

60989.q: Why is the word “Gypsy” considered problematic today?
a: It is a derogatory name given by outsiders
It is a protected brand name
It comes from the Romani language
It only refers to people from India
60989.e: The name was given by the majority society and is linked to prejudice and persecution. The groups themselves use names such as Roma, Sinti or Yenish.
60989.m: Roma and Sinti prefer their own names to “Gypsy”.

60990.q: What does the European Holocaust Memorial Day for Sinti and Roma on 2 August commemorate?
a: The murder of the last prisoners of the “Gypsy camp” at Auschwitz-Birkenau in 1944
The start of the Second World War in 1939
60990.e: On the night of 2 to 3 August 1944, the SS murdered the roughly 4,300 Sinti and Roma remaining in that section of the Birkenau camp. The European Parliament recognised the memorial day in 2015.
60990.m: On 2 August the genocide of the Sinti and Roma is remembered.

60991.q: What does the Roma flag show in the middle?
60991.e: The flag is blue at the top for the sky and green at the bottom for the earth. In the middle is a red wheel, recalling the origins in India and life on the move.
60991.m: The Roma flag shows a red wheel on blue and green.

60992.q: Which two groups did the Federal Council recognise as national minorities of Switzerland in 2016?
60992.e: The Federal Council recognised the Yenish and Sinti, using their own names, as a national minority under the Council of Europe's Framework Convention.
60992.m: The Yenish and Sinti are recognised as a national minority in Switzerland.

60993.q: What is the genocide of the Sinti and Roma under National Socialism often called in Romani?
60993.e: Porajmos means something like “the devouring”. Some people prefer the term Samudaripen, which means “mass murder”.
60993.m: The genocide of the Roma is called the Porajmos.

60994.q: Which migration route leads mainly from Libya and Tunisia to Italy and Malta?
60994.e: Via the Central Mediterranean route, people mainly reach Lampedusa and Sicily. According to the International Organization for Migration, it is the deadliest known migration route in the world.
60994.m: The Central Mediterranean route is the most dangerous migration route in the world.

60995.q: Which migration route leads from Turkey to Greek islands such as Lesbos?
60995.e: On this route the crossing is short, but the boats are often overcrowded. In 2015 hundreds of thousands reached the EU this way.
60995.m: The Eastern Mediterranean route links Turkey with the Greek islands.

60996.q: Which agreement was meant to reduce crossings from Turkey to Greece from March 2016?
60996.e: Turkey agreed to take back migrants who had reached Greece irregularly. In return, the EU promised, among other things, billions in aid for refugees in Turkey.
60996.m: The 2016 EU-Turkey Statement sharply reduced arrivals on the Greek islands.

60997.q: Which Italian naval operation rescued tens of thousands of people for a year after the boat disaster off Lampedusa in 2013?
60997.e: After the disaster of 3 October 2013, with over 360 dead, Italy launched Operation Mare Nostrum. At the end of 2014 it was replaced by the smaller EU operation Triton.
60997.m: Mare Nostrum was Italy's large rescue operation in the Mediterranean.

60998.q: Which rule of the Dublin Regulation puts a particular burden on Mediterranean countries?
a: Usually the country of first entry is responsible for the asylum procedure
Asylum seekers may freely choose their destination country
Every country takes in the same number of asylum seekers
Asylum applications are only examined in Brussels
60998.e: Because many people arrive first in Italy, Greece, Malta or Spain, these countries are often responsible. Switzerland also applies Dublin as an associated state.
60998.m: Under Dublin, the country of first entry is usually responsible for an asylum application.

60999.q: Which two Spanish cities on the North African coast are protected by high border fences?
60999.e: Ceuta and Melilla are Spanish exclaves in North Africa and therefore EU territory. Again and again, people try to get over the fences.
60999.m: Ceuta and Melilla are Spanish cities on the coast of North Africa.

61000.q: According to UNHCR, roughly how many people came to Europe across the Mediterranean in 2015?
61000.e: In 2015 over a million people reached Europe by sea, most of them Greece. Many were fleeing the war in Syria.
61000.m: In 2015 about a million people came to Europe across the Mediterranean.

61001.q: Why could a no vote on the Frontex proposal in May 2022 have been risky for Switzerland?
a: Its Schengen membership would have been at risk
Switzerland would have had to leave the UN
The franc would have been replaced by the euro
The army would have had to be disbanded
61001.e: Frontex is the border agency of the Schengen countries, which include Switzerland. Voters accepted the proposal on 15 May 2022 with about 71.5 per cent.
61001.m: In 2022 Switzerland clearly said yes to a higher Frontex contribution.

61002.q: Which group of islands is the destination of the dangerous Atlantic route from West Africa to Spain?
61002.e: Boats set off from the coasts of Morocco, Mauritania, Senegal or the Gambia and sometimes travel over 1,000 km across the open Atlantic. The Canaries belong to Spain and therefore to the EU.
61002.m: The Atlantic route leads from West Africa to the Canary Islands.

61003.q: Roughly how many inhabitants does the Netherlands have (as of 2024)?
61003.e: In 2024, according to the statistics office CBS, the Netherlands passed the mark of 18 million inhabitants.
61003.m: The Netherlands has about 18 million inhabitants.

61004.q: Roughly how high is the population density of the Netherlands in relation to its land area?
61004.e: With about 18 million people and about 34,000 km² of land, that makes just over 500 inhabitants per km². This puts the Netherlands among the most densely populated larger countries in Europe.
61004.m: The Netherlands is one of the most densely populated larger countries in Europe.

61005.q: Roughly how does the population density of the Netherlands compare with that of Switzerland?
a: It is about two to two and a half times as high
It is about half as high
It is about ten times as high
61005.e: With about 9 million people on 41,285 km², Switzerland has about 220 inhabitants per km². In relation to its land area, the Netherlands has over 500.
61005.m: The Netherlands is more than twice as densely populated as Switzerland.

61006.q: What is the largely agricultural zone in the middle of the Randstad called?
61006.e: The “Green Heart” is meant to keep the cities of the Randstad apart and protect them from urban sprawl. It consists mainly of pastures, polders and lakes.
61006.m: The Groene Hart is the green centre of the Randstad.

61007.q: Which province was created in 1986 almost entirely on land reclaimed from the sea?
61007.e: Flevoland consists almost entirely of polders that were drained in the former Zuiderzee in the 20th century. Only small parts, such as the former island of Urk, were land before.
61007.m: Flevoland is the youngest province of the Netherlands.

61008.q: Which town in Flevoland was built on reclaimed land from the 1970s and grew to be the largest town in the province?
61008.e: Almere was built as an overspill town for Amsterdam. Today over 200,000 people live there, more than in any other town in the province.
61008.m: Almere is a planned town on polder land near Amsterdam.

61009.q: Why has the population of the Netherlands been growing for years, even though the fertility rate is below 2 children per woman?
a: Because of land reclaimed from the sea
Because of very many multiple births
61009.e: According to the statistics office CBS, population growth has been mostly due to immigration for years. Births alone would not keep the population stable in the long run.
61009.m: Immigration makes the population of the Netherlands grow.

61010.q: Following the plans of which engineer was the Zuiderzee closed off and partly drained?
61010.e: Cornelis Lely designed the Zuiderzee Works, which were approved in 1918. The newly gained land provided space for farming and new towns in the densely populated country.
61010.m: Cornelis Lely planned the draining of the Zuiderzee.

61012.q: Which European capital lies outside the Blue Banana, which was seen in France as a warning sign?
61012.e: Paris lies west of the belt that stretches from England via the Benelux countries and the Rhine valley to northern Italy. The study therefore showed that France was in danger of being left behind by Europe's core area.
61012.m: Paris is not in the Blue Banana.

61013.q: Which spatial economic model does the Blue Banana illustrate with its dense core and the weaker outer regions of Europe?
61013.e: The Blue Banana is considered Europe's economic centre, while regions such as southern Spain, southern Italy or eastern Europe count as the periphery. The concept therefore shows spatial inequality.
61013.m: In the core-periphery model, the Blue Banana stands for Europe's core.

61015.q: In the classic version, which area forms the southern end of the Blue Banana?
a: Northern Italy around Milan and Turin
61015.e: In the south, the Blue Banana ends in the industrial region of northern Italy with Milan, Turin and Genoa. Lyon and Barcelona lie outside it.
61015.m: In the south, the Blue Banana ends in northern Italy.

61016.q: In the classic version, where does the Blue Banana begin in the north-west?
61016.e: The belt begins in the old industrial regions of north-west England around Manchester and Liverpool and runs via London to the English Channel.
61016.m: North-west England forms the start of the Blue Banana.

61017.q: What is the fast-growing area along the Mediterranean coast from Valencia to northern Italy often called, as a counterpart to the Blue Banana?
61017.e: Because of its growth in high-tech, services and tourism, the northern Mediterranean arc is also called the “Sunbelt” or “Golden Banana”.
61017.m: The Golden Banana lies on the Mediterranean.

61018.q: What is the EU spatial concept of 1999 called that describes the core area as a five-sided shape between London, Paris, Milan, Munich and Hamburg?
61018.e: In the European Spatial Development Perspective (ESDP), the economic core was described as a “Pentagon” with five corner cities. Unlike the Blue Banana, it includes Paris.
61018.m: The EU Pentagon links five major economic centres.

61019.q: Which description fits the Blue Banana best geographically?
a: A polycentric axis of cities with a high density of economic activity
A single large area around one metropolis
A rural farming corridor with little industry
A thinly populated border region in the east
61019.e: The Blue Banana is made up of many cities and urban areas without a single centre. It brings together a large part of Europe's population, industry and purchasing power.
61019.m: The Blue Banana is a belt of many centres.

61020.q: Which three cities did Saskia Sassen study in her 1991 work “The Global City”?
a: New York, Paris and Hong Kong
61020.e: Saskia Sassen showed that New York, London and Tokyo act as control centres of the world economy. Financial markets and business services are concentrated there.
61020.m: Saskia Sassen coined the term global city using New York, London and Tokyo.

61021.q: What makes London, together with New York, one of the most important “global cities”?
a: Its concentration of financial markets and company headquarters
The largest population in the world
The largest container port in the world
61021.e: Global cities are control centres of the world economy. Banks, stock exchanges, insurers and consultancies with worldwide networks are concentrated in London and New York.
61021.m: London and New York are the most connected world cities.

61022.q: What nickname does the City of London, the historic financial district, have?
61022.e: The City of London is only about one square mile in size, but it is home to the Bank of England and many banks and insurers.
61022.m: The City of London is also called the Square Mile.

61023.q: In which former port area did Canary Wharf, London's second big financial centre, develop?
61023.e: After the docks declined, the Docklands were redeveloped from the 1980s. Canary Wharf became a base for international banks.
61023.m: Canary Wharf is in the redeveloped Docklands.

61024.q: Which Mayor of London later became British Prime Minister?
61024.e: Boris Johnson was Mayor of London from 2008 to 2016, including during the 2012 Olympic Games. From 2019 to 2022 he was Prime Minister. London has had a directly elected mayor since 2000.
61024.m: Boris Johnson was first Mayor of London, then Prime Minister.

61025.q: With which measure has London charged a fee for driving into the city centre since 2003?
61025.e: The Congestion Charge is a city-centre road charge intended to reduce traffic and fund public transport.
61025.m: The Congestion Charge is London's city-centre road charge.

61026.q: Which London airport handles the most passengers?
61026.e: Heathrow in west London handles by far the most passengers and is one of the largest hubs in Europe.

61027.q: Roughly how many inhabitants did Greater London have in the 2021 census?
61027.e: The 2021 census counted about 8.8 million inhabitants for Greater London. That is about as many as the whole of Switzerland.
61027.m: Greater London has about as many inhabitants as Switzerland.

61028.q: What is meant by gentrification, a term coined in 1964 using the example of London neighbourhoods?
a: The upgrading of a neighbourhood that pushes out poorer residents
The building of new suburbs in the countryside
The decline of neighbourhoods as people move away
The conversion of flats into offices
61028.e: The sociologist Ruth Glass described how middle-class families moved into working-class areas such as Islington. Rents and prices rose, and the existing residents had to move away.
61028.m: In gentrification, better-off people push out poorer residents.

61029.q: What does the French term “banlieue” mean?
a: The ring of suburbs around a big city
A port district by a river
61029.e: Banlieue means the suburbs around a core city, especially around Paris. In everyday use the term is often linked with socially deprived large housing estates.
61029.m: The banlieue is the ring of suburbs around a French city.

61030.q: What are the large housing estates built mainly between 1950 and 1975 in the Paris suburbs called?
61030.e: The grands ensembles were built to tackle the housing shortage after the Second World War. They are large estates of tower blocks and long slab blocks built with industrial methods.
61030.m: Grands ensembles are the large post-war housing estates.

61031.q: What does the abbreviation HLM stand for in French housing?
61031.e: HLM refers to social housing with capped rents (“housing at moderate rent”). In many banlieues the share of such homes is very high.
61031.m: HLM flats are French social housing.

61032.q: Which department north of Paris is considered the poorest department in mainland France?
61032.e: Seine-Saint-Denis, number 93, has high unemployment and a low average income. The neighbouring Hauts-de-Seine, by contrast, is one of the richest departments.
61032.m: Seine-Saint-Denis is the poorest department in mainland France.

61033.q: What sparked weeks of unrest in the French suburbs in October 2005?
a: The death of two teenagers who had hidden from the police
A sharp rise in petrol prices
The closure of a large car factory
A lost World Cup final of the national football team
61033.e: In Clichy-sous-Bois two teenagers died in an electricity substation where they had hidden from a police check. The unrest spread to many towns, and the government declared a state of emergency.
61033.m: The riots of 2005 revealed the tensions in the banlieues.

61034.q: Which ring motorway physically separates the city of Paris from the neighbouring banlieues?
61034.e: The Boulevard périphérique, completed in 1973, roughly follows the boundary of the city of Paris. It is seen as a physical and symbolic barrier between the core city and the suburbs.
61034.m: The Périphérique separates Paris from its suburbs.

61035.q: What is the large metro project called that is meant to link the Paris suburbs directly with each other through new orbital lines?
61035.e: The Grand Paris Express is planned to create about 200 kilometres of new metro lines. Many lines run tangentially through the banlieue without crossing the city centre.
61035.m: The Grand Paris Express links the suburbs with each other.

61036.q: Which 1995 film by Mathieu Kassovitz is about the lives of young men in a Paris banlieue?
61036.e: “La Haine” shows a day after riots on a large housing estate. The black-and-white film strongly shaped the public image of the banlieue.
61036.m: “La Haine” is the best-known banlieue film.

61037.q: Which street layout shapes the city plan of Moscow?
61037.e: Main roads radiate outwards from the Kremlin and are crossed by several rings such as the Boulevard Ring, the Garden Ring and the MKAD.
61037.m: Moscow is laid out radially and concentrically around the Kremlin.

61038.q: What is the MKAD in Moscow?
a: A ring motorway around the city
61038.e: The Moscow Ring Road is about 109 kilometres long and was long regarded as the city boundary. It fits Moscow's radial-concentric city plan.
61038.m: The MKAD is Moscow's ring motorway.

61039.q: In which year did the first line of the Moscow Metro open?
61039.e: The Moscow Metro began operating in 1935. Its splendid stations were meant to represent the Soviet Union as “palaces for the people”.
61039.m: The Moscow Metro has been running since 1935.

61040.q: What are the seven monumental high-rise buildings built in Moscow under Stalin called?
61040.e: The Seven Sisters were built between 1947 and 1957 in the so-called wedding-cake style. The largest is the main building of Lomonosov University.
61040.m: Stalin's skyscrapers are called the Seven Sisters.

61041.q: What is the high-rise district called that was built as an international business centre on the banks of the Moskva?
61041.e: Moscow City is a district of office and residential tower blocks west of the centre, with some of the tallest buildings in Europe.
61041.m: Moscow City is the high-rise district of the Russian capital.

61042.q: In which year is Moscow first mentioned in a chronicle?
61042.e: The Hypatian Chronicle mentions Moscow in 1147 in connection with Prince Yuri Dolgoruky. This year is regarded as the year it was founded.

61043.q: In which year did Moscow become the capital again after St Petersburg had held this role for a long time?
61043.e: Peter the Great had moved the capital to St Petersburg in 1712. In 1918 the Bolsheviks made Moscow the seat of government again.
61043.m: Moscow has been the capital again since 1918.

61044.q: Why was Moscow enlarged by large areas called “New Moscow” in 2012?
61044.e: In 2012 large areas in the south-west were incorporated, and the city's area grew about two and a half times. New residential areas, workplaces and government buildings are planned there.
61044.m: New Moscow is meant to relieve the overcrowded centre.

61045.q: Which major event is considered the trigger for the tourism boom in Barcelona?
61045.e: For the 1992 Olympic Games, beaches, the harbour and the transport network were rebuilt. Afterwards the number of visitors rose sharply.
61045.m: Tourism in Barcelona has been booming since the 1992 Olympics.

61046.q: What did Barcelona announce in 2024 about licences for holiday flats?
a: They are all to expire by 2028
They are only to go to hotels
They are to be free in future
61046.e: In June 2024 Mayor Jaume Collboni announced that the roughly 10,000 licences for tourist flats would not be renewed by 2028. The flats are to be used by local people again.
61046.m: Barcelona wants to allow no more holiday flats by 2028.

61047.q: Which measure did Barcelona take from 2015 against mass tourism in the city centre?
61047.e: Under Mayor Ada Colau, Barcelona used a special plan to limit the number of tourist accommodations in the centre. New hotels could no longer be built there.
61047.m: From 2015 Barcelona stopped new hotels being built in the centre.

61048.q: What did demonstrators spray tourists with in Barcelona in summer 2024 to protest against mass tourism?
61048.e: In July 2024 thousands marched through the city and squirted guests in restaurants with water pistols. The protest was against rising rents and overcrowded neighbourhoods.
61048.m: The 2024 protests became known for their water pistols.

61049.q: Which park in Barcelona has limited access to its Monumental Zone with tickets and quotas since 2013?
61049.e: Park Güell, designed by Antoni Gaudí, was overcrowded. Since 2013 there has been a charge to enter the Monumental Zone, and numbers per hour are limited.
61049.m: Park Güell limits visitor numbers with tickets.

61050.q: With which charge does Barcelona make tourists contribute to the costs of tourism?
a: A tourist tax per overnight stay
An entry fee at the city boundary
A road toll for hire cars
A surcharge on every train ticket
61050.e: Anyone staying overnight in Barcelona pays a tourist tax per person per night, which has been raised several times. Venice, by contrast, has an entry fee for day visitors.
61050.m: Barcelona charges a tourist tax on overnight stays.

a: Tourism that excessively harms quality of life and the visitor experience
Trips with more than three overnight stays
61051.e: Overtourism is when too many visitors overload the infrastructure, push up rents and drive out local people. The term spread from about 2016.
61051.m: Overtourism means too much tourism for a place.

61052.q: What is the process called in which residents are pushed out because flats are turned into holiday lets?
61052.e: In touristification, a neighbourhood is increasingly geared towards visitors. In Barcelona this particularly affects the old town and Barceloneta.
61052.m: Touristification drives local people out of popular neighbourhoods.

61053.q: Why was Amsterdam's canal ring added to the UNESCO World Heritage list?
a: As an example of a planned 17th-century town extension
As the oldest seaport in the world
61053.e: In 2010 UNESCO recognised the canal ring as an outstanding example of a planned town extension. Canals, streets and houses were laid out to an overall plan during the Golden Age.
61053.m: The canal ring is World Heritage as a planned town extension.

61054.q: How do the three main canals, the Herengracht, Keizersgracht and Prinsengracht, run in Amsterdam?
a: As half-rings around the old town
Dead straight from north to south
Radiating out from the central station
As a cross through the city centre
61054.e: The three main canals were laid out in the 17th century as parallel half-rings around the medieval old town. The Herengracht is on the inside, the Prinsengracht on the outside.
61054.m: The main canals lie like half-rings around Amsterdam's old town.

61055.q: What was the outermost canal around Amsterdam's canal ring originally used for?
a: As the defensive moat of the enlarged city
As a store of drinking water
As a harbour for ocean-going ships
61055.e: The Singelgracht used to be the defensive moat of the enlarged city. Today it forms the outer boundary of the World Heritage area.
61055.m: Amsterdam's outermost canal used to be a defensive moat.

61056.q: What do most of the historic houses on Amsterdam's canals stand on?
61056.e: The ground of peat and clay is soft. That is why long wooden piles were driven down to a layer of sand that could bear the weight.
61056.m: Amsterdam's canal houses stand on wooden piles.

61057.q: What are the beams with hooks on the gables of many canal houses for?
a: For hoisting up goods and furniture
61057.e: The stairs in the narrow houses are steep and tight. So goods and furniture were pulled up through the windows on a rope over the hook.
61057.m: The gable hook is used to hoist loads into the house.

61058.q: On which canal is the Anne Frank House?
61058.e: Anne Frank hid with her family in the Secret Annexe at Prinsengracht 263. Today it is a museum.
61058.m: The Anne Frank House is on the Prinsengracht.

61059.q: Which river does the name Amsterdam come from?
61059.e: Amsterdam grew up at a dam on the Amstel. “Amstelredamme” became today's name.
61059.m: Amsterdam is named after a dam on the Amstel.

61060.q: Which canal was originally the moat of the medieval town and today forms the innermost ring?
61060.e: Until the end of the 16th century the Singel surrounded the town as a defensive moat. After that, the town was extended beyond it.
61060.m: The Singel used to be Amsterdam's town moat.

61061.q: What was the main reason for building the canal ring?
a: A planned extension for the growing trading city
61061.e: Amsterdam grew strongly in the 17th century. The city therefore planned canals for transport and drainage, as well as building land for rich merchants.
61061.m: The canal ring was a planned town extension.

61062.q: What is the former Jewish quarter in Prague's Old Town called?
61062.e: Josefov is named after Emperor Joseph II. Among the buildings that survive are the Old-New Synagogue and the Old Jewish Cemetery.
61062.m: Josefov is the Jewish quarter of Prague.

61063.q: Under which ruler did construction of the Charles Bridge begin in 1357?
61063.e: Emperor Charles IV had the stone bridge built to replace the destroyed Judith Bridge. It has borne his name since 1870.
61063.m: The Charles Bridge is named after Charles IV.

61064.q: Since which year has Prague been the capital of the independent Czech Republic?
61064.e: On 1 January 1993 Czechoslovakia split peacefully into the Czech Republic and Slovakia. Prague remained the Czech capital, and Bratislava became the capital of Slovakia.
61064.m: Prague has been the Czech capital since 1993.

61065.q: What is on the Old Town Hall in Prague and is considered one of the oldest working examples of its kind?
61065.e: The astronomical clock, the Orloj, dates from 1410. Every hour, figures of the apostles move past.
61065.m: The Prague Orloj is an astronomical clock.

61066.q: Which event in Prague in 1618 is considered the trigger of the Thirty Years' War?
61066.e: In 1618 Protestant nobles threw two imperial governors out of a window of Prague Castle. The conflict escalated into the Thirty Years' War.
61066.m: The Defenestration of Prague in 1618 started the Thirty Years' War.

61067.q: In which square did the large rallies of the Velvet Revolution take place in Prague in 1989?
61067.e: Hundreds of thousands gathered in Wenceslas Square in November 1989. The peaceful protests brought communist rule to an end.
61067.m: Wenceslas Square was the centre of the Velvet Revolution.

61068.q: What in Prague is part of the UNESCO World Heritage list?
61068.e: Since 1992 the historic centre with the Old Town, the Lesser Town and Hradčany has been on the World Heritage list. It includes many buildings from the Middle Ages, the Baroque period and Art Nouveau.
61068.m: Prague's whole historic centre is World Heritage.

61069.q: Who has their official seat in Prague Castle today?
61069.e: Prague Castle was the seat of the kings of Bohemia and is today the official seat of the president. It is considered one of the largest castle complexes in the world.
61069.m: The Czech president resides in Prague Castle.

61070.q: In which building does the European Commission have its headquarters in Brussels?
61070.e: The star-shaped Berlaymont building in the European Quarter has been the seat of the Commission for decades. The Justus Lipsius building was long used by the Council of the EU.
61070.m: The EU Commission is based in the Berlaymont.

61071.q: Where is the official seat of the European Parliament, with its regular plenary sessions?
61071.e: According to the EU treaties, the Parliament meets regularly in Strasbourg. Committees and additional sessions, however, take place in Brussels.
61071.m: The European Parliament has its official seat in Strasbourg.

61072.q: Apart from the EU institutions, which international organisation has its headquarters in Brussels?
61072.e: NATO's headquarters is in north-east Brussels. The OSCE is based in Vienna, the Council of Europe in Strasbourg and the OECD in Paris.
61072.m: NATO also has its headquarters in Brussels.

61073.q: Which official languages apply in the Brussels-Capital Region?
61073.e: The Brussels-Capital Region is officially bilingual. In everyday life, French is mostly spoken.
61073.m: Brussels is officially French- and Dutch-speaking.

61074.q: Which Belgian region completely surrounds the Brussels-Capital Region?
61074.e: Brussels lies like an island in Flemish territory, although mostly French is spoken there. The region is made up of 19 municipalities.
61074.m: The Brussels-Capital Region lies in the middle of Flanders.

61075.q: For which event was the Atomium in Brussels built?
a: For the founding of the EEC in 1957
61075.e: The Atomium shows a hugely enlarged unit cell of an iron crystal and was the landmark of Expo 58.
61075.m: The Atomium was built for Expo 58.

61076.q: Which founding father of European unity is the central roundabout in Brussels' European Quarter named after?
61076.e: The Rond-point Schuman, with the metro station of the same name, lies between the Commission and the Council. In 1950 Robert Schuman proposed the European Coal and Steel Community.
61076.m: The Schuman roundabout is the heart of the European Quarter.

61077.q: In which public register should interest representatives who want to influence the EU institutions in Brussels sign up?
61077.e: Brussels is considered one of the biggest lobbying centres in the world. Interest representatives are recorded in the joint Transparency Register of the Parliament, the Council and the Commission.
61077.m: Lobbyists in Brussels sign up to the Transparency Register.

61078.q: What is being built in Hamburg's HafenCity on former port land?
a: A new urban district with homes, offices and culture
61078.e: HafenCity is being built on about 157 hectares of former port land. It is one of the largest inner-city development projects in Europe.
61078.m: HafenCity is a new urban district on old port land.

61079.q: Which architecture firm designed the Elbphilharmonie in HafenCity?
61079.e: The Basel firm Herzog & de Meuron placed a glass concert hall on top of an old warehouse. The concert hall opened in January 2017.
61079.m: The Elbphilharmonie was designed by architects from Basel.

61080.q: On which existing structure was the Elbphilharmonie built?
61080.e: The brick building of Kaispeicher A from the 1960s forms the base. Above it, at about 37 metres, there is a public plaza.
61080.m: The Elbphilharmonie sits on Kaispeicher A.

61081.q: How is HafenCity protected from storm floods?
a: The buildings stand on raised mounds of earth.
A high ring dyke surrounds the district.
A barrier closes off the harbour basin.
All buildings stand on floating pontoons.
61081.e: Instead of dykes, the ground is built up to about 7.5 metres above sea level. The waterside promenades, on the other hand, are allowed to flood.
61081.m: HafenCity protects itself with raised mounds instead of dykes.

61082.q: What do town planners call HafenCity's principle of combining living, working and leisure in the same district?
61082.e: In HafenCity, homes, offices, shops, schools and culture are close together. This mixed use is meant to create short journeys and keep the district lively all day.
61082.m: Mixed use brings living, working and leisure together.

61083.q: In the end, how much did the Elbphilharmonie cost taxpayers, when 77 million euros had originally been planned?
61083.e: According to the Hamburg Senate, the cost to the city rose to about 789 million euros, about ten times as much. The Elbphilharmonie is therefore seen as an example of costs spiralling out of control on major projects.
61083.m: The Elbphilharmonie cost about ten times more than planned.

61084.q: Which warehouse district next to HafenCity has been a UNESCO World Heritage Site together with the Kontorhaus district since 2015?
61084.e: The Speicherstadt was built from 1883 for the free port and is the largest historic warehouse complex in the world. Together with the Chilehaus in the Kontorhaus district, it is World Heritage.
61084.m: The Speicherstadt has been World Heritage since 2015.

61085.q: What is the planned 245-metre skyscraper at the Elbe bridges called, whose construction stopped in 2023 because of the investor's financial problems?
61085.e: The Elbtower was meant to become Hamburg's tallest building. When the Signa group ran out of money at the end of 2023 and filed for insolvency, the building site came to a standstill.
61085.m: Construction of the Elbtower stalled in 2023.

61086.q: What is the 1947 urban development plan called, under which Copenhagen is to expand along railway lines?
61086.e: The Finger Plan provides for corridors of settlement along suburban railway lines, like the fingers of a hand. Green wedges are left free in between.
61086.m: Copenhagen grows along its railway lines according to the Finger Plan.

61087.q: Which shopping street in Copenhagen became one of Europe's first long pedestrian zones in 1962?
61087.e: Strøget was closed to cars in 1962. Its success encouraged the city to redesign more streets and squares for pedestrians and cyclists.
61087.m: Strøget is Copenhagen's famous pedestrian zone.

61088.q: Which Danish architect and urban planner became known for the concept of “Cities for People”?
61088.e: Jan Gehl studied how people use public spaces and shaped Copenhagen's pedestrian- and cycle-friendly planning.
61088.m: Jan Gehl planned cities for people instead of cars.

61089.q: What are cycle bridges such as Cykelslangen in Copenhagen's harbour for?
a: They take bikes quickly across the water without steps
They give pedestrians a viewing platform
They keep ships away from the city centre
They generate electricity from solar panels
61089.e: Cykelslangen means “bicycle snake”. The raised bridge from 2014, for bikes only, links harbour neighbourhoods without steps or junctions.
61089.m: Dedicated cycle bridges make cycling in Copenhagen fast.

61090.q: What are the cycle superhighways that Copenhagen is building for commuters?
a: Wide, direct cycle routes to neighbouring municipalities
61090.e: The Supercykelstier are wide, lit and signposted cycle routes. They are meant to make longer commutes by bike attractive too. The network is to cover several hundred kilometres.
61090.m: Cycle superhighways link Copenhagen with the surrounding area.

61091.q: Roughly what speed are the traffic lights of the “green wave” for cyclists in Copenhagen set for?
61091.e: Anyone riding at about 20 km/h on main routes reaches the next traffic light when it is green. This keeps bike traffic flowing without stops.
61091.m: The green wave is matched to the speed of bikes.

61092.q: Which statement about cycling in Copenhagen is true?
